On the trivial bundle $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ take the graph section of the identity, with solution set $\{0\}$ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.solutionSet_graphSection_id⟧ and tame germ data ⟦Chapter3/NonVacuityG · TrivialBundle.isScFredholmSectionTame_graphSection⟧, and $t(x) = 1/2 + \arctan(x)/\pi$ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.arctanTime⟧, a $C^\infty$ function with values in $(0, 1)$ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.contDiff_arctanTime⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.arctanTime_mem_Ioo⟧. Both ends are empty ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.arctanTime_preimage_eq_empty⟧, and $t'(x) = 1/(\pi(1 + x^2)) \ne 0$ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.hasFDerivAt_arctanTime⟧, so $dt(x)$ is onto in the identity chart ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.hasSurjDerivAt_arctanTime⟧. So the 2021 definition is satisfiable ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.isSubmersiveGenCompactHomotopy_witness⟧; the same data are not a generalized compact homotopy in the earlier sense, as $0$ is not a value of $t$ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.not_isGenCompactHomotopy_witness⟧.

**Lemma 5.3.16 (preprint 5.23) under (3)** ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · lemma_5_3_16⟧. *Statement.* If $dt(x)$ is onto, then in a chart the derivative $\ell$ on $T_zO$ is non-zero, $\ker\ell$ has a one-dimensional complement $Z$, and the conclusions of Lemma 5.3.16 hold. *Proof.* Take $v$ with $\ell(DR(z)v) = 1$; so $\ell \ne 0$. A vector on which $\ell$ is non-zero spans a complement of $\ker\ell$ ⟦Chapter5/Homotopy · exists_isCompl_ker_of_ne_zero⟧, and §V.23 applies ⟦Chapter5/Homotopy · lemma_5_3_16_preprint⟧. $\square$ This is the hypothesis $dt(x) \ne 0$ that §V.23 found missing from Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): the 2021 condition (3) supplies it. That $Z$ can be chosen smooth is not formalized; Theorem 5.3.15 itself is proved without it (§§V.36–V.41; gap G.48).

**Theorem 5.5.5 (preprint 5.32).** The 2017 and 2021 statements print the exponent $p$ that the preprint omits in (1) and (2); the theorem is proved as printed there, with the exponent (§V.43; gap G.50).

### V.33 Remark 5.3.8 (preprint 5.16): Theorem 5.3.10 relative to a compact part, and the cobordism

Remark 5.3.8 joins two transversal sections $f_0$, $f_1$ by an sc-Fredholm arc $(t, x) \mapsto f_t(x)$ with compact solution set and says that a small perturbation vanishing near $t = 0, 1$ makes the arc transversal, its solution set a compact cobordism; "the reader will be able to carry out this construction". Two things are needed: Theorem 5.3.10 (preprint 5.18) for a section that is already in general position off a compact part of its zeros, and the arc itself. The arc lives on $[0, 1] \times X$ in the text; it is read on $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ with the time window $[0, 1]$ (reading D2 of Part VI), so that no tame structure on $[0, 1] \times X$ is needed (Findings, Chapter 5, item 186; gap G.44).

**A chart criterion** ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isGeneralPositionGerm_of_sup_eq⟧. If in a tame chart centred at a zero $y$ the linearization $\mathrm{Lin}_f(0)$ is onto and $\ker\mathrm{Lin}_f(0) + T^R_0O = T_0O$ on level $0$, then $(f, y)$ is in general position. This is the second half of the argument of §V.19, now for any section: the kernel has an algebraic complement inside $T^R_0O$ ⟦Chapter5/GeneralPosition · exists_compl_le_of_sup_eq⟧, §V.16 gives good position, the kernel is then the tangent space of the solution set, finite-dimensional and smooth (§V.17), and it has an sc-complement inside $T^R_0O$ ⟦Chapter4/LocalStructure · exists_scComplement_le⟧. Conversely general position gives $\ker\mathrm{Lin}_f(0) + T^R_0O = T_0O$ in every tame chart centred at $y$ ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isParamGP_elim0_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧. Two consequences: if $(g, y)$ is in general position, the family $F(\lambda, x) = g(x) + \sum\lambda_it_i(x)$ is in general position at $(0, y)$ whatever sections are added ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isGeneralPositionGerm_paramSection_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧, and the lift $\tilde g(r, x) = g(x)$ to $\mathbb R^m \times X$ is in general position at every $(r_0, y)$, since in the product chart $\mathrm{Lin}_{\tilde g}(0)(a, u) = \mathrm{Lin}_g(0)u$ ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isGeneralPositionGerm_paramLift⟧. General position, like good position, depends only on the germ of the section ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isGeneralPositionGerm_congr_nhds⟧.

**The perturbation step relative to an open set** ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · exists_null_isGeneralPositionGerm_paramSlice⟧. Let $G$ have tame germ data, $N$ be an auxiliary norm, $W$ open with $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in W \mid N(G(x)) \le 1\}$ compact, and $t_1, \dots, t_m$ sc⁺-sections with $N(t_i) \le 1$ such that $F$ is in general position at $(0, y)$ for every zero $y$ of $G$. Then there are $\delta > 0$ and a null set $CV$ such that for $|\lambda| < \delta$, $\lambda \notin CV$, $N(\sum\lambda_it_i) \le 1$ and $G + \sum\lambda_it_i$ is in general position at every zero in $W$. This is the mechanism of §V.20 with $s_0 = 0$ and only the zeros in $W$ controlled: openness of general position near the zero slice, compactness of the zeros over a small parameter ball inside the margin, Theorem 4.3.1 (preprint 4.23) and the Sard step.

**Theorem 5.3.10 relative to a compact part** ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · theorem_5_3_10_relative_hyp⟧. Let $X$ be tame with sc-smooth bump functions, $G$ with tame germ data, $N$ auxiliary, $K \subseteq W$ with $K$ compact and $W$ open, such that $(G, x)$ is in general position at every zero $x \notin K$ and $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in W \mid N(G(x)) \le 1\}$ is compact. Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an sc⁺-section $p$ supported in $W$ with $N(p) \le \varepsilon$ and $(G + p, x)$ in general position at every zero. *Proof.* Sections supported in $W$ make $F$ general at $(0, y)$ for the zeros $y$ near the compact $K \cap S_G$, by (i)–(ii) of §V.19 at finitely many centres ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · exists_sections_isGeneralPositionGerm_near⟧; at the other zeros $F$ is general because $G$ is (the chart criterion). The relative step, for the norm $N/\eta$ with $\eta = \min(\varepsilon, 1)$, gives $p = \sum\lambda_it_i$ with the zeros in $W$ in general position. A zero outside $W$ has a neighbourhood on which $p$ vanishes, since $\operatorname{supp}p \subseteq W$ is closed, so $G + p = G$ there; such a zero is a zero of $G$ not in $K$, in general position, and germ locality concludes. $\square$ The text's theorem is the case $K = S_G$, $W = U$; here $S_G$ need not be compact.

**The margin** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark538 · exists_margin_of_isCompact⟧. For a compact set $K$ of zeros of an sc-Fredholm section $f$ and an open $V \supseteq K$, some open $W$ with $K \subseteq W \subseteq V$ has $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in W \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact: the local step of Theorem 5.2.2 (§V.6) at the points of $K$, finitely many of them.

**Remark 5.3.8 relative to a time function** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark538 · remark_5_3_8_relative⟧. Let $X$ be tame with sc-smooth bump functions, $F$ with tame germ data, $N$ auxiliary, $\tau : X \to \mathbb R$ continuous, $c < a$, $b < d$. Suppose $(F, x)$ is in general position at every zero with $\tau(x) \notin (a, b)$, and the zeros with $\tau \in [c, d]$ form a compact set. Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are $c < c' < a$, $b < d' < d$ and an sc⁺-section $p$ with $N(p) \le \varepsilon$, vanishing where $\tau \notin (c', d')$, such that $F + p$ is in general position at every zero and its zeros with $\tau \in [c, d]$ are compact. *Proof.* The zeros over $[a, b]$ are compact; the margin gives $W$ around them inside $\tau^{-1}(c', d')$, and Theorem 5.3.10 relative to that compact set gives $p$ supported in $W$. $\square$

**The arc** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark538 · remark_5_3_8_arc⟧. For $F(t, x) = f_t(x)$ a section of the pull-back of $P$ to $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ with tame germ data, in general position at its zeros with $t \notin (a, b)$, $0 < a$, $b < 1$, and with compact zeros over $[0, 1]$, the instance $\tau = t$, $[c, d] = [0, 1]$ gives an sc⁺-section $s$ with $N(s) \le \varepsilon$, $s(t, \cdot) = 0$ for $t \notin (c', d')$, and $F + s$ in general position at every zero with compact zeros over $[0, 1]$. "$f_0$, $f_1$ transversal" is read as general position of $F$ at the zeros near $t = 0, 1$; for $X$ without boundary and $F$ stationary near the ends it is the transversality of $f_0$, $f_1$. Its orientation, Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42), is formalized in Part VI (gap G.66).

**The cobordism between admissible sections** ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · exists_cobordism⟧, the form Theorem 6.7.1 uses (Part VI). Let $U \supseteq S_f$ be open with $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 2\}$ compact ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · exists_adapted_margin⟧, and $s_0, s_1$ allowable with $f + s_i$ in general position at every zero. There is an sc⁺-section $S$ of the pull-back to $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ with $S(t, \cdot) = s_0$ for $t \le 1/8$, $S(t, \cdot) = s_1$ for $t \ge 7/8$, $S = 0$ over $X \setminus U$, $N(S) \le 2$, $\tilde f + S$ in general position at every zero, and compact zeros over every $[a, b]$. *Proof.* $S = \hat s + p$, where $\hat s = (1 - \chi)\tilde s_0 + \chi\tilde s_1$ with the $C^\infty$ cut-off $\chi$, $0$ for $t \le 3/16$ and $1$ for $t \ge 13/16$ ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · cylCut⟧, an sc⁺-section ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isScPlusSection_cylInterp⟧; near the ends $\tilde f + \hat s$ is the lift of $f + s_i$, general by the lift lemma; $p$ comes from the relative theorem for $G = \tilde f + \hat s$, the pulled-back auxiliary norm ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · StrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.pullback⟧, $W = (1/8, 7/8) \times U$ and $K$ the zeros over $[3/16, 13/16]$. $\square$ The homotopy version is ⟦Chapter6/ProperHomotopy2021 · exists_homotopy_cobordism⟧.

### V.34 Theorem 5.3.12 (preprint 5.19): the dense form

Theorems 5.3.5 and 5.3.10 have dense forms (§§V.15, V.20); Theorem 5.3.12 is printed with "arbitrarily small", and §V.22 proves that form. The dense form is proved too (gap G.45).

**The generic form around a given section** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_DenseGoodPosition · theorem_5_3_12_param_rel⟧. Let $f$ have tame germ data, $N$ be auxiliary, $U \supseteq S_f$ open with $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact, $(f, x)$ in good position at the zeros $x \in \partial X$, and $s_0$ an sc⁺-section supported in $U$, with $N(s_0) \le 1 - \varepsilon$ and support disjoint from $\partial X$. Then there are allowable $t_1, \dots, t_m$ supported in $U \setminus \partial X$, $\delta > 0$ and a null $CV$ such that for $|\lambda| < \delta$, $\lambda \notin CV$, the section $s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i$ is allowable, its support misses $\partial X$, and $f + s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i$ is transversal and in good position at every zero. *Proof.* The proof of §V.22 with $g = f + s_0$ in place of $f$. Off the support of $s_0$, $g = f$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_DenseGoodPosition · sectionAdd_eq_of_not_mem_support⟧, so near $\partial X$ the zeros of $g$ are those of $f$, in good position, and germ locality ⟦Chapter3/Chapter5BridgeG · StrongBundle.IsGoodPositionGermTame.congr_nhds⟧ carries this to $g$; $g$ has tame germ data (§V.15, step 2), and its zeros lie in the compact margin (Remark 5.3.4 (preprint 5.12), §V.10). Steps 1–5 of §V.22 then apply to $g$; on the slices the value of a sum at a zero is read off ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_DenseGoodPosition · paramSlice_apply_of_isZeroAt⟧. $\square$ For a section, "vanishing near $\partial X$" and "support disjoint from $\partial X$" are the same ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_DenseGoodPosition · eventually_isZeroAt_nhdsSet_iff⟧.

**The dense form** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_DenseGoodPosition · theorem_5_3_12_dense⟧. Let $X$ admit bump functions, $f$ have tame germ data and compact solution set, $N$ be auxiliary, and $(f, x)$ be in good position at the zeros on $\partial X$. There is an open $U \supseteq S_f$ with $S_{f+s}$ compact for every $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$, and for every $s' \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ vanishing near $\partial X$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ an $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ vanishing near $\partial X$ with $N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le \varepsilon$ for all $x$, $f + s$ transversal and in good position at every zero, and $S_{f+s}$ compact and, if non-empty, a tame sub-M-polyfold with the structure of a manifold with boundary with corners. *Proof.* $U$ from Theorem 5.2.2 (preprint 5.5), compactness by Remark 5.3.4 (§V.10). With $\varepsilon' = \min(\varepsilon, 1)$ and $s_0 = (1 - \varepsilon'/2)s'$, $N(s_0) \le 1 - \varepsilon'/2$ and $\operatorname{supp}s_0 \subseteq \operatorname{supp}s'$ misses $\partial X$; the generic form gives $t$, $\delta$, $CV$; the ball of radius $\min(\delta, \varepsilon'/(2m + 2))$ is not null, so it contains a $\lambda \notin CV$, and $s = s_0 + \sum\lambda_it_i$ has $N(s - s') \le \varepsilon'/2 + m|\lambda| \le \varepsilon'$, exactly as in §V.15. $\square$

### V.35 Remark 5.3.14 (preprint 5.21): isomorphic end problems

Definition 5.3.13 asks $(f|X_i, P|Y_i) = (f_i, P_i)$; Remark 5.3.14 proposes to read the equalities up to isomorphism and to make the isomorphisms part of the data. Formalized as follows (gap G.47; Findings, Chapter 5, item 100).

**Isomorphic problems** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsProblemIso⟧. $(P, f)$ and $(P', f')$ are isomorphic if there is a strong bundle isomorphism $(h, \Phi)$, with inverse $(g, \Psi)$, carrying $f$ to $f'$: $\Phi \circ f = f' \circ h$. Strong bundle isomorphisms are those of the formalization of Chapter 8 ⟦Chapter8/StrongBundleMap · StrongBundle.IsStrongBundleIso⟧ (the file imports them, a forward import that builds). The relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsProblemIso.refl⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsProblemIso.symm⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsProblemIso.trans⟧. A strong bundle map sends the zero of the fibre over $x$ to the zero over $h(x)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsStrongBundleMap.map_fiberZero⟧, so the base map of the inverse carries $S_{f'}$ onto $S_f$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsProblemIso.image_solutionSet⟧, and compactness of the solution sets is invariant ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsProblemIso.isCompact_solutionSet_iff⟧.

**Ends up to isomorphism.** For a sub-M-polyfold $A \subseteq X$, the restricted problem — $f|A$ in the pull-back bundle, as in §V.23 — is isomorphic to a given problem ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.EndIso⟧; end isomorphisms compose with isomorphisms of the given problem ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.EndIso.trans⟧ and give compact end solution sets ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.EndIso.isCompact_solutionSet⟧. A *generalized compact homotopy between $(P_0, f_0)$ and $(P_1, f_1)$* is a generalized compact homotopy in the 2021 sense (§V.32) with end isomorphisms at $t^{-1}(0)$ to $(P_0, f_0)$ and at $t^{-1}(1)$ to $(P_1, f_1)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsGenCompactHomotopyBetween⟧. It is invariant under isomorphism of the end problems ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsGenCompactHomotopyBetween.congr_left⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsGenCompactHomotopyBetween.congr_right⟧, its end solution sets are compact ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsGenCompactHomotopyBetween.isCompact_solutionSet_left⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsGenCompactHomotopyBetween.isCompact_solutionSet_right⟧, and every generalized compact homotopy is one between its own restrictions, with identity isomorphisms ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Remark5314 · StrongBundle.IsSubmersiveGenCompactHomotopy.isGenCompactHomotopyBetween⟧ — so the notion is satisfiable whenever Definition 5.3.13 is (§V.32).

### V.36 Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): the statement, and "Morse-type"

Theorem 5.3.15 says: let $P$ be a strong bundle over a tame M-polyfold with sc-smooth bump functions, $(f, t)$ a generalized compact homotopy (Definition 5.3.13) whose ends $X_i = t^{-1}(i)$ have no boundary and carry problems in general position, with $\partial X = X_0 \sqcup X_1$, and $N$ an auxiliary norm. Then there is an open $U \supseteq S_f$ with $S_{f+s}$ compact for $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ an $s_0 \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ with $N(s_0) \le \varepsilon$, vanishing near $\partial X$, such that (1) $(f + s_0, x)$ is in general position at every zero and (2) $t : S_{f+s_0} \to [0, 1]$ has only Morse-type critical points. The proof (pp. 223–228) finds that $d(t|S)$ has no zeros near $\partial S$, builds at each critical point $x$ of $t|S$ sections with Lemmas 5.3.16 and 5.3.17 that make $(\lambda, y) \mapsto d(t \circ \Phi_\lambda)(y)$ transversal to the zero section near $(0, x)$, through a trivialization $\Phi_\lambda : S \to S_\lambda$ and the second derivative of the equation, unites the sections of finitely many critical points, and concludes with "a parameterized version of Sard's theorem". The formal proof keeps this outline and changes one device: Lagrange multipliers on level sets of the solution manifold of $f + \sum\mu_j\sigma_j$ replace $\Phi_\lambda$ (§§V.38–V.40). §§V.36–V.41 retell it (gap G.48; Findings, Chapter 5, items 101, 178, 183).

**The ends** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · StrongBundle.IsGeneralPositionAtEnds⟧. For $i = 0, 1$ and every proof that $t^{-1}(i)$ is a sub-M-polyfold: the induced M-polyfold has no boundary, and the restriction of $f$ to the pull-back bundle (§V.23) is in general position at each of its zeros. The text's $(f_i, P_i)$ are these restrictions (Definition 5.3.13 (2) as read in §V.32), or problems isomorphic to them (§V.35).

**Smooth parametrizations** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam⟧. "Morse-type critical points" is not defined in the text, and $S_{f+s_0}$ is a manifold with boundary with corners. It is read through parametrizations. A *smooth parametrization* of $A \cap G$, $G \subseteq X$ open, by a set $\Omega$ of a normed space $E$ consists of $p$, continuous on $\Omega$ with $p(\Omega) = A \cap G$, and $q : X \to E$ with sc-smooth components and $q \circ p = \mathrm{id}$ on $\Omega$, such that $h \circ p$ is $C^\infty$ on $\Omega$ for every sc-smooth $h : X \to \mathbb R$. A point $x$ of $A$ is a *regular point or a Morse-type critical point of $t|A$* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · MPolyfold.IsMorseOrRegularPoint⟧ if some parametrization by a set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ with unique derivatives, $x = p(u_0)$, has the property: if $d(t \circ p)(u_0) = 0$, then $\Omega$ is a neighbourhood of $u_0$ and the Hessian of $t \circ p$ at $u_0$ is injective. So critical points are interior and non-degenerate, and boundary points must be regular. $t$ *has only Morse-type critical points on $A$* if every point of $A$ is such a point ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · MPolyfold.HasOnlyMorseCriticalPoints⟧. Any finite-dimensional parameter space and open $\Omega$ will do ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · MPolyfold.isMorseOrRegularPoint_of_param⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.comp_equiv⟧. In a chart the notion is the classical one ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · HasOnlyMorseCriticalPointsOn⟧.

**Independence of the parametrization.** For two parametrizations $p$, $p'$ through one point, the transition $\theta = q' \circ p$ is $C^\infty$ on $\Omega$, $\theta(u) = u'$ and $p' \circ \theta = p$ near $u$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvariance · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.transition⟧; the chain rule within the parameter sets ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvarianceClause · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.hasFDerivWithinAt_transition⟧ gives $D(q \circ p')(u') \circ D(q' \circ p)(u) = 1$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvarianceClause · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.fderivWithin_transition_comp⟧. Hence $d(t \circ p')(u') \ne 0$ implies $d(t \circ p)(u) \ne 0$, at boundary points too ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvarianceClause · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.fderivWithin_ne_zero_congr⟧; $\Omega'$ a neighbourhood of $u'$ makes $\Omega$ one of $u$, by the inverse function theorem for the transition ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvarianceClause · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.mem_nhds_congr⟧; and at an interior critical point the second-order chain rule ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · fderiv_fderiv_comp_apply⟧, whose first-order term vanishes there, conjugates the two Hessians by the invertible $D\theta(u)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvariance · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.hessian_injective_congr⟧. So the whole clause transfers ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvarianceClause · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.morseClause_congr⟧: if $x$ is a regular or Morse-type critical point of $t|A$, then in *every* smooth parametrization of $A$ around $x$ by a set with unique derivatives a critical point is interior with injective Hessian ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalInvarianceClause · MPolyfold.IsMorseOrRegularPoint.morseClause⟧. The comparison with the charts of the Mathlib manifold structure that the project builds on solution sets is not formalized.

**Theorem 5.3.15** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Final · theorem_5_3_15⟧. *Statement.* $X$ with sc-smooth bump functions, $(f, t)$ a generalized compact homotopy in the 2021 sense ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · StrongBundle.IsSubmersiveGenCompactHomotopy⟧ — so $X$ tame, $f$ with tame germ data and compact solution set, $t$ sc-smooth with values in $[0, 1]$ and $dt(x)$ onto at every smooth $x$ — with the end hypotheses above, $\partial X = t^{-1}(0) \cup t^{-1}(1)$, and $N$ auxiliary. Then: an open $U \supseteq S_f$ with $S_{f+s}$ compact for $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ an $s_0 \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ with $N(s_0(x)) \le \varepsilon$ for all $x$, $s_0 = 0$ near $\partial X$, (1) $(f + s_0, x)$ in general position at every $x \in S_{f+s_0}$ and (2) $t$ with only Morse-type critical points on $S_{f+s_0}$. No hypothesis is added; the bump functions on the $X_i$ are not assumed. The hypotheses are satisfiable: the witness of §V.32 has empty ends and $\partial\mathbb R = \emptyset = X_0 \cup X_1$ ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · GenCompactHomotopyWitness.isSubmersiveGenCompactHomotopy_witness⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · theorem_5_3_15_generalPosition_witness⟧. *Proof.* $s_0 = s_1 + s_2$: $s_1$ gives (1) (§V.37); $s_2$ comes from the covering argument for $f + s_1$ (§§V.38–V.40) ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · theorem_5_3_15_hyp⟧, whose local data are derived from the implicit function theorem and Definition 5.3.13 (3) (§V.41) ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.hasMorseLocalData⟧. $\square$ The hidden hypothesis $dt(x) \ne 0$ of the preprint (§V.23) is the 2021 condition (3) (§V.32); of $\partial X = X_0 \sqcup X_1$ the proof uses $\partial X \subseteq X_0 \cup X_1$ for (1) and $t(\partial X) \subseteq \{0, 1\}$ for (2).

### V.37 Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): compactness and general position, from the ends

"In view of the assumption that $(f_i, X_i)$ are already in general position" the text perturbs away from $\partial X$. What this needs is general position of $(f, x)$ at the zeros $x \in \partial X$.

**From the restriction to $X$** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · isGeneralPositionGerm_of_restrict⟧. Let $f$ have tame germ data, $A \subseteq X$ be a sub-M-polyfold without boundary with $f|A$ sc-smooth in the pull-back bundle, and $a \in A$ a zero with $(f|A)'(a)$ onto. Then $(f, a)$ is in general position in $X$. *Proof.* Take the tame chart $c$ of the germ data, centred at $a$. The sub-chart of $A$ built from $c$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · subChartOf⟧ and the chart of the pull-back bundle over it ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · subPullbackData⟧ make $\varphi \circ \iota \circ \psi^{-1}$ the inclusion $\varphi(W \cap A) \subseteq O$, and the principal part of $f|A$ is $\hat f$ on $\varphi(W \cap A)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · principal_restrictSection_subPullback⟧. Surjectivity of $(f|A)'(a)$ is chart independent, and the derivative of a retraction is the identity on the tangent space of a smaller retract ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · scDeriv_apply_eq_self_of_retract_subset⟧, so every $k$ in the fibre is $D(\hat f \circ r)(z)v$ for some $v$ tangent to $\varphi(W \cap A)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · exists_scDeriv_eq_of_isLinSurjAt_restrict⟧. Since $A$ has no boundary, these tangent vectors lie in $E_z$: the reduced tangent space is chart independent ⟦Chapter2/ReducedTangentIntrinsic · MPolyfold.reducedTangentFiber_eq⟧, and in a chart of $A$ at a point of index $0$ the point is interior, so $T^R_aA = T_aA$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · mem_minimalSubspaceWith_of_isWithoutBoundary⟧. So $\mathrm{Lin}_f(0)$ is onto already on a subspace of $T^R_0O$, $\ker\mathrm{Lin}_f(0) + T^R_0O = T_0O$, and the chart criterion (§V.33) concludes. $\square$ Of the end hypotheses only the surjectivity of $f_i'(x)$ and $d_{X_i} \equiv 0$ are used; the kernel complement in $X_i$ and the degeneracy index of $x$ in $X$ are not.

**At the boundary** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · StrongBundle.IsSubmersiveGenCompactHomotopy.isGeneralPositionGerm_of_mem_boundary⟧. If $\partial X \subseteq t^{-1}(0) \cup t^{-1}(1)$, a zero $x \in \partial X$ lies in an end, a sub-M-polyfold without boundary on which the restriction is in general position, hence onto; the previous lemma gives $(f, x)$ in general position.

**Compactness and conclusion (1)** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Ends · theorem_5_3_15_generalPosition⟧, the hypotheses of §V.36. *Proof* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_GeneralPosition · theorem_5_3_15_generalPosition_hyp⟧. $U$ from Theorem 5.2.2 (preprint 5.5); compactness of $S_{f+s}$ for $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ by Remark 5.3.4 (§V.10). General position at the zeros on $\partial X$ holds at the zeros of an open $W_b \supseteq S_f \cap \partial X$ (openness, §V.18) ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_GeneralPosition · exists_isOpen_isGeneralPositionGerm_of_forall⟧; Theorem 5.3.10 relative to the compact part $K = S_f \setminus W_b$ (§V.33), with the perturbation supported in $U \setminus \partial X$, gives $s_0$ small, vanishing near $\partial X$, with $(f + s_0, x)$ in general position at every zero. $\square$

### V.38 Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): the parametrized Sard step, and Lagrange multipliers

The text's last step is "a parameterized version of Sard's theorem" (p. 228). Here it is proved in a chart from the inverse function theorem and Sard's lemma in equal dimensions, which Mathlib has.

**Parametric transversality in equal dimensions.** A surjective $L : \Lambda \times E \to F$ with $\dim E = \dim F$ is completed by a linear $T : \Lambda \times E \to \Lambda$, a projection onto $\ker L \cong \Lambda$, to an isomorphism $(L, T)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · exists_clm_prod_equiv⟧. *The local step* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · exists_isOpen_measure_image_fst_eq_zero⟧: near a point where $G'(p_0)$ is onto, $(G, T)$ is a local diffeomorphism by the inverse function theorem; in its coordinates the zeros of $G$ form a graph over $\Lambda$, a parameter $\lambda$ of a zero at which $\partial_zG$ is not injective is a critical value of a map between spaces of the same dimension $\dim\Lambda$, and Sard's lemma in equal dimensions makes these parameters null. *The theorem* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · ae_forall_injective_of_surjective⟧: if $G : \Lambda \times E \to F$ is $C^1$ on an open $W$, $\dim E = \dim F$, and $G'(p)$ is onto at every zero $p \in W$, then for almost every $\lambda$, at every zero $(\lambda, z) \in W$, $\partial_zG(\lambda, z)$ is injective. Countably many local steps cover $W$.

**Morse functions for almost every parameter** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · ae_hasOnlyMorseCriticalPointsOn⟧. If $g : \Lambda \times E \to \mathbb R$ is $C^2$ on the open $W$ and $(\lambda, z) \mapsto \partial_zg(\lambda, z) \in E^*$ — the text's $(\lambda, y) \mapsto d(t \circ \Phi_\lambda)(y)$ in a chart — has a surjective derivative at its zeros, then for almost every $\lambda$, $g(\lambda, \cdot)$ has only Morse-type critical points on its slice: apply the previous theorem to $G = \partial_zg$, with $\dim E^* = \dim E$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · finrank_clm_real⟧ and $\partial_zG$ the Hessian ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · fderiv_slice_eq⟧. The hypothesis is satisfiable: for a $C^2$ function $h$ and almost every linear form $\ell$, $h + \ell$ has only Morse-type critical points, since $D(\partial_zg)(\ell, z)(\delta\ell, 0) = \delta\ell$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_ParametricMorse · ae_hasOnlyMorseCriticalPointsOn_add_linear⟧.

**Lagrange multipliers.** For a constraint $h : V \to F_c$, $F_c$ finite-dimensional, and $T : V \to \mathbb R$, the Lagrangian is $L(v, c) = T(v) - c(h(v))$, $c \in F_c^*$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · lagrangian⟧. $(v, c)$ is critical iff $h(v) = 0$ and $dT(v) = c \circ dh(v)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · fderiv_lagrangian_eq_zero_iff⟧; when $dh(v)$ is onto, a functional vanishing on $\ker dh(v)$ factors through $dh(v)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · exists_clm_comp_eq_of_ker_le⟧, so a critical point of $T$ on $\{h = 0\}$ has a multiplier. Near a regular point the level set is the image of a $C^\infty$ map $\gamma$ on an open set of $\ker dh(v)$, with an affine left inverse and $\operatorname{im}d\gamma(u) = \ker dh(\gamma(u))$ at every point ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · exists_levelSet_param⟧ (the classical implicit function theorem). The multiplier is *non-degenerate* if the Hessian of $L$ at $(v, c)$ is injective ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · IsLagrangeNondegenerate⟧. *The bordered Hessian* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseLagrange · injective_hessian_comp_of_lagrange⟧: if $\gamma$ parametrizes $\{h = 0\}$ near $\gamma(u)$, $c$ is a multiplier there and the Lagrangian is non-degenerate, the Hessian of $T \circ \gamma$ at $u$ is injective. By the second-order chain rule and $dh \circ D^2\gamma = -D^2h(d\gamma, d\gamma)$ (from $h \circ \gamma = 0$), the Hessian of $T \circ \gamma$ is the $v$-Hessian of $L$ on $\ker dh$; a vector $a$ in its kernel gives the kernel vector $(d\gamma(u)a, \delta c)$ of the Hessian of $L$, with $\delta c$ from the factorization through $dh$, so $d\gamma(u)a = 0$ and $a = 0$.

**The family of level sets.** For $\mu$, $B_1, \dots, B_d : V \to F_c$, the constraints $h_\lambda = \mu - \sum\lambda_iB_i$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · famConstraint⟧ and the gradient of the Lagrangian of the family, $(\lambda, v, c) \mapsto D_{(v, c)}(T - c(h_\lambda))$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · famGradient⟧. *The transversality (5.13)–(5.14) in Lagrange form* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · surjective_fderiv_famGradient⟧: if $d\mu(v_0)$ is onto and the forms $\sum\delta_i\,c(dB_i(v_0)\,\cdot)$, over the $\delta$ with $\sum\delta_iB_i(v_0) = 0$, restrict onto the dual of $\ker d\mu(v_0)$, then the derivative of the gradient at $(0, v_0, c)$ is onto. The gradient has a component in $V^*$ and one in $F_c$. The direction $\delta v$ reaches every value of the $F_c$-component, $d\mu(v_0)$ being onto ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · fderiv_famGradient_point⟧; the direction $\delta c$ gives $-\delta c \circ d\mu(v_0)$ in $V^*$, all functionals vanishing on $\ker d\mu(v_0)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · fderiv_famGradient_mult⟧; and the direction $\delta\lambda$ with $\sum\delta_iB_i(v_0) = 0$ gives the forms of the hypothesis, onto the dual of $\ker d\mu(v_0)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · fderiv_famGradient_param⟧. Only first derivatives of $\mu$ and $B_i$ at $v_0$ enter; the text differentiates the equation $f(\Phi_\lambda(z)) + \sum\lambda_is_i(\Phi_\lambda(z)) = 0$ twice.

**The Sard step for the family** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · ae_isLagrangeNondegenerate_family⟧. Let $T$, $\mu$, $B_i$ be $C^\infty$ on the open $\Omega$, $d\mu(v_0)$ onto, and the hypothesis above hold for every multiplier $c$ at $v_0$ for $\lambda = 0$. Then there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and an open $\Omega' \ni v_0$ such that for almost every $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| < \varepsilon$, at every $v \in \Omega'$ with $h_\lambda(v) = 0$, $dh_\lambda(v)$ is onto and every multiplier at $v$ is non-degenerate. Surjective operators into a finite-dimensional space form an open set ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseFamily · isOpen_setOf_surjective_clm⟧ and the multiplier of a regular level set depends continuously on the point, so the transversality holds near every $(0, v_0, c)$; the parametric Sard theorem above, applied to the Lagrangian of the family on $\Lambda \times (V \times F_c^*)$, gives the rest. This is the text's open neighbourhood $U(x)$ of p. 227.

### V.39 Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): the families $a_i\sigma$, and transversality at one centre

**The solution manifold of a family.** For sc⁺-sections $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_k$ let $M = \{(\mu, y) \mid f(y) + \sum\mu_j\sigma_j(y) = 0\} \subseteq \mathbb R^k \times X$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · famZero⟧. The sections are taken of the form $s_i = a_i \cdot \sigma_{g(i)}$, $a_i$ sc-smooth functions and $g : \{1, \dots, d\} \to \{1, \dots, k\}$ — the form $g \cdot s_e$ of the section in the proof of Lemma 5.3.17 (§V.23). Then $y$ is a zero of $f + \sum\lambda_ia_i\sigma_{g(i)}$ iff $(\Lambda(\lambda, y), y) \in M$, $\Lambda(\lambda, y)_j = \sum_{g(i) = j}\lambda_ia_i(y)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · famShift⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · fiberComb_smul_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · isZeroAt_paramSlice_smul_iff⟧. So $S_\lambda$ lies in the fixed $M$, and $\lambda$ enters through the sc-smooth map $\Lambda$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · isScSmoothMap_famShift⟧, sc-smooth into $\mathbb R^k$ because its components are ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · isScSmoothMap_rn_of_components⟧. No trivialization $\Phi_\lambda$ and no second derivative of $f$ are needed.

**The local statement** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · ae_isMorseOrRegularPoint_famSlice⟧. Let $M$ be smoothly parametrized by $p : \Omega \to M \cap G$, $\Omega$ open in a finite-dimensional space, $p(v_0) = (0, y_0)$; let $t$ and $a_1, \dots, a_d$ be sc-smooth and $S_\lambda = \{y \mid (\Lambda(\lambda, y), y) \in M\}$. Suppose $\mu \circ p$ has a surjective derivative at $v_0$ ($\mu$ the projection to $\mathbb R^k$), and for every $c$ with $d(t \circ p)(v_0) = c \circ d(\mu \circ p)(v_0)$ the forms $\sum\delta_ic_{g(i)}\,d(a_i \circ p)(v_0)$, over the $\delta$ with $\Lambda(\delta, y_0) = 0$, restrict onto the dual of $\ker d(\mu \circ p)(v_0)$. Then there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and an open $O \ni y_0$ such that for almost every $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| < \varepsilon$ every point of $S_\lambda \cap O$ is a regular point or a Morse-type critical point of $t|S_\lambda$. *Proof.* In the parameter space of $p$, with $T = t \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ p$ and $B_i = (a_i \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ p)e_{g(i)}$, $S_\lambda$ near $y_0$ is the level set $\{h_\lambda = 0\}$; the Sard step for the family (§V.38) applies. At a point of the level set, the level set parametrization composed with $p$ is a smooth parametrization of $S_\lambda$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseParam · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.of_levelSet⟧; a critical point of $t$ on it has a multiplier, non-degenerate, so the bordered Hessian is injective, and the point is interior because $\Omega'$ is open. $\square$

**Multipliers and critical points.** A Lagrange multiplier of $t$ on $M$ at $(0, y)$ makes $y$ a critical point of $t|S_f$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseTransfer · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.fderivWithin_eq_zero_of_multiplier⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · not_isRegularPointOn_of_multiplier⟧. So at a regular point $y$ of $t|S_f$ there is no multiplier, and the hypothesis of the local statement holds vacuously. Regular points form an open subset ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseTransfer · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.exists_isOpen_regular⟧ and satisfy the clause of §V.36, also for a set that coincides with $A$ near the point ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseTransfer · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.isMorseOrRegularPoint_of_regular_of_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · MPolyfold.IsRegularPointOn⟧.

**The functions.** At a critical point $x$, with one section $\sigma_x$ and the parametrization $(p_x, q_x)$ of $M_x = \{f + \mu\sigma_x = 0\} \subseteq \mathbb R \times X$, the functions are $a_0 = 1$ and $a_i = \arctan(q_{x,i}(0, \cdot))/2$, the bounded coordinates of the parametrization: $|a_i| \le 1$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · abs_arctan_div_two_le_one⟧, and $\arctan(\cdot)/2$ is $C^\infty$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · contDiff_arctan_div_two⟧ with non-vanishing derivative.

**The transversality survives in the larger family** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseTransfer · exists_spanning_of_group⟧. Let $M_1 \subseteq \mathbb R \times X$ be the $j$-th one-parameter slice of $M \subseteq \mathbb R^k \times X$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_MorseTransfer · inclJ⟧, both smoothly parametrized near $(0, y)$, the functions $a_0 = 1$, $a_i = \arctan(q_{1,i}(0, \cdot))/2$ built from the left inverse $q_1$ of the parametrization of $M_1$, and every multiplier of $t$ on $M_1$ at $(0, y)$ non-zero. Then for every multiplier $c$ of $t$ on $M$ at $(0, y)$, $c_j \ne 0$, and the forms $\sum\delta_ic_j\,d(a_i \circ p)$, $\sum\delta_ia_i(y) = 0$, restrict onto the dual of $\ker d(\mu \circ p)$: the hypothesis of the local statement. Restricted to the slice, $c$ gives the multiplier $c_j$ on $M_1$, non-zero; the differentials of the coordinates $q_{1,i}$, and so of the $a_i$, restrict onto the dual of the tangent space of the solution set at $y$; and the constant $a_0 = 1$, whose differential vanishes, adjusts any $\delta$ to meet $\sum\delta_ia_i(y) = 0$. The multipliers on $M_x$ at $(0, y)$ are non-zero exactly when $(0, y)$ is not critical for $t$ on $M_x$, an open condition (above) that defines $U(x)$. This is the text's "by construction, the smooth map has, at every point $(0, y)$ satisfying $d(t|S)(y) = 0$, a linearization which is surjective" (p. 227); when the families of several centres are united it needs this argument (Findings, Chapter 5, item 183).

### V.40 Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): the covering argument

**The local data.** For a section $g$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · StrongBundle.HasMorseLocalData⟧: (A1) for all sc⁺-sections $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_k$ and every zero $y \notin \partial X$, the solution set of $g + \sum\mu_j\sigma_j$ has a smooth parametrization around $(0, y)$ by an open set on which $\mu$ is a submersion ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · HasFamilyParam⟧; (A2) every zero $x \notin \partial X$ has, inside every open $W \ni x$ and with arbitrarily small $N$, an sc⁺-section $\sigma$ for which $(0, x)$ is a regular point of $t$ on the solution set of $g + \mu\sigma$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · HasRegularFamilyParam⟧; (A3) the zeros on $\partial X$ are regular points of $t|S_g$.

**The covering argument** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · exists_morse_perturbation_hyp⟧. Let $X$ be tame, $f$ with tame germ data and compact $S_f$, in general position at every zero, $N$ auxiliary, $t$ sc-smooth, $V \supseteq S_f$ open, and (A1)–(A3) hold for $f$. Then there is an open $U$, $S_f \subseteq U \subseteq V$, with $S_{f+s}$ compact for $s \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ an $s_0 \in \Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ with $N(s_0) \le \varepsilon$, vanishing near $\partial X$, $(f + s_0, x)$ in general position at every zero, and only Morse-type critical points of $t$ on $S_{f+s_0}$. *Proof.*

1. *The critical set.* The critical points $C$ of $t|S_f$ form a closed, hence compact, subset of $S_f$ (regular points form an open set, §V.39), and $C \cap \partial X = \emptyset$ by (A3).
2. *The centres.* At $x \in C$, (A2) gives a small $\sigma_x$ supported in $V \setminus \partial X$ near $x$ and a parametrization of $M_x$ with $(0, x)$ regular for $t$; the regular points form an open $U(x)$. Finitely many $U(x_1), \dots, U(x_k)$ cover $C$.
3. *The family.* $\sigma_j = \sigma_{x_j}$, the functions $1$ and $\arctan(q_{x_j,i}(0, \cdot))/2$ of §V.39, and the sections $s_i = a_i\sigma_{g(i)}$, allowable and supported in $V \setminus \partial X$.
4. *General position.* $f$ is in general position at every zero, so the family is in general position at every $(0, y)$ (§V.33), and the relative step gives a null set off which the small slices are in general position at every zero ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · exists_null_isGeneralPositionGerm_paramSlice⟧ — Theorem 5.3.10's mechanism.
5. *The local statements.* Every zero $y$ of $f$ has an open $O_y$ and a null set. For $y \in \partial X$ the perturbations vanish near $y$, so $S_\lambda = S_f$ there, and the regularity of (A3) persists on an open set. For $y \notin \partial X$, (A1) parametrizes $M$ at $(0, y)$ with $\mu$ a submersion; if $y$ lies in some $U(x_j)$, the hypothesis of §V.39's local statement comes from the survival of the transversality, and otherwise $y$ is regular and the hypothesis is vacuous. The local statement gives $O_y$ and the null set.
6. *Size.* For small $|\lambda|$, $N(\sum\lambda_is_i) \le \varepsilon$ and the sum is allowable.
7. *Compactness.* Finitely many $O_y$ cover $S_f$, and the zeros of the slices for small $|\lambda|$ lie in their union: the compactness argument of §V.13 in the margin of Theorem 5.2.2.
8. *The parameter.* Off the finitely many null sets a small $\lambda$ exists; $s_0 = \sum\lambda_is_i$. Every zero of $f + s_0$ lies in some $O_y$, where it is regular or a Morse-type critical point, and $(f + s_0, \cdot)$ is in general position at every zero. $\square$

**With the ends** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · theorem_5_3_15_hyp⟧: the hypotheses of §V.36 and (A1)–(A3) for every perturbed section $f + s$ ($s$ sc⁺, vanishing near $\partial X$, with compact solution set and general position at every zero). Let $\eta = \min(\varepsilon, 1)/2$. §V.37 gives $U$ and $s_1$ with $N(s_1) \le \eta$, vanishing near $\partial X$, $f_1 = f + s_1$ in general position at every zero; $S_{f_1}$ is compact and inside $U$. The covering argument for $f_1$ inside $V = U$ gives $s_2$ with $N(s_2) \le \eta$. Then $f + (s_1 + s_2) = f_1 + s_2$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · sectionAdd_sectionAdd_eq⟧, $N(s_1 + s_2) \le \min(\varepsilon, 1)$ ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · StrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.auxLe_sectionAdd⟧, its support lies in $U$, and it vanishes near $\partial X$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_Morse · isZeroAt_sectionAdd_of_isZeroAt⟧. $\square$

### V.41 Theorem 5.3.15 (preprint 5.22): the local data from the implicit function theorem

(A1)–(A3) hold for every section $g$ with tame germ data in general position at every zero, when $X$ has bump functions and $t$ is as in Definition 5.3.13 ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.hasMorseLocalData⟧: $t$ sc-smooth with values in $[0, 1]$, $dt(x)$ onto at every smooth $x$ (the 2021 condition (3), read in a chart ⟦Chapter5/Book2021 · MPolyfold.HasSurjDerivAt⟧), and $\partial X \subseteq t^{-1}(0) \cup t^{-1}(1)$.

**Parametrizations from tangent germ data** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalParam · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.exists_isSmoothParam⟧. For regular tangent germ data $D$ of $M$ at $x$ (Definition 3.2.1 (2) (preprint 3.25)), $p = D.\varphi^{-1} \circ \Gamma$ on $\Omega = V \cap O_E$, $O_E$ open in the finite-dimensional $N$, is a smooth parametrization of $M$ with $p(0) = x$ and $q = \beta \cdot (\pi \circ D.\varphi)$, $\beta$ a bump function equal to $1$ near $x$ and supported in the chart domain, the cut-off of §V.23 ⟦Chapter5/Homotopy · chartLinCutoff⟧; $h \circ p$ is $C^\infty$ because $\Gamma$ is sc-smooth on a finite-dimensional domain (§V.14, step 2). *At a zero in general position* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.exists_isSmoothParam_solutionSet⟧, the index form of Theorem 3.6.8 (§V.17) gives $D$; the parametrization is by a set of $\mathbb R^n$ with unique derivatives ($V$ is relatively open in a partial quadrant), and by an open set when $d_X(y) = 0$, since the degeneracy index of the tame chart is $d_X(y)$ and at index $0$ the partial quadrant is the whole space ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.exists_isOpen_of_mem_nhds⟧.

**Kernel vectors are tangent vectors.** For a smooth parametrization $p$ of $A$ and a chart $\varphi$ with retraction $R$ around $p(u_0)$, let $S$ be a retraction whose retract lies in $\varphi(A)$ and passes through $z = \varphi(p(u_0))$. Every $w \in T_z$ of that retract has a $v$, namely $D(q \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ S)(z)w$, with $d(g \circ p)(u_0)v = D(g \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ R)(z)w$ for all sc-smooth $g$, at interior and boundary points alike ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · MPolyfold.IsSmoothParam.exists_fderivWithin_eq_scDeriv⟧; the chosen sc-derivative is any bounded operator that restricts to the level-$1$ derivative ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · scDeriv_eq_of_hasFDerivWithinAt⟧. At a zero in general position, every strong bundle chart carries a retraction $S$ with retract in $\varphi(S_f)$ through $\varphi(y)$ and $\operatorname{range}DS(z) = \ker\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · StrongBundle.exists_retract_range_eq_linKer⟧, by the equivalence of §V.18 ⟦Chapter5/GeneralPosition · exists_isGeneralPositionGerm_iff⟧. Together: every $w \in \ker\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is tangent to every smooth parametrization of $S_f$ through $y$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · StrongBundle.exists_fderivWithin_eq_scDeriv_of_mem_linKer⟧. Since condition (3) is stated in an existential chart, one change of chart for the derivative of a function is needed ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · MPolyfold.exists_scDeriv_eq_chart_change⟧.

**(A1)** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.hasFamilyParam⟧. The family $F(\mu, y) = g(y) + \sum\mu_j\sigma_j(y)$ is in general position at $(0, y)$ (§V.33), so its solution set has a parametrization around $(0, y)$ — open for $y \notin \partial X$ — whose tangent vectors include $\ker F'(0, y)$ in the product chart ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.exists_isSmoothParam_famZero⟧. In the product chart the derivative of $\mu_j$ is $(\delta a, \delta u) \mapsto \delta a_j$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · scDeriv_pc0_fst_apply⟧. Since $g'(y)$ is onto, every $\delta\mu$ has a $w$ with $g'(y)w = -\sum\delta\mu_j\hat\sigma_j(y)$, i.e. $(\delta\mu, w) \in \ker F'(0, y)$; so $d(\mu \circ p)(v_0)$ is onto.

**(A2)** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.exists_hasRegularFamilyParam⟧. Let $x \notin \partial X$ be a zero, $W \ni x$ open, $\eta > 0$. In a tame chart centred at $x$, $dt(x) \ne 0$ and $E_\infty$ is dense in $E_0$, so there is a smooth $v_1$ with $dt(x)(Dr(0)v_1) \ne 0$. $w_1 = Dr(0)v_1$ and $k = \mathrm{Lin}(0)w_1$ are smooth points, because $Dr(0)$ and $D(\hat g \circ r)(0)$ are sc-operators at the smooth point $0$ and sc-operators map smooth points to smooth points ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · IsScOperator.apply_mem_smooth⟧. Lemma 5.3.3 (preprint 5.11) gives an sc⁺-section through $\Phi^{-1}(0, k)$ supported in $W$, rescaled by $\theta = \eta/(N(e) + 1)$ to $\sigma$; then $(-1/\theta, w_1) \in \ker F'(0, x)$, and the derivative of $t \circ \mathrm{pr}_2$ in the product chart ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · scDeriv_pc0_snd_apply⟧ is $dt(x)w_1 \ne 0$ on it: $(0, x)$ is a regular point of $t$ on the solution set of $g + \mu\sigma$. Neither the open mapping theorem nor density in the fibre is needed. This is where the text's $b(e_i)$, in an algebraic complement $Z$ (Lemma 5.3.16), is replaced: Lemma 5.3.3 reaches only smooth points of the fibre, and $-c\,g'(x)w_1$ is one because $w_1$ is smooth.

**(A3) at every corner** ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalData · StrongBundle.isRegularPointOn_of_extremum⟧. *The extremum lemma* ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · scDeriv_eq_zero_of_extremum⟧: if $U$ is relatively open in a partial quadrant $C = T^{-1}([0, \infty)^n \oplus W)$ and an sc¹ function $\tau$ on $U$ has a minimum or a maximum at a level-$1$ point $z$, then $D\tau(z)e = 0$ for every $e \in E_z$. A direction $e \in E_z$ keeps at $0$ the coordinates that vanish at $z$, so $z + se \in C$ for small $|s|$ of both signs; for $e$ of level $1$, $s \mapsto \tau(z + se)$ is differentiable with an extremum at $0$; the level-$1$ vectors are dense in $E_z$ ⟦Chapter5/Theorem5315_LocalTangent · mem_closure_levelOne_minimalSubspaceWith⟧ and $D\tau(z)$ is continuous on $E_0$. At a zero $x \in \partial X$, $t(x) \in \{0, 1\}$ and $0 \le t \le 1$, so $t$ has an extremum, and $dt(x)$ vanishes on $E_x \supseteq T^R_xX$, whatever the codimension of $T^R_xX$. General position gives $T_xX = \ker g'(x) + T^R_xX$ ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isParamGP_elim0_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧ and $dt(x) \ne 0$, so $dt(x)$ does not vanish on $\ker g'(x)$, the tangent space of the parametrization: $x$ is a regular point of $t|S_g$. No hypothesis on the degeneracy index $d_X(x)$ is needed; of $\partial X = X_0 \sqcup X_1$ only $t(\partial X) \subseteq \{0, 1\}$ enters here, and "the $X_i$ have no boundary" only in §V.37.

**The theorem.** With (A1)–(A3) for every perturbed section, `theorem_5_3_15_hyp` (§V.40) is the theorem without hypothesis (§V.36). Theorem 5.3.15 holds as printed, with Definition 5.3.13 read in its 2021 form.

### V.42 Theorem 5.5.10 (preprint 5.37): every chart has the approximation property

§V.25 proved "(i) ⇒ (ii)" for restricted charts, because the text's $\operatorname{cl}_X(W) \subseteq U$ does not follow from $\operatorname{cl}_C(V) \subseteq O$ (Findings, Chapter 5, item 111). Every chart has the property, by a different route ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · hasApproxProperty_of_isChart⟧, and Theorem 5.5.10 holds with "every chart" ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · theorem_5_5_10_every_chart⟧.

**Tools on $X$.** With sc-smooth partitions of unity, disjoint closed sets have sc-smooth Urysohn functions ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · MPolyfold.AdmitsScPartitionsOfUnity.exists_urysohn⟧, and a continuous function with values in $[0, 1]$ and support closed in an open set is approximated within $\varepsilon$ by sc-smooth functions with closed support in that set ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · MPolyfold.AdmitsScPartitionsOfUnity.exists_approx⟧ — the argument of §V.25 on $X$ itself.

**The shells.** Let $f : O \to [0, 1]$ be continuous with support in $V = O \cap W$, $\operatorname{cl}V \subseteq O$, and $F = f \circ \varphi$ on the chart domain; $F$ extended by $0$ need not be continuous (§V.25). Write the chart domain as $\{d > 0\}$ with $d$ continuous ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · exists_continuous_pos_iff⟧. Take sc-smooth $\kappa_n$, $1$ on $\{d \ge 1/(n + 1)\}$ and $0$ on $\{d \le 1/(n + 2)\}$, and the weights $\lambda_n = \kappa_n\prod_{j<n}(1 - \kappa_j)$, which telescope to $1$ on the chart domain and are locally finite. Where $\lambda_n \ne 0$, $\kappa_{n+1} = 1$, so $F = F\kappa_{n+1}$ there; $F\kappa_{n+1}$ has support closed in $X$, and its approximation $\hat g_n$ has closed support in the chart domain. $g = \sum_n\lambda_n\hat g_n$ is finite near each point, hence sc-smooth, with values in $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · sum_mul_mem_Icc⟧, and within $\varepsilon$ of $F$ as a convex combination of $\varepsilon$-approximations ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_ApproxEveryChart · abs_sub_sum_mul_le⟧. Read in the chart, $g$ gives the approximation on $O$. $\square$ The restricted charts of §V.25 are kept.

### V.43 Theorem 5.5.5 (preprint 5.32): Bonic–Frampton

**The statement** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.theorem_5_5_5⟧. On the real $L^p(\mu)$ of any measure space, $p \ge 1$, $F(f) = \|f\|^p$ is (1) $C^\infty$ for $p$ an even integer, (2) $C^{p-1}$ for $p$ an odd integer, (3) $C^{[p]}$ for $p$ not an integer — as printed (gap G.50; Findings, Chapter 5, items 117, 120, 179).

**Weighted products** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LpWeightedProduct · BonicFrampton.wMul⟧. For $w \in L^q$ with $q^{-1} + m/p = 1$, $(h_1, \dots, h_m) \mapsto \int w\prod h_i$ is a continuous $m$-linear form of norm $\le \|w\|_q$, by the generalized Hölder inequality ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LpWeightedProduct · BonicFrampton.eLpNorm_prod_le⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LpWeightedProduct · BonicFrampton.norm_wMul_le⟧. *The even case* ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LpWeightedProduct · BonicFrampton.theorem_5_5_5_even⟧: $\|f\|^{2k} = \int f^{2k}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LpWeightedProduct · BonicFrampton.norm_rpow_eq_integral⟧ is the diagonal of the $2k$-linear form with weight $1 \in L^\infty$, hence $C^\infty$.

**The general case.** Let $g_j$ be the $j$-th derivative of $|t|^p$, of the form $a_j\max(t, 0)^{p-j} + b_j\max(-t, 0)^{p-j}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.gK⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.hasDerivAt_gK⟧. Two one-variable estimates for such homogeneous kernels carry the analysis: $|g(s + t) - g(s)| \le \varepsilon|s|^r + C_\varepsilon|t|^r$ for $r > 0$, from the continuity of $z^r$ at $1$ and homogeneity ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.kern_sub_le⟧, and the first-order remainder bound $|t|(\varepsilon|s|^{r-1} + C_\varepsilon|t|^{r-1})$ by the mean value theorem ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.taylor1_le⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.gK_taylor_le⟧. For $j < p$, $g_j(f) \in L^{p/(p-j)}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.memLp_gK⟧, and the exponents form Hölder triples ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.holderTriple_qE⟧. The forms $T_j(f) = \int g_j(f)\prod h_i$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.Tj⟧ are continuous in $f$ (the first estimate, integrated) ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.continuous_Tj⟧, and the derivative of $T_j$ is $T_{j+1}$ curried (the second estimate with Hölder $L^p \times L^{p/(p-j-1)} \to L^{p/(p-j)}$) ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.hasFDerivAt_Tj⟧. So $(T_j)$ is a Taylor series of $\|\cdot\|^p$ up to every integer $n < p$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.hasFTaylorSeriesUpTo_normRpow⟧, and $\|\cdot\|^p$ is $C^n$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_BonicFrampton · BonicFrampton.contDiff_normRpow_of_lt⟧. Case (2) is $n = 2k < 2k + 1$, case (3) is $n = [p] < p$. No calculus of Nemytskii operators is needed beyond these two estimates.

### V.44 The Sobolev remark after Theorem 5.5.5

After Theorem 5.5.5 the text says that the usual norms of $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ have the differentiability of $\|\cdot\|_{L^p}$, that $\beta(\|x\|^p)$ is a bump function of $L^p$, that $W^{1,4}(\Omega)$ with $E_m = W^{1+m,4}(\Omega)$ admits sc-smooth bump functions, while on $W^{1,3/2}(\Omega)$ the straightforward bump is only sc¹, and it asks whether an sc-smooth one exists (pp. 230–231). Formalized, with the sc-structure built on one domain (row V5.76, narrower; gap G.51; Findings, Chapter 5, items 118, 185).

**$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.Wsub⟧. For $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and $p \ge 1$: the tuples $(v_\alpha)_{|\alpha| \le k}$ in the $\ell^p$-product of copies of $L^p(\Omega)$ with $\int_\Omega v_0\,\partial^\alpha\varphi = (-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi$ for all test functions $\varphi$ on $\Omega$. Each identity is a continuous functional ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.wk⟧, so the subspace is closed ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.isClosed_Wsub⟧, a Banach space with $\|u\|^p = \sum_\alpha\|D^\alpha u\|^p_{L^p}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.norm_rpow_W⟧; weak derivatives are unique on open $\Omega$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.Dop_zero_injective⟧.

**The norms and the bumps.** Any norm with $\|u\|^p = \sum_i\|T_iu\|^p_{L^p}$, $T_i$ continuous linear, has the differentiability of Theorem 5.5.5 ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · SobolevRemark.theorem_5_5_5_sum⟧, which is the first claim ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.remark_5_5_5_sobolev⟧. For $\beta$ smooth with compact support, $\beta(\|x\|^p)$ has bounded support ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · SobolevRemark.bump_comp_rpow⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · SobolevRemark.hasContDiffBump_of_rpow⟧; "non-vanishing $\beta$" is read as $\beta(0) \ne 0$, as in the Hilbert example of p. 229. This gives bumps of $L^p$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · SobolevRemark.hasContDiffBump_Lp⟧ and of $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.remark_5_5_5_sobolev_bump⟧, $C^\infty$, $C^{p-1}$ or $C^{[p]}$ in the three cases.

**From level $0$ to the sc-structure.** A $C^\infty$ bump on $E_0$ gives the sc-smooth bump property of every local model on $E$: rescale and translate it to $x$ as in Proposition 5.5.8 (§V.24); it is $C^\infty$ on $E_0$, hence sc-smooth (Corollary 1.2.5 (preprint 1.20)), and composed with the retraction ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · LocalModel.hasBumpProperty_of_hasContDiffBump⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · MPolyfold.admitsBumpFunctions_of_hasContDiffBump⟧. Hence every sc-Banach space with $E_0 \cong W^{1,4}(\Omega)$ admits sc-smooth bump functions, as do its local models and the M-polyfolds modelled on it ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark3 · SobolevRemark.remark_5_5_5_W14⟧; on $W^{1,3/2}(\Omega)$ the bump $\beta(\|x\|^{3/2})$ is $C^1 = C^{[3/2]}$ on $E_0$, hence sc¹ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark1 · exists_isSck_bump⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark3 · SobolevRemark.remark_5_5_5_W1_3_2⟧. These use only the level $0$: they hold for every sc-structure on these spaces and every $\Omega$. The closing question is a question, not a claim.

**The sc-structure $E_m = W^{1+m,p}(\Omega)$** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark3 · SobolevRemark.sobolevSc⟧, with the inclusions $W^{k+1,p} \to W^{k,p}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.inclW⟧, injective on open $\Omega$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark2 · SobolevRemark.inclW_injective⟧, takes the compactness of the inclusions and the density of $E_\infty$ as hypotheses; $\Omega = \emptyset$ is the trivial instance ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevRemark3 · SobolevRemark.sobolevSc_hyps_empty⟧. Both are proved for $\Omega = (0, 1) \subset \mathbb R^1$ and every $p > 1$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube5 · SobolevCube.cubeSc⟧:

1. *The Volterra operator* $Vg(x) = \int_0^xg$ is compact on $L^p(0, 1)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube1 · SobolevCube.isCompactOperator_V⟧: by Hölder $|Vg(x) - Vg(y)| \le \|g\|\,|x - y|^{1-1/p}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube1 · SobolevCube.abs_Vf_sub_le⟧, so the image of the unit ball is uniformly close to step functions on a grid of $N$ intervals ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube1 · SobolevCube.dist_V_le⟧, hence totally bounded.
2. *Rellich.* A function with weak derivative $0$ is constant ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube2 · SobolevCube.eq_cst_of_weakDeriv_zero⟧, so every component of $u \in W^{k,p}$ is a constant plus $V$ of the next one ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube2 · SobolevCube.eq_cst_add_V⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube3 · SobolevCube.comp_eq_cst_add_V⟧, with the constant bounded by the norm ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube4 · SobolevCube.abs_cst_le⟧; the inclusion $W^{k+1,p} \to W^{k,p}$ is compact ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube4 · SobolevCube.isCompactOperator_inclW_cube⟧.
3. *Density.* Polynomials are dense ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube2 · SobolevCube.denseRange_poly⟧; approximating the top derivative and integrating gives smooth approximations on every level ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube5 · SobolevCube.exists_smooth_approx⟧, so $E_\infty$ is dense ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube5 · SobolevCube.dense_smoothLvl_cube⟧.

On this structure the claims hold for the text's sc-structure ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube5 · SobolevCube.remark_5_5_5_W14_cube⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube5 · SobolevCube.remark_5_5_5_W14_instance⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SobolevCube5 · SobolevCube.remark_5_5_5_W1_3_2_cube⟧. Cubes in $\mathbb R^n$, $n \ge 2$, and other bounded domains — where, as we read it, a regular boundary is presupposed — are not done; hence the row is narrower.

### V.45 Theorem 5.5.13 (preprint 5.40): Toruńczyk

The statement recorded in §V.26 ⟦Chapter5/PartitionsOfUnity · TorunczykStatement⟧ — $C^k$ partitions of unity iff a coordinate-wise $C^k$ homeomorphic embedding into some $c_0(\Gamma)$ — holds for every real Banach space and every $k \in \mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · theorem_5_5_13⟧ (gap G.52). The coordinates of $c_0(\Gamma)$ are $1$-Lipschitz ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · abs_cz_sub_le⟧ and only finitely many exceed a given $\varepsilon$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · finite_cz_gt⟧.

**(⇒)** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · torunczyk_forward⟧. For each $n$ take a $C^k$ partition of unity $(\rho_{n,c})_{c \in V}$ subordinate to the balls $B(c, 1/(n + 1))$, and $h(x) = (\rho_{n,c}(x)/(n + 1))_{(n,c)}$. It lies in $c_0(\mathbb N \times V)$, since the partitions are locally finite and the weights tend to $0$; it is continuous, because up to $\varepsilon$ only finitely many $n$ matter; its coordinates are $C^k$; and it is an embedding: if $h(y)$ is close to $h(x)$, some coordinate $(n, c)$ large at $x$ is still non-zero at $y$, so $y$ and $x$ share a ball of radius $1/(n + 1)$.

**(⇐)** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · torunczyk_backward⟧, through $C^k$ Urysohn functions ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · exists_contDiff_urysohn_of_embedding⟧ and Mathlib's bump coverings ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · admitsContDiffPartitionsOfUnity_of_urysohn⟧. With a $C^\infty$ bump $\theta$, $1$ on $[-1/2, 1/2]$ and $0$ outside $(-3/5, 3/5)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · thetaB⟧, the *lattice bumps* are $b_{n,\sigma}(x) = \prod_\gamma\theta((n + 1)h(x)(\gamma) - \sigma(\gamma))$ for finitely supported $\sigma : \Gamma \to \mathbb Z$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · latticeBump⟧. Near a point all but finitely many factors are $1$, so they are $C^k$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · contDiff_latticeBump⟧ (locally finite sums and products of $C^k$ functions are $C^k$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · contDiff_finsum_of_locallyFinite⟧); for fixed $n$ they are locally finite in $\sigma$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · locallyFinite_latticeBump⟧; at $x$, the bump of the rounding $\sigma$ of $(n + 1)h(x)$ equals $1$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · exists_latticeBump_eq_one⟧, and its support lies in $\{y \mid \|h(y) - h(x)\| \le 2/(n + 1)\}$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · tsupport_latticeBump_subset_ball⟧. For disjoint closed $s$, $t$, the bumps whose support misses $s$ or misses $t$ cover $V$, $h$ being an embedding; Michael's products, which multiply the bumps of level $n$ by $\eta$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_Torunczyk · etaB⟧ of the sums of the levels $m < n$, make them locally finite across $n$, and the quotient of the sum over the bumps on the side of $t$ by the sum of all is the Urysohn function.

### V.46 Theorem 5.5.16 (preprint 5.43) for separable spaces, and Corollary 5.5.17 (preprint 5.44) without hypothesis

**$E_0$ is separable** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · ScBanach.separableSpace_zero⟧, for every sc-Banach space: the inclusion $E_1 \to E_0$ is a compact operator with dense range; the range of a compact operator lies in $\bigcup_nnK$ with $K$ compact, so it is separable ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · IsCompactOperator.isSeparable_range⟧, and a space with a dense separable subset is separable. So in the sc-calculus Theorem 5.5.16 is needed only for separable spaces (Findings, Chapter 5, item 184).

**The separable case.** From a $C^k$ bump, a $C^k$ function $\psi : V \to [0, 1]$, $1$ on $B(0, 1)$, supported in $B(0, R)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · HasContDiffBump.exists_one_on_ball⟧. For disjoint closed $s$, $t$: a countable cover of $t$ by balls $B(x_n, r_n)$ whose $R$-fold enlargements miss $s$ (Lindelöf), $\psi_n = \psi((\cdot - x_n)/r_n)$, and the telescoping products $f_n = \psi_n\prod_{j<n}(1 - \psi_j)$ with $\sum_{n<N}f_n = 1 - \prod_{n<N}(1 - \psi_n)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · sum_range_mul_prod_one_sub⟧ give a $C^k$ Urysohn function ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · exists_contDiff_urysohn_of_separable⟧, and bump coverings give $C^k$ partitions of unity ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · admitsContDiffPartitionsOfUnity_of_separable⟧: Theorem 5.5.16 for separable spaces, the Bonic–Frampton construction ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · godefroyTroyanskiWhitfieldZizlerStatement_of_separable⟧.

**Corollary 5.5.17 (preprint 5.44)** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · corollary_5_5_17_unconditional⟧. If $\|v\|^2 = b(v, v)$ on $E_0$, the local model has the sc-smooth approximation property, with no further hypothesis: $E_0$ is separable, has the $C^\infty$ bump $\tau(1 - b(v, v))$ (§V.26), hence $C^\infty$ partitions of unity, and Proposition 5.5.11 (preprint 5.38) applies. The M-polyfold form ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_SeparablePOU · MPolyfold.admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_of_hilbert_unconditional⟧ drops the hypothesis of §V.26.

**Hilbert spaces of any density** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_HilbertPOU · admitsContDiffPartitionsOfUnity_of_hilbertSpace⟧. For a Hilbert basis $(b_\gamma)$, $x \mapsto (\|x\|^2, (\langle b_\gamma, x\rangle)_\gamma)$ maps into $c_0$ with $C^\infty$ coordinates, and it is a homeomorphic embedding by a Kadec–Klee estimate in $\ell^2$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_HilbertPOU · l2_inverse_estimate⟧: if $|v_\gamma - u_\gamma| \le \delta$ for all $\gamma$ and $|\|v\|^2 - \|u\|^2| \le \delta$, then $\|v - u\|^2 \le n\delta^2 + 2\delta + 2n\delta(2\|u\| + \delta) + 4\,\mathrm{tail}_F(u)$, with $F$ a set of $n$ coordinates carrying most of $u$. Toruńczyk (⇐) concludes ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_HilbertPOU · godefroyTroyanskiWhitfieldZizlerStatement_of_hilbertSpace⟧.

### V.47 Theorem 5.5.16 (preprint 5.43): every WCG Banach space

⟦Chapter5/GapP1_GTWZ · theorem_5_5_16⟧. A weakly compactly generated Banach space with a $C^k$ bump admits $C^k$ partitions of unity, for every $k$ (gap G.53). The recorded statement ⟦Chapter5/PartitionsOfUnity · GodefroyTroyanskiWhitfieldZizlerStatement⟧ leaves completeness out; the theorem assumes it, the text's "Banach". The route follows Deville–Godefroy–Zizler, reorganized so that neither Krein's theorem nor the Eberlein–Šmulian theorem nor a transfinite recursion is needed.

**Bases** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_C0Base · IsRelC0Base⟧. A *base relative to $Q$* is a locally $c_0$-finite family of $C^k$ functions with values in $[-1, 1]$ whose cozero sets are $Q$-small. A base gives partitions of unity: $x \mapsto (f_i(x))_i$ is a coordinate-wise $C^k$ embedding into $c_0(I)$, and Toruńczyk applies ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_C0Base · admitsContDiffPartitionsOfUnity_of_isRelC0Base⟧; conversely $f_{(c,n)} = \rho_{n,c}/(n + 1)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_C0Base · exists_isRelC0Base_of_admits⟧. Bases transfer along operators ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_C0Base · IsRelC0Base.comp⟧, and a bump gives a cut-off ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_C0Base · HasContDiffBump.exists_cutoff⟧. *The gluing lemma* ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_C0Base · isRelC0Base_glue⟧: if $X$ has a $C^k$ bump, $\Delta_i$, $Q_i$ are operators with $\|\Delta_i\| \le C$, $(\|\Delta_ix\|)_i \in c_0$ for every $x$, every $x \ne 0$ is close to some $Q_ix$ with $\Delta_ix \ne 0$, and each $Q_i$ carries a base relative to $Q_i$, then $X$ has a base. The new functions are $(m + 1)^{-1}(N + 1)^{-1}\psi((m + 1)\Delta_iy)\,\chi((N + 1)(y - Q_iy))\,g_{ij}(y)$ and $(N + 1)^{-1}\chi((N + 1)y)$, with $\psi = 1 - \chi$.

**Projections from Lindenstrauss pairs** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · IsLPair⟧. For $K$ weakly compact with dense span, a *Lindenstrauss pair* $(A, D)$: $A$ a $\mathbb Q$-subspace, $D$ a set of functionals norming $A$, and $A \cap K$ dense in $K$ for the topology of $D$. It gives a norm-one projection onto $\operatorname{cl}A$ along $D_\perp$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · IsLPair.exists_proj⟧, by weak compactness (the finite intersection property) and Mazur's theorem; the convexity of $K$ (Krein) is not used. A monotone closure operator $S \mapsto (A(S), D(S))$, an $\omega$-iteration of finitary operations with global choices of norming functionals and witnesses ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · lclA⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · lclD⟧, yields a pair ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · isLPair_lcl⟧ of finite character ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · lclA_finite⟧ and of cardinality at most $\max(\#S, \aleph_0)$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_LindenstraussPair · card_lcl⟧.

**The resolution of the identity** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_WCGPRI · priP⟧. With $e$ enumerating a dense set by the ordinals below $\mu$, $P_\alpha$ is the projection of the closure of $\{e_\beta \mid \beta < \alpha\}$. The projections commute, $P_\mu = 1$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_WCGPRI · priP_top⟧, and the family is continuous at limit ordinals ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_WCGPRI · PRICont⟧ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_WCGPRI · priP_cont⟧ because the closure has finite character — so no recursion over the ordinals is needed. For such a family the increments of $x$ are in $c_0$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_WCGPRI · pri_finite⟧, and $x$ is approximated by some $P_{\alpha+1}x$ with a non-zero increment, through the least $\beta$ with $P_\beta x = x$ ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_WCGPRI · pri_approx⟧.

**The induction** ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_GTWZ · admitsContDiffPartitionsOfUnity_of_wcg_card⟧, strong induction on a cardinal $\kappa$ bounding a dense set. For $\kappa \le \aleph_0$ the space is separable (§V.46). Otherwise the pieces $P_{\alpha+1}X$ are WCG ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_GTWZ · IsWCG.of_proj⟧, carry a $C^k$ bump ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_GTWZ · HasContDiffBump.submodule⟧, and have dense sets of smaller cardinality ⟦Chapter5/GapP1_GTWZ · exists_dense_card_le⟧, so by induction they admit partitions of unity, hence bases; with $\Delta_\alpha = P_{\alpha+1} - P_\alpha$ and $Q_\alpha = P_{\alpha+1}$ the gluing lemma gives a base of $X$, and partitions of unity.

### V.48 Weak sequential compactness in reflexive spaces

The text uses without comment that a bounded sequence in a reflexive Banach space has a weakly convergent subsequence (proof of Proposition 5.2.7, "after perhaps taking a subsequence"), and that the compact inclusion $F_1 \to F_0$ maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent ones (proof of Lemma 5.1.5). Mathlib has the sequential Banach–Alaoglu theorem only for the dual of a separable space, so both are proved here. A space is *reflexive* if the canonical map $F \to F^{**}$ is onto ⟦Chapter5/PartitionsOfUnity · IsReflexive⟧ (the definition of §V.26); finite-dimensional spaces are reflexive ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · isReflexive_of_finiteDimensional⟧. *Weak convergence* $u_k \rightharpoonup h$ is $g(u_k) \to g(h)$ for every $g \in F^*$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · WeakTendsto⟧. Weakly convergent sequences are bounded, by uniform boundedness ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · WeakTendsto.exists_bound⟧, and the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous, $\|h\| - \varepsilon < \|u_k\|$ eventually ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · WeakTendsto.eventually_norm_gt⟧.

**Weak sequential compactness** ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · exists_subseq_weakTendsto⟧: in a reflexive $F$ every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence; also with a bound that holds only eventually ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · exists_subseq_weakTendsto_of_eventually⟧. *Step 1.* The closed span $M$ of the sequence is separable, so countably many norm-one functionals $g_d$ norm the points of $M$. *Step 2.* The values $(g_d(u_k))_d$ lie in a cube $\prod_d[-C, C]$, compact and metrizable; a subsequence makes every $g_d(u_k)$ converge. *Step 3.* The images $J(u_k)$ in the bidual lie in a weak*-compact ball (Banach–Alaoglu). Every weak* cluster point is $J(p)$ for some $p \in M$, by reflexivity and Hahn–Banach, and the $g_d$ determine $p$; so the subsequence has one cluster point, and a sequence in a compact set with one cluster point converges. **Two consequences.** A compact operator maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent ones ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · WeakTendsto.tendsto_of_isCompactOperator⟧. In a reflexive space, a bounded sequence whose image under an injective bounded operator converges to the image of $h$ converges weakly to $h$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_WeakSeqCompact · weakTendsto_of_bounded_of_tendsto⟧: every subsequence has a weakly convergent subsequence, whose limit is $h$ by injectivity.

### V.49 Definition 5.1.4 (2017: 5.2; not in the preprint) and Lemma 5.1.5 (2017: 5.2; not in the preprint)

**Definition 5.1.4** (restated) ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.HasReflexiveFibers⟧: $P : Y \to X$ has reflexive $(0, 1)$-fibres if every $x \in X$ lies in the domain of a strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas whose model has $F_1$ reflexive. The text asks for an equivalent atlas of such charts; this is read as "the reflexive compatible charts cover $X$", which is the same, since chart domains are of the form $P^{-1}(V)$. It holds if every chart of the given atlas is reflexive ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.hasReflexiveFibers_of_atlas⟧. In a chart $c$ the fibre part of a point $y \in Y_{0,1}$ is $h \in F_1$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundleChart.liftOneSnd⟧.

**Lemma 5.1.5** ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · lemma_5_1_5⟧: let $y_k \in Y_{0,1}$ with $P(y_k) \to x$ on level $0$, and $\Psi$, $\Psi'$ charts around $x$ with $F_1$, $F'_1$ reflexive; then the fibre parts $h_k$ converge weakly in $F_1$ iff the $h'_k$ converge weakly in $F'_1$. The strong form ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · lemma_5_1_5_limit⟧ identifies the limits, which the text's proof uses implicitly: if $h_k \rightharpoonup h$ (and only $F'_1$ needs to be reflexive), there is one $y \in Y_{0,1}$ over $x$ with $\Psi$-part $h$, $y_k \to y$ in $Y$, and $h'_k$ converges weakly to the $\Psi'$-part of $y$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.weakTendsto_transfer⟧. *Step 1, the limit point.* $h_k \rightharpoonup h$ in $F_1$ gives $h_k \to h$ in $F_0$, through the compact inclusion (§V.48). The limit $(a, h)$ lies in the local model $K$, because the retraction is continuous on $U \triangleleft F$ and fixes $K$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundleChart.mem_K_of_tendsto⟧; it is a point $y$ of $Y_{0,1}$ with $y_k \to y$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.exists_limit_of_weakTendsto⟧. *Step 2, the other chart.* The $h'_k$ are bounded in $F'_1$, by the local comparison of the norms $|\cdot|_1$ of two charts (Lemma 5.1.2), and converge in $F'_0$ to the fibre part of $y$, because $y_k \to y$ in $Y$ and $\Psi'$ is continuous; so they converge weakly in the reflexive $F'_1$ (§V.48) ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.weakTendsto_liftOneSnd_of_tendsto⟧. Fibre parts are read in a chart only for large $k$.

### V.50 Definitions 5.1.6 and 5.1.7 (2017: 5.3 and 5.4; not in the preprint): mixed convergence and reflexive auxiliary norms

**Definition 5.1.6** ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.MixedTendsto⟧: $y_k \in Y_{0,1}$ is mixed convergent to $y \in Y_{0,1}$ if $P(y_k) \to P(y)$ in $X_0$ and, in some chart around $P(y)$ with $F_1$ reflexive, the fibre parts converge weakly. The text's "in view of this lemma we can define" is proved: the fibre parts then converge weakly in every compatible reflexive chart around $P(y)$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.MixedTendsto.weakTendsto_of_isChart⟧, and $y_k \to y$ in $Y$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.MixedTendsto.tendsto_oneVal⟧, both by Lemma 5.1.5. *Mixed convergent subsequences* ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.exists_mixedTendsto_subseq⟧: if $P(y_k) \to x$ and $N(y_k) \le r$ for an auxiliary norm $N$, a subsequence is mixed convergent; the fibre parts in a reflexive chart are bounded by Lemma 5.1.2, and §V.48 applies.

**Definition 5.1.7** ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.IsReflexiveAuxNorm⟧: a reflexive auxiliary norm is an auxiliary norm with $N(y) \le \liminf_kN(y_k)$ whenever $y_k$ is mixed convergent to $y$. The text prints $\liminf_{k \to 0}$; presumably $k \to \infty$. The $\liminf$ is taken in the extended reals, so that an unbounded sequence has $\liminf = \infty$. Equivalent forms: if $N(y_k) \le r$ infinitely often then $N(y) \le r$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.IsReflexiveAuxNorm.le_of_frequently_le⟧, and a criterion through eventual bounds ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.le_liminf_coe_of_eventually⟧.

### V.51 Proposition 5.1.8 (2017: 5.2; not in the preprint): reflexive auxiliary norms exist

**Proposition 5.1.8** ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · proposition_5_1_8⟧: with reflexive $(0, 1)$-fibres a reflexive auxiliary norm exists ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · proposition_5_1_8_exists⟧, and for an auxiliary norm $N_0$ and a reflexive one $N_1$ there is a continuous $f : X \to (0, \infty)$ with $f(x)N_0 \le N_1 \le f(x)^{-1}N_0$ on the fibre over $x$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · proposition_5_1_8_compare⟧. The text leaves the proof to the reader. *Existence.* The norm of Proposition 5.1.3 (preprint 5.3) built over the reflexive compatible charts, $N(w) = \sum_i\rho_i(P(w))\,|\Phi_i[1](w)|_1$ for a partition of unity $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to their domains, is an auxiliary norm by Lemma 5.1.2 (preprint 5.2). *Lower semicontinuity* ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.le_liminf_gluedNorm⟧: near $P(y)$ only finitely many terms are nonzero; $\rho_i(P(y_k)) \to \rho_i(P(y))$; in each chart the fibre parts converge weakly, by the chart independence of §V.50, and the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous (§V.48). So $N$ is a reflexive auxiliary norm ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.isReflexiveAuxNorm_gluedNorm⟧. *Comparison.* A reflexive auxiliary norm is an auxiliary norm, and Proposition 5.1.3 (preprint 5.3) compares any two. Two tools for later chapters: $(g \circ P) \cdot N$ is again a (reflexive) auxiliary norm for continuous $g > 0$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.IsReflexiveAuxNorm.comp_mul⟧, and with reflexive fibres every auxiliary norm lies between two reflexive ones ⟦Chapter5/P3R_Reflexive2021 · StrongBundle.exists_reflexiveAuxNorm_sandwich⟧.

### V.52 Definition 5.2.6 and Proposition 5.2.7 (2017: 5.6 and 5.3; not in the preprint)

**Definition 5.2.6** ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · StrongBundle.HasReflexiveLocalCompactness⟧: $f$ has the reflexive local compactness property if for every reflexive auxiliary norm $N$ and every $x$ there is an open $U(x) \ni x$ with $\operatorname{cl}_X\{q \in U(x) \mid N(f(q)) \le 1\}$ compact. The text prints $N(f(x)) \le 1$ inside the set; presumably $N(f(q))$. $N(f(q)) \le 1$ includes $f(q) \in Y_{0,1}$, as in §V.32. The standing assumptions of the text (reflexive fibres, $f$ sc-smooth and regularizing) are hypotheses of the statements that use it.

**Proposition 5.2.7** (stronger) ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · proposition_5_2_7⟧. With the text's hypotheses: (1) every $x \in X_0 \setminus X_1$ has a neighbourhood on which $N(f(q)) > 1$; (2) so has every $x$ with $N(f(x)) > 1$. *(2) for every continuous section* ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · StrongBundle.exists_nhds_not_auxLe⟧. If not, $x$ is a limit of points $x_k$ with $N(f(x_k)) \le 1$; $X$ is metrizable (Theorem 2.3.10), so a sequence suffices. A subsequence of $f(x_k)$ is mixed convergent to some $y$ (§V.50), and $f(x_k) \to y$ in $Y$, so $y = f(x)$ by continuity of $f$; lower semicontinuity gives $N(f(x)) \le 1$. *(1)*: for a regularizing $f$, $f(x) \notin Y_{0,1}$ at $x \notin X_1$, so $N(f(x)) = \infty$ ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · StrongBundle.not_auxLe_of_not_mem_levelSet⟧, and (2) applies. The reflexive local compactness property is not used, and (2) needs only continuity of $f$. In other words, $\{x \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ is closed ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · StrongBundle.isClosed_setOf_auxLe⟧.

**The remark after Proposition 5.2.7** (stronger) ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · StrongBundle.closure_auxLe_subset⟧: the closure of $\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ lies in $\{x \in \operatorname{cl}_XU \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$, for every $U$ and no compactness assumption, since the second set is closed. The text prints $\{x \in X \mid \dots\}$ in the closure; presumably $x \in U$, which is what the argument above it uses.
