### V.53 Theorem 5.2.8 (2017: 5.4; not in the preprint) and Remarks 5.2.9, 5.2.10 (2017: 5.1, 5.2)

**Theorem 5.2.8** (stronger) ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · theorem_5_2_8⟧. Hypotheses as in the text: $X$ tame, reflexive $(0, 1)$-fibres, $f$ sc-Fredholm with compact solution set $S$ and the reflexive local compactness property, $N$ a reflexive auxiliary norm, and $U_\partial$ an open neighbourhood of $S_\partial = S \cap \partial X$ in $\partial X$ with $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U_\partial \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact; "open in $\partial X$" is read as $U_\partial = W \cap \partial X$ with $W$ open. Conclusion: an open $U \supseteq S$ with $U \cap \partial X = U_\partial$ and $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact. Tameness and the sc-Fredholm property are not used; the theorem holds for every continuous section of a strong bundle with reflexive fibres over any M-polyfold ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · theorem_5_2_8_of_continuous⟧. *Step 1, the boundary part.* Finitely many $U(\bar x_1), \dots, U(\bar x_\ell)$ of Definition 5.2.6 cover the compact $\operatorname{cl}\{x \in U_\partial \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$; with the open set $\{N \circ f > 1\}$ (§V.52) they form $\tilde U$, which contains $U_\partial$. *Step 2, the interior part.* $S \setminus \tilde U$ is compact and misses $\partial X$; finitely many $U(x) \setminus \partial X$ cover it, and their union with $\tilde U$ is an open $U'$. *Step 3, compactness.* $\{x \in U' \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ lies in the finite union of the compact sets $\operatorname{cl}\{q \in U(x_i) \mid N(f(q)) \le 1\}$, because on $\{N \circ f > 1\}$ there is nothing to add. *Step 4, the boundary.* $U = U' \cap (W \cup (X \setminus \partial X))$ contains $S$, has $U \cap \partial X = U_\partial$, and its controlled set is a closed subset of the compact union. Witness for all hypotheses at once: the trivial bundle $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^n$ with the section $\mathrm{id}$ (solution set $\{0\}$, $U_\partial = \emptyset$) ⟦Chapter5/P3R_ReflexiveCompactness2021 · TrivialBundle.theorem_5_2_8_witness⟧.

**Remark 5.2.9** restates Theorem 5.2.8 in words: if $(U_\partial, N)$ controls compactness on the boundary, some $(U, N)$ with $U \cap \partial X = U_\partial$ controls it on $X$. **Remark 5.2.10**, that the theorem is crucial for inductive perturbation arguments, has no mathematical content to formalize.

### V.54 Definition 5.4.1 (2017: 5.11; not in the preprint): sc⁺-sections over the boundary

**Definition 5.4.1** (restated) ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.IsBoundaryScPlusSection⟧: a section $s$ of $W|\partial X \to \partial X$ is an sc⁺-section over $\partial X$ if its restrictions to the local faces at every $x \in \partial X$ are sc⁺-sections. Read chart-wise: on $\partial X$, $s$ is a section with values in $W_{0,1}$, and for every tame strong bundle chart $\Phi$ around $x$, every tame presentation $T$ of the corner of its model and every $i \in I(\varphi(x))$, the local representative $\Phi[1] \circ s \circ \varphi^{-1}$ restricted to the face germ $O \cap \{t_i = 0\}$ at $\varphi(x)$ is an sc⁺-section of $K \to O$ near $\varphi(x)$ (Part XII, §XII.8). That $s(x) \in W_{0,1}$ is stated outright, so that $N(s(x))$ in Theorem 5.4.2 is defined at every boundary point. The definition quantifies over all tame charts and presentations; its witness is the zero section, for every strong bundle ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.isBoundaryScPlusSection_fiberZero⟧. The text's $\operatorname{supp}(s)$ is the closure of $\{x \in \partial X \mid s(x) \ne 0_x\}$ ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.boundarySupport⟧.

### V.55 Theorem 5.4.2 (2017: 5.9; not in the preprint): the ∂-extension theorem

**Theorem 5.4.2** ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · theorem_5_4_2⟧. Let $P : W \to X$ be a strong bundle over a tame M-polyfold admitting sc-smooth partitions of unity, $s$ an sc⁺-section over $\partial X$, $N$ an auxiliary norm, $\tilde U$ an open neighbourhood of $\operatorname{supp}(s)$, and $f : X \to [0, \infty)$ continuous, supported in $\tilde U$, with $N(s(x)) < f(x)$ on $\operatorname{supp}(s)$. Then there is an sc⁺-section $\tilde s$ with (1) $N(\tilde s) \le f$, (2) $\operatorname{supp}(\tilde s) \subset \tilde U$, (3) $\tilde s|\partial X = s$. The text gives a sketch: Proposition 12.3.7 locally, glued by a partition of unity. "Strong bundle over a tame M-polyfold" is the project's tame strong bundle, whose base is tame and every point of which lies in a tame strong bundle chart; this fixes the spaces in the lowest universe, and the core below takes only the chart hypothesis. *Step 1, the local step* ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.exists_local_extension⟧. At $x \in \partial X$, in a tame chart, Proposition 12.3.7 (Part XII, §XII.8) extends the local representative of $s$ near $\varphi(x)$; a boundary point of $X$ is a boundary point of the model ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.degIndex_ne_zero_of_mem_boundary⟧. Cut off by a bump function equal to $1$ near $x$ (Proposition 5.5.3 (preprint 5.30)), the extension becomes a global sc⁺-section agreeing with $s$ on $\partial X$ near $x$, by the locality of sc⁺ ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.isScPlusSection_of_locally_p3b⟧. *Step 2, local bounds* ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.exists_local_bounded⟧. Every $x$ has an open $U \ni x$ and an sc⁺-section $\sigma$ with $N(\sigma) \le f$ on $U$ and $\sigma = s$ on $\partial X \cap U$. At $x \in \operatorname{supp}(s)$, $\sigma$ is the local extension, and $N(\sigma) < f$ near $x$ by continuity of $N \circ \sigma$ and of $f$. Elsewhere $\sigma = 0$ ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.aux_fiberZero⟧: off $\partial X$, and on $\partial X \setminus \operatorname{supp}(s)$, where $s$ vanishes on a neighbourhood. *Step 3, gluing* ⟦Chapter5/P3B_BoundaryExtension2021 · StrongBundle.exists_boundary_extension⟧. With an sc-smooth partition of unity $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to these $U_i$, $\tilde s = \sum_i\rho_i\sigma_i$ is sc⁺ by locality; $N(\tilde s) \le \sum_i\rho_iN(\sigma_i) \le f$ by the triangle inequality and homogeneity of $N$; on $\partial X$, $\tilde s = \sum_i\rho_is = s$ since $\sum_i\rho_i = 1$. (2) follows from (1): where $f = 0$, $N(\tilde s) = 0$, so $\operatorname{supp}(\tilde s) \subset \operatorname{supp}(f) \subset \tilde U$. That $\tilde U$ is open and contains $\operatorname{supp}(s)$ is kept from the text and not used.

## Part VI. Linearizations, orientations and invariants (HWZ Chapter 6, §§6.2–6.8 (preprint §§6.1–6.7))

Chapter 6 builds the orientation theory of sc-Fredholm sections and, at its end, the invariant of oriented proper sections. At a smooth point $x$ it collects the linearizations of $f$ into a convex set $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ of Fredholm operators (§6.2 (preprint §6.1)); it fixes the conventions for determinant lines and for the isomorphism attached to a four-term exact sequence (§6.3 (preprint §6.2)); it defines the determinant $\det(T) = \lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda^*(\operatorname{coker}T)$ of a Fredholm operator, compares it with the determinants of $PT$ for good left-projections $P$ and of the stabilizations $T_\varphi$, and builds the determinant line bundle $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ over the Fredholm operators (§§6.4–6.5 (preprint §§6.3–6.4)); it then restricts that bundle to $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, propagates its orientations along sc-smooth paths of $X$, first in small neighbourhoods (Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35)) and then globally, as a functor on the path category (Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37)), puts a topology on the orientation space (Theorem 6.6.17, new in 2021), and defines orientability and orientations of $f$, orients the solution set (Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41)) and the sections $f + s$ over $X \times [0, 1]$ (Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42)) (§6.6 (preprint §6.5)); §6.7 (preprint §6.6) defines the admissible perturbations and the invariant $\Psi_{(f,o)} : H^*_{dR}(X, \partial X) \to \mathbb R$ and proves that it is well defined and invariant under proper oriented homotopies (Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43)); and the appendix §6.8 (preprint §6.7) proves Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) and Proposition 6.4.11 (preprint 6.12). This Part retells §6.2 (preprint §6.1) (§VI.1); §6.3 (preprint §6.2) — determinant lines, Definition 6.3.1 (preprint 6.3) and Proposition 6.3.2 (preprint 6.4), the isomorphism $\Phi_E$, Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) and Proposition 6.3.5 (preprint 6.6) (§§VI.2–VI.3); §6.6 (preprint §6.5) — orientations over $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ (§VI.9), Proposition 6.6.3 (preprint 6.28) (§VI.10), Lemmas 6.6.4–6.6.6 (preprint 6.29–6.31) (§§VI.11–VI.13), the push-forward (§§VI.14–VI.15), Lemma 6.6.8 (preprint 6.33), Lemma 6.6.10 (preprint 6.34) and Proposition 6.6.7 (preprint 6.32) (§§VI.16–VI.17), Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35) and Definition 6.6.12 (preprint 6.36) (§§VI.18–VI.19), the path category (§VI.20), the comparison of charts (§VI.21), the transport and Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37) (§§VI.22–VI.23), Definitions 6.6.14–6.6.16 (preprint 6.38–6.40) (§VI.24), Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41) (§VI.25) and Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42) (§VI.26); **What is proved, and what is not.** *Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43) is proved, with the hypotheses of the text only* — $X$ tame with sc-smooth bump functions — and so is the case $\partial X = \emptyset$ after it (§VI.27; rows V6.76, V6.77 restated; gaps G.54, G.55 closed). The proof follows the text's: one admissible perturbation defines $\Psi$, Stokes' theorem makes it a map on cohomology, and a cobordism $S_F$ over $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ compares two perturbations and two ends of a homotopy; the decomposition of $\partial S_F$ is replaced by a cut-off in time. Theorems 6.6.11, 6.6.13, 6.6.17 and 6.6.18 (preprint 6.35, 6.37, —, 6.41) are proved, the last three with the text's hypotheses (§§VI.18, VI.23, VI.33, VI.25); Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41) in the book's shape, the solution set a compact Mathlib manifold with boundary and corners carrying a continuous tangent orientation which is the Fredholm one, read compatibly in any two charts, and the paragraph after it on perturbed solution sets (gaps G.67–G.69 closed). Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42) gives an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.6.16 (preprint 6.40), the 2021 convention $e$ first, with no sign (§VI.26; gap G.66 closed). Proved besides: Propositions 6.3.2, 6.3.5, 6.4.10, 6.4.11, 6.4.13, 6.4.15, 6.5.4, 6.5.7, 6.5.8, 6.6.1, 6.6.7 (preprint 6.4, 6.6, Lemma 6.11, 6.12, —, 6.15, 6.20, 6.23, 6.24, 6.26, 6.32), Lemmas 6.3.3, 6.4.4, 6.4.14, 6.5.1, 6.5.2, 6.5.5, 6.5.9, 6.6.6, 6.6.8–6.6.9, 6.6.10 (preprint 6.5, —, 6.14, 6.17, 6.18, 6.21, 6.25, 6.31, 6.33, 6.34) and Lemma 6.10 (preprint), Corollary 6.4.12 (preprint 6.13), Lemma 6.5.3 (preprint 6.19) for general topological vector bundles (§VI.35; G.59 closed), Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29) with property (P) for the slices and Lemma 6.6.5 (preprint 6.30) as a statement about manifolds, with $\pi$ a submersion and $L$ a smooth vector bundle (§VI.36; G.62, G.63 closed), Proposition 6.6.3 (preprint 6.28) with (1) as printed in 2021 and with (1′), on $\mathbb R$ and on $[0, 1]$ (§VI.10; G.61 closed), the equivalence of Definitions 6.6.14 and 6.6.15 (preprint 6.38 and 6.39), the sc-Fredholm property of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ on every level (§VI.1; G.64 closed), the facts on paths recalled before Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) (§VI.37; G.56 closed), the alternative determinant and the identification (6.25) (preprint (95)) (§VI.34; G.57, G.58 closed), Proposition 6.4.13, last sentence (§VI.33; G.81 closed), property (2) of Theorem 6.6.17 without further hypotheses (§VI.33; G.90 closed), the orientation bundle, the $\mathbb Z_2$-action and $\det_f$ after it (§VI.38; G.91 closed), and the classical determinant bundle at the opening of §6.6 (§VI.34). Every definition of the chapter is formalized. **Gaps:** G.54–G.64, G.66–G.69, G.81, G.90, G.91 closed (G.61 since 2026-11-13, with Proposition 6.6.3 (1) in its 2021 wording); G.65 (paths and families on $[0, 1]$) in part; no gap is open. **Narrower rows**, with their reasons: V6.48, Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35) — the statement does not introduce the section $f$ (presumably an omission; it is read for an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data), and $U$ is not shown contractible in itself, the preprint's (1); the 2021 form of (1), a smaller $U'$ contractible in $U$, is proved, and (1′) is what the proof uses; V6.80, the remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable — it does not hold as we read it for finite-dimensional $E$, $F$ (Lean counterexample `exists_two_lineOrientation_det_of_finiteDimensional`) and is proved for infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and under complex structures, not for all Banach spaces; V6.81, the classical case — $C^1$ maps in place of smooth ones, and a topological, not smooth, line bundle. Several places needed more than a reading. The projection of the proof of Lemma 6.10 (preprint) does not lie below the two given projections as we read it, and the lemma is proved by another construction (§VI.4). The isomorphism $\Phi_E$ of formula (94) does not vary continuously in the topology of $\mathrm{DET}$ where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ changes parity, as we read it, so the propagation uses $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}T}\Phi_E$ (§VI.14). Proposition 6.6.3 (1) is proved in its 2021 wording, a smaller $U'$ contractible in $U$; the preprint's "$U$ is sc-smoothly contractible" is not established by its proof as we read it, and the proofs use (1′) (§§VI.10, VI.18). The form $\bar\omega = p_1^*\omega \wedge p_2^*dt$ of the proof of Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43) has one degree too many for the comparison, as we read it, and $p_1^*\omega$ is used (§VI.27). Seven proofs the text omits are supplied: the orientability of a line bundle over a convex set (§VI.9), the general position of Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29) (§VI.11), the "simple computation" of Lemma 6.6.8 (preprint 6.33) (§VI.16), the covering argument of Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37) (§VI.22), the equivalence of Definitions 6.6.14 and 6.6.15 (preprint 6.38 and 6.39) (§VI.24), the construction of the topology of Theorem 6.6.17 (§VI.33), and the orientation of the cobordism on its ends in Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43) (§VI.27).

**Six structural choices.** (1) *Chart points.* $T_xX$ carries no linear structure in the formalization (gaps G.6, G.7, G.13 of Chapter 2), so $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ are made at a *chart point* $(c, z)$ of $x$, with operators $T_zO = Dr(z)E \to K_z = \rho(z)F$ on level $0$, and they are identified between charts by explicit transition maps (§VI.21); the text's $f - s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$ is $f + s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$. (2) *Global sections, from bump functions.* The text assumes sc-smooth partitions of unity from §6.3 (preprint §6.2) on, "to simplify the presentation" (p. 241 (preprint p. 203)). The formalization assumes sc-smooth bump functions, which partitions of unity give (§V.25), and uses them only to make global sc⁺-sections (Findings, Chapter 6, item 43); Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43) assumes them in its statement. (3) *Families on $\mathbb R^n$, and on $[0, 1]^n$.* Paths, homotopies and families are first sc-smooth maps on $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^n$ whose conditions are imposed on $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$, and $X \times [0, 1]$ is read as $\mathbb R^n \times X$ with the pull-back $\pi^*P$ of the bundle along the projection, the parameter first (decision D2, as for Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) in §III.49; Findings, Chapter 6, item 102). Most of these statements now also hold as printed, on the M-polyfolds $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n \times X$ (§VI.37); what is still read on $\mathbb R$ is listed in gap G.65 (§VI.30). The cobordism of Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43) lives over $\mathbb R^1 \times X$. (4) *The sign $\alpha(T) = (-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}T}$* at both end points of every propagation (§VI.14). (5) *(1′), and orientable neighbourhoods as pairs $V \subseteq U$*, since what the proofs use of Proposition 6.6.3 (preprint 6.28) is (1′) rather than contractibility (§§VI.10, VI.19). (6) *Dyadic subdivisions* in place of the finite coverings of the proof of Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37) (§VI.22). An orientation of a line is a ray (Mathlib's `Module.Ray`); an orientation of a topological line bundle is a choice of rays given near every point by a continuous nowhere-zero section; an orientation of a Mathlib manifold is a continuous tangent orientation (§VI.25).

Throughout, $E$ and $F$ are real Banach spaces, $T : E \to F$ is bounded, $R(T)$ is its range and $\operatorname{coker}T = F/R(T)$; $T$ is Fredholm if $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{coker}T$ are finite-dimensional, with index $\dim\ker T - \dim\operatorname{coker}T$. A *line* is a one-dimensional real space. $P : Y \to X$ is a strong bundle over an M-polyfold, both paracompact and Hausdorff, and from §VI.10 on $X$ is tame with sc-smooth bump functions and $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (Definition 3.6.4 (preprint 3.51)), the reading of Chapter 5 (Part V). A strong bundle chart $c$ has base chart $\varphi$, retraction $r$ on an open set $U$ of a partial quadrant $C$, retract $O = r(U)$, and fibre projections $\rho(u)$; the *principal part* of a section is its fibre coordinate in the chart. $\mathbb R^1$ is the M-polyfold of the parameter $t$, with $t$ the point of $\mathbb R^1$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · pt1⟧, and $(\tau, t)$ the point of $\mathbb R^2$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · pt2⟧; $\kappa$ is Mathlib's smooth transition function, $0$ on $(-\infty, 0]$, $1$ on $[1, \infty)$.

### VI.1 Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1): the space $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$

§6.2 (preprint §6.1) (pp. 237–240 (preprint pp. 200–201)) works at a smooth point $x$. Since $f(x)$ is a smooth point of the fibre, there is an sc⁺-section $s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$ — in a chart, $s(y) = R(y, f(x))$ — and $(f - s)'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is sc-Fredholm. Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1) collects these linearizations, perturbed by sc⁺-operators, into $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$; the index is the index of any member, and Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) says that it is constant along sc-smooth paths.

**The chart point** (V6.1). A chart point of $x$ is a strong bundle chart $c$ of the atlas whose base chart contains $x$, with the level-$1$ point $z$ of the model over $\varphi(x)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint⟧. In it $T_xX$ is $T_zO = Dr(z)E$, the range of the derivative of the retraction ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.T⟧, and $Y_x$ is $K_z = \rho(z)F$, the range of the fibre projection over $z$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.K⟧; both are closed, as ranges of continuous projections, hence Banach spaces. An sc⁺-operator $T_xX \to Y_x$ is level $0$ of an sc⁺-operator between these sc-subspaces ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.IsScPlusOp⟧.

**Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1)** (V6.1). $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, at the chart point $p$, is the set of the operators $(f + s)'(x) + a : T_zO \to K_z$ for an sc⁺-section $s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$ and an sc⁺-operator $a$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.mem_linSet_iff⟧. The linearization of $f + s$ at its zero $x$ is the derivative at $z$ of the principal part composed with $r$, restricted to $T_zO$ — the $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ of Part III. Replacing the text's $s$ by $-s$ turns $f - s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$ into $f + s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$.

**Two sections differ by an sc⁺-operator.** For two sections $s$, $t$ with $(f + s)(x) = (f + t)(x) = 0$, the principal parts of $f + s$ and $f + t$ differ by that of the sc⁺-section $s - t$, whose derivative at $z$, followed by $\rho(z)$, is level $0$ of an sc⁺-operator: the derivative of an sc⁺-map is sc⁺ on the shifted levels. So $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is $(f + s)'(x)$ plus all the sc⁺-operators, for any one $s$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.exists_isScPlusOp_linAt_eq⟧, and two members differ by an sc⁺-operator ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.isScPlusOp_sub_of_mem_linSet⟧. The paragraph before the definition puts this as "$(f - s)'(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm operator if and only if $(f - s)'(x)$ is"; it is read with $(f - t)'(x)$ in the second place (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 41).

**Not empty.** The text makes its section locally, in a chart. The formalization uses global sc⁺-sections: $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is not empty when $P$ has sc⁺-sections through the smooth points of its fibres, one through $-f(x)$ giving a member ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet_nonempty⟧, and bump functions give such sections ⟦Chapter3/IndexLocallyConstantLocal · MPolyfold.AdmitsBumpFunctions.hasScPlusSectionsThrough⟧. This is the hidden hypothesis of the definition: an sc⁺-section through $f(x)$.

**Fredholm, of one index.** Every member is Fredholm on level $0$, with the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ of the germ at $x$ (§III.49) ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.isFredholm_isIndexAt_of_mem_linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.exists_index_linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.fredholmIndex_of_mem_linSet⟧. The proof: $f + s$ has germ data at $x$ (an sc-Fredholm germ plus an sc⁺-germ is one), so its linearization at the zero $x$ is Fredholm of the index of the germ, through the conjugation to a basic germ (Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52), §III.30); adding an sc⁺-operator, compact on level $0$, keeps the Fredholm property and the index; and the index of the germ does not depend on the choices. *The members are sc-Fredholm on every level*, as the text says, all of one index ⟦Chapter6/LinSetFredholm · ChartPoint.exists_isScFredholm_of_mem_linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSetFredholm · ChartPoint.definition_6_2_1_linSet_isScFredholm⟧: for $L = (f + s)'(x) + a$, the section $f + s$ is sc-Fredholm with a zero at $x$, so its linearization $T_zO 	o K_z$ is sc-Fredholm, between these sc-subspaces with their induced sc-structures (row V3.96); $a$ is level $0$ of an sc⁺-operator; and an sc-Fredholm operator plus an sc⁺-operator is sc-Fredholm of the same index on every level (Proposition 1.1.11). The level-$0$ operator is $L$, so the indices agree. The determinant lines use level $0$ only (gap G.64 closed; Findings, Chapter 6, items 40, 122).

**Convex** ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.convex_linSet⟧. $(1 - \tau)(L + a) + \tau(L + b) = L + ((1 - \tau)a + \tau b)$, and the sc⁺-operators form a vector space. The text notes this on preprint p. 219, where Proposition 6.6.1 (preprint 6.26) needs it.

**Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2)** (V3.98). The constancy of the index along sc-smooth paths was formalized with Chapter 3 and is retold in §III.49: for paths on $\mathbb R$, with the text's hypotheses — tame germ data, no bump functions, the locally defined sc⁺-sections of Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1). It is not repeated here. The facts on paths recalled before it on preprint p. 201 — an M-polyfold is locally path connected, and two smooth points in one path component are joined by an sc⁺-smooth path — are formalized, with paths on $[0, 1]$ (§VI.37; gap G.56 closed; Findings, Chapter 6, items 42, 124).

### VI.2 Determinant lines, Definition 6.3.1 (preprint 6.3), Proposition 6.3.2 (preprint 6.4)

**$\lambda(E)$ and $\lambda^*(E)$** (V6.2). For a finite-dimensional real space $E$, $\lambda(E) = \Lambda^{\max}E$ is the top exterior power ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPow⟧ and $\lambda^*(E)$ its dual ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowDual⟧; both are lines ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · finrank_maxPow⟧, $\lambda(\{0\}) = \mathbb R$ being the zeroth exterior power. A family $a_1, \dots, a_n$ with $n = \dim E$ has its wedge $a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge⟧. Two rules carry every computation of the chapter. A change of basis multiplies the wedge by its determinant ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_eq_det_smul⟧, also when only one block of a two-block wedge $a \wedge b$ is changed ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_basis_left⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_basis_right⟧; and adding to the vectors of one block vectors of the span of the other does not change the wedge ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_add_left⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_add_right⟧. For $v \ne 0$ in a line, $v^*$ is the functional with $v^*(v) = 1$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · dualVec⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · dualVec_self⟧, and that value determines it ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · eq_dualVec_of_apply_eq_one⟧. For $\dim E = \dim F$ and $\Phi : E \to F$, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi a_n$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap_wedge⟧, with $\lambda(\Psi\Phi) = \lambda(\Psi)\lambda(\Phi)$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap_comp⟧, and $\lambda(\Phi) \ne 0$ iff $\Phi$ is bijective ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap_ne_zero_iff⟧; $\lambda^*(\Phi)$ is its dual ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowDualMap⟧ (pp. 241–243 (preprint pp. 203–204)).

**Definition 6.3.1 (preprint 6.3)** (V6.3). $\iota : \lambda(E^*) \to \lambda^*(E)$ is $\iota(e_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge e_n^*)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \det(e_i^*(a_j))$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual_wedge_wedge⟧. The formula is alternating and multilinear in both families, so it descends to the exterior powers; that is the text's well-definedness. $\iota$ is a nonzero map of lines ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual_ne_zero⟧, and for a basis with its dual basis $\iota(e_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge e_n^*) = (e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual_wedge_dualBasis⟧, since the matrix is the identity. The text's matrix $(e_i^*(a_j))$ is the transpose of the one of Mathlib's pairing, with the same determinant (preprint p. 204).

**Proposition 6.3.2 (preprint 6.4)** (V6.4) ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · proposition_6_3_2⟧. For an isomorphism $\Phi : E \to F$, $\lambda^*(\Phi) \circ \iota = \iota \circ \lambda(\Phi^*)$. Both sides, evaluated at $f_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge f_n^*$ and $a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n$, give $\det(f_i^*(\Phi a_j))$: the left side by the definition of $\lambda^*(\Phi)$, the right side because $(\Phi^*f_i^*)(a_j) = f_i^*(\Phi a_j)$ (p. 243 (preprint p. 205)).

### VI.3 Four-term exact sequences: $\Phi_E$, Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5), Proposition 6.3.5 (preprint 6.6)

**The data of (91)** (V6.5). Let $\mathbf E : 0 \to A \xrightarrow{\alpha} B \xrightarrow{\beta} C \xrightarrow{\gamma} D \to 0$ be an exact sequence of finite-dimensional spaces ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact⟧. A *choice* ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice⟧ consists of a complement $Z$ of $\alpha(A)$ in $B$, a complement $V$ of $\beta(B)$ in $C$, bases $a$ of $A$, $d$ of $D$, $b'$ of $Z$, and the $\gamma$-preimages $c$ in $V$ of the basis $d$. Then $\alpha(a), b'$ is a basis of $B$, and $c, \beta(b')$ is one of $C$, because $\beta$ maps $Z$ isomorphically onto $\beta(B)$ and $\gamma$ maps $V$ isomorphically onto $D$. Formula (91) assigns to the choice the value $(\alpha(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \alpha(a_n) \wedge b'_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b'_{m-n}) \otimes (c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_l \wedge \beta(b'_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \beta(b'_{m-n}))^*$ as the image of $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_l)^*$, with the text's two ordering conventions ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice.value⟧. $\Phi_E : \lambda(A) \otimes \lambda^*(D) \to \lambda(B) \otimes \lambda^*(C)$ is the linear map of lines defined by one fixed choice ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.canonicalChoice⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.phi⟧; it is nonzero ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.phi_ne_zero⟧, hence an isomorphism ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.phiEquiv⟧ (preprint p. 206).

**Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5)** (V6.6) ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.lemma_6_3_3⟧. The text: $\Phi_E$ does not depend on the choices. The formalization proves the strongest form: $\Phi_E$, defined from one choice, maps the source element $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_l)^*$ of *any other* choice to the right-hand side of (91) computed with that choice. This is the form every later computation uses — $\gamma^P_T$ is always evaluated in bases adapted to the problem at hand (Findings, Chapter 6, item 1). The proof is §6.8.1 (preprint §6.7.1) (§VI.28).

**Proposition 6.3.5 (preprint 6.6)** (V6.7). With the contraction $\bar\iota(v \otimes b \otimes \varphi) = \varphi(v)\,b$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · contractDual⟧, (92) defines $\Psi_E(c \otimes h) = \bar\iota(c \otimes \Phi_E(h))$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.psi⟧. The proposition ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.proposition_6_3_5⟧: $\Psi_E$ maps the wedge of the basis $c, \beta(b')$ of $C$, tensored with $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_l)^*$, to $\alpha(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \alpha(a_n) \wedge b'_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b'_{m-n}$. By Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) in its strong form, $\Phi_E$ of the source is the value of (91) for this choice, and the dual wedge evaluated on the wedge is $1$. The wedge in $C$ is taken in the order of (91); the statement exchanges the names of its two blocks (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 2) (preprint p. 207).

### VI.4 Determinants of Fredholm operators, good left-projections, and Lemma 6.10 (preprint)

**Definition 6.4.1 (preprint 6.7)** (V6.8). $\det(T) = \lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda^*(F/R(T))$ ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · linDet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · fredholmDet⟧, a line for $T$ Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · finrank_fredholmDet⟧. Equal operators have identified determinants ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · linDetEquivOfEq⟧: $PQT$ and $PT$ are the same operator when $P \le Q$, but not the same expression, and Proposition 6.4.11 (preprint 6.12) compares their determinants. The alternative definition $\lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$ mentioned after the definition is naturally isomorphic to $\det(T)$ through $\iota$ (§VI.34; gap G.57 closed) (preprint p. 208).

**Definition 6.4.2 (preprint 6.8)** (V6.9). An orientation of $T$ is a ray of $\det(T)$ ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · FredholmOrientation⟧; there is one ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · nonempty_fredholmOrientation⟧, and exactly two ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · exists_two_fredholmOrientation⟧ (preprint p. 208).

**Definition 6.4.3 (preprint 6.9) and the facts after it** (V6.10). A *good left-projection* for $T$ is a bounded projection $P : F \to F$ with $\dim F/R(P) < \infty$ and $R(PT) = R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj⟧; $\Pi_T$ is their set ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · goodLeftProjs⟧. $P \le Q$ iff $P = PQ = QP$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE⟧, a partial order ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE.refl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE.antisymm⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE.trans⟧. A good left-projection is Fredholm of index $0$ — $\ker P$ is a complement of $R(P)$, of dimension $\dim F/R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.isFredholm⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.fredholmIndex_eq_zero⟧ — so $PT$ is Fredholm with $\mathrm{ind}(PT) = \mathrm{ind}(T)$ when $T$ is, by the index of a composite ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.isFredholm_comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.fredholmIndex_comp⟧. For $P, P' \in \Pi_T$, $R(P) \cap R(P')$ has finite codimension ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.finiteDimensional_quotient_inf⟧. And $\Pi_T \ne \emptyset$ for $T$ Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · exists_isGoodLeftProj⟧ — the projection onto $R(T)$ along a finite-dimensional complement is one — which the text uses from Proposition 6.4.10 (preprint Lemma 6.11) on without stating it (Findings, Chapter 6, item 3) (preprint p. 208).

**Lemma 6.10 (preprint)** (V6.11) ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · lemma_6_10_preprint⟧. *For $P, P' \in \Pi_T$ there is $P'' \in \Pi_T$ with $P'' \le P$ and $P'' \le P'$*, for any bounded $T$. The text's $P''$ projects onto $R(P) \cap R(P')$ along a complement assembled from $\ker P$, $\ker P'$ and a further piece, and $P'' = P''P$ needs $\ker P \subseteq \ker P''$. As we read it, this does not hold in general: on $\mathbb R^2$ with $T = 1$, let $P$ project onto the $x$-axis along the $y$-axis and $P'$ along the diagonal; $R(P) \cap R(P')$ is the $x$-axis, and a projection onto it below both would equal both ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · lemma_6_10_text_reading_preprint⟧. The lemma holds with a smaller range. *Step 1.* $K = \ker P + \ker P'$ is finite-dimensional, each kernel having the dimension of a finite-dimensional quotient. *Step 2.* $K$ has a closed complement $N$ (finite-dimensional subspaces are complemented, by Hahn–Banach), and $R'' = R(P) \cap R(P') \cap N$ is closed, of finite codimension, and meets $K$ only in $0$. *Step 3.* $R''$ has a complement $C \supseteq K$, topological because the quotient by $R''$ is finite-dimensional; $P''$ is the projection onto $R''$ along $C$. *Step 4.* $\ker P \subseteq C = \ker P''$ gives $P''P = P''$, and $R'' \subseteq R(P)$ gives $PP'' = P''$; the same for $P'$. *Step 5.* $R(P''T) = P''(R(PT)) = P''(R(P)) = R''$, since $P''$ is the identity on $R'' \subseteq R(P)$. Nothing uses that $T$ is Fredholm. The 2017 version drops the lemma and remarks that a common lower bound need not exist; with the order of Definition 6.4.3 (preprint 6.9), used by both versions, it always exists, as we read it, so the preprint's route to Lemma 6.5.9 (preprint 6.25) is sound and is the one formalized (Findings, Chapter 6, item 4) (preprint pp. 208–209).

### VI.5 Proposition 6.4.10 (preprint Lemma 6.11), $\gamma^P_T$, Proposition 6.4.11 (preprint 6.12) and Corollary 6.4.12 (preprint 6.13)

**Proposition 6.4.10 (preprint Lemma 6.11)** (V6.12). For $P \in \Pi_T$, the sequence $\mathbf E(T, P) : 0 \to \ker T \to \ker(PT) \to F/R(P) \to \operatorname{coker}T \to 0$, with the inclusion ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqJ⟧, $x \mapsto Tx + R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqPhi⟧ and $y + R(P) \mapsto (I - P)y + R(T)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqPi⟧, is exact ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · proposition_6_4_10⟧, a four-term exact sequence of §VI.3 ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeq⟧. The four checks use only $P^2 = P$ and $R(PT) = R(P)$. At $\ker(PT)$: if $PTx = 0$ and $Tx \in R(P)$, then $Tx \in R(P) \cap \ker P = 0$. At $F/R(P)$: the last map is well defined because $(I - P)R(P) = 0$; it kills $[Tx]$ for $x \in \ker(PT)$, since $(I - P)Tx = Tx$; and if $(I - P)y = Tx$, then $PTx = 0$ and $y - Tx = Py \in R(P)$. Onto: $Py = PTe$ for some $e$, and then $(I - P)(y - Te) = y - Te$, which has the class of $y$ in $\operatorname{coker}T$ (preprint p. 209).

**The isomorphism $\gamma^P_T$** (V6.13). $\gamma^P_T : \det(T) \to \det(PT)$ is $\Phi_{\mathbf E(T,P)}$ followed by the identification of $\lambda^*(F/R(P))$ with $\lambda^*(F/R(PT))$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj_tmul⟧ — the text's "recalling $R(P) = R(PT)$" (Findings, Chapter 6, item 5). By Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) it is given on wedges by (91) for any choice ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj_wedge_tmul⟧ (preprint p. 210).

**Proposition 6.4.11 (preprint 6.12)** (V6.14). *For $P \le Q$ in $\Pi_T$, $QT$ is Fredholm, $P \in \Pi_{QT}$, and $\gamma^P_{QT} \circ \gamma^Q_T = \gamma^P_T$*, up to the identification of $\det(P(QT))$ with $\det(PT)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · proposition_6_4_11⟧. $P \in \Pi_{QT}$ because $R(PQT) = R(PT) = R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · IsGoodLeftProj.of_projLE⟧. The identity is a computation in adapted bases ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · comp_comp_eq_of_projLE⟧, the proof of §6.8.2 (preprint §6.7.2), retold in §VI.29 (preprint p. 211).

**Corollary 6.4.12 (preprint 6.13)** (V6.15) ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · corollary_6_4_12⟧. For $P \le S$ and $P \le R$ in $\Pi_T$, $(\gamma^P_{RT})^{-1} \circ \gamma^P_{ST} = \gamma^R_T \circ (\gamma^S_T)^{-1}$. Proposition 6.4.11 (preprint 6.12) twice gives $\gamma^P_{ST}\gamma^S_T = \gamma^P_T = \gamma^P_{RT}\gamma^R_T$; rearranging gives the claim. So the left side, the comparison of two local frames through a common lower bound, does not depend on the lower bound (preprint p. 211).

### VI.6 The stabilization: Lemma 6.4.14 (preprint 6.14), formula (94), Proposition 6.4.15 (preprint 6.15), Definition 6.4.16 (preprint 6.16)

**Lemma 6.4.14 (preprint 6.14)** (V6.16). For $T$ Fredholm and $\varphi : \mathbb R^n \to F$ with $T_\varphi(e, r) = Te + \varphi r$ onto, the sequence $0 \to \ker T \xrightarrow{j} \ker T_\varphi \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathbb R^n \xrightarrow{[\varphi]} F/R(T) \to 0$, with $j(e) = (e, 0)$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabJ⟧, $\pi(e, r) = r$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabPi⟧ and $[\varphi](r) = \varphi(r) + R(T)$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabClass⟧, is exact ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · lemma_6_4_14⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabSeq⟧. $j$ is injective; $\ker\pi \cap \ker T_\varphi$ is $\{(e, 0) \mid Te = 0\} = j(\ker T)$; for $(e, r) \in \ker T_\varphi$, $\varphi r = -Te \in R(T)$, and conversely $\varphi r = -Te$ puts $(e, r)$ in $\ker T_\varphi$; $[\varphi]$ is onto because $T_\varphi$ is. A stabilizing $\varphi$ exists for every Fredholm $T$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · exists_surjective_coprod⟧: send a basis of $\mathbb R^n$ to representatives of a basis of the cokernel. The proof writes $j(e) = (0, e)$, read as $(e, 0)$ (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 8) (pp. 251–256 (preprint pp. 211–212)).

**Formula (94)** (V6.17). $\psi : \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to \lambda^*(\{0\})$ maps $(e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n)^*$ to $1^*$ for the standard basis ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stdWedge⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabOne⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabPsi⟧. Then $\psi((c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n)^*) = \det[c_1, \dots, c_n]^{-1}\,1^*$ for every basis ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabPsi_dualVec⟧: $c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n = \det[c]\,e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n$, and the dual vectors scale inversely (p. 256 (preprint p. 212)).

**Proposition 6.4.15 (preprint 6.15)** (V6.18). Since $T_\varphi$ is onto, $\det(T_\varphi) = \lambda(\ker T_\varphi) \otimes \lambda^*(\{0\})$, and $\iota_\varphi = (1 \otimes \psi) \circ \Phi_{\mathbf E}$, for the sequence $\mathbf E$ of Lemma 6.4.14 (preprint 6.14), is an isomorphism $\det(T) \to \det(T_\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabIota⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabIota_bijective⟧. The formula ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · proposition_6_4_15⟧: for a basis $a$ of $\ker T$, vectors $\bar c_1, \dots, \bar c_m$ with $[\varphi](\bar c_i)$ a basis of $F/R(T)$, and $\bar b_i = (b_i, r_i)$ completing $(a, 0)$ to a basis of $\ker T_\varphi$, $\iota_\varphi(h) = \det(\bar c, r)^{-1}\,((a_1, 0) \wedge \dots \wedge (a_k, 0) \wedge \bar b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \bar b_l) \otimes 1^*$. These data are a choice of (91) for $\mathbf E$ — $Z$ the span of the $\bar b_i$, $V$ the span of the $\bar c_j$ — so Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) gives $\Phi_{\mathbf E}(h) = ((a, 0) \wedge \bar b) \otimes (\bar c \wedge r)^*$, and (94) turns the second factor into $\det(\bar c, r)^{-1}1^*$. To form $\det(\bar c, r)$ one needs $m + l = n$: the statement takes it as a hypothesis, and it is proved to hold always ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stab_card_eq⟧; that the $r_i$ and $\bar c_j$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^n$, which the text notices, is proved — the $r_i$ span $\pi(\ker T_\varphi) = \ker[\varphi]$, and the $\bar c_j$ a complement of it ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · isCompl_range_stabPi_span⟧. The statement calls $\psi$ "$\varphi$" (possible misprint). The identification (95) and the maps $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$, $V \otimes \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ after the proposition are formalized separately (§VI.34; gap G.58 closed); the statements here use only (94) (Findings, Chapter 6, items 9, 10) (preprint p. 213).

**Definition 6.4.16 (preprint 6.16)** (V6.19). For Fredholm $T$, $S$, the operator $T \oplus S$ has $\ker(T \oplus S) \cong \ker T \times \ker S$ and $\operatorname{coker}(T \oplus S) \cong \operatorname{coker}T \times \operatorname{coker}S$, through the inclusions of the factors ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · kerInl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · kerInr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · cokerInl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · cokerInr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · kerProdEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · cokerProdEquiv⟧; the dimensions add ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · finrank_ker_prodMap⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · finrank_coker_prodMap⟧, so $T \oplus S$ is Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · isFredholm_prodMap⟧. The map $\det(T) \otimes \det(S) \to \det(T \oplus S)$, $h \otimes h' \mapsto (a \wedge a') \otimes (d \wedge d')^*$, is defined by the formula in one choice of bases ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumVec⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumDet⟧, satisfies it for every choice ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumVec_eq_smul⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · definition_6_4_16⟧ — a change of bases multiplies source and target by the same product of determinants, the block wedges by the block determinants — and is an isomorphism ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumDet_bijective⟧. "Natural" is read as the formula for every choice, as in Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 11) (p. 258 (preprint p. 214)).

### VI.7 Local determinant bundles: Lemmas 6.5.1–6.5.3 (preprint 6.17–6.19), Proposition 6.5.4 (preprint 6.20), Lemma 6.5.5 (preprint 6.21)

**Lemma 6.5.1 (preprint 6.17)** (V6.20). The Fredholm operators form a subspace of $L(E, F)$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · FredholmOp⟧. *For a bounded $T$, $P \in \Pi_T$ and a topological complement $Y$ of $\ker(PT)$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for $\|S - T\| < \varepsilon$, $P \in \Pi_S$ and $PS|_Y : Y \to R(P)$ is a topological isomorphism* ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · lemma_6_5_1⟧. *Step 1.* $PT|_Y$ is injective, since $Y \cap \ker(PT) = 0$, and onto $R(P)$, since $PT(E) = PT(Y)$ and $R(PT) = R(P)$; as a bijection between the Banach spaces $Y$ and $R(P)$ (both closed) it is an isomorphism by the open mapping theorem. *Step 2.* $\|PS|_Y - PT|_Y\| \le \|P\|\,\|S - T\|$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · projRestrict⟧, and the invertible operators form an open set. *Step 3.* $R(PS) \supseteq PS(Y) = R(P)$, so $P \in \Pi_S$. That $T$ is Fredholm is not used (Findings, Chapter 6, item 20); a topological complement is an algebraic complement with a continuous projection (p. 258 (preprint p. 214)).

**Lemma 6.5.2 (preprint 6.18)** (V6.21). A *local determinant chart* is the data $(T, P, Y, \varepsilon)$ of Lemma 6.5.1 (preprint 6.17) with its conclusions ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart⟧. For $k \in \ker(PT)$, $y(k, S) = -(PS|_Y)^{-1}PSk$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.ySol⟧ is continuous in $(k, S)$, inversion being continuous, and $k + y(k, S) \in \ker(PS)$. The map $(S, k) \mapsto (S, k + y(k, S))$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.kerMap⟧ is onto $\bigcup_{\|S - T\| < \varepsilon}\{S\} \times \ker(PS)$, inverted by the continuous projection onto $\ker(PT)$ along $Y$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.kerProj⟧: for $w \in \ker(PS)$ write $w = k + y$ with $y \in Y$; then $PSy = -PSk$, so $y = y(k, S)$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.lemma_6_5_2⟧. "Is a trivial vector bundle" is stated as this trivialization and its inverse (Findings, Chapter 6, item 21) (preprint p. 215).

**Lemma 6.5.3 (preprint 6.19) and Proposition 6.5.4 (preprint 6.20)** (V6.22). For a basis $k$ of $\ker(PT)$, $k_i(S) = k_i + y(k_i, S)$ is a continuous frame of the kernels ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.kerFrame⟧, and with a constant basis $e$ of $F/R(P) = F/R(PS)$, $\omega(S) = (k_1(S) \wedge \dots \wedge k_n(S)) \otimes (e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_l)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.frame⟧ is a nowhere-zero frame ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.frame_ne_zero⟧ of $\mathrm{DET}(T, P, \varepsilon) = \bigcup_S\det(PS)$. The frames of two charts with the same $P$ differ by a continuous nowhere-zero factor ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · proposition_6_5_4⟧: the determinant of the matrix expressing one kernel frame in the other, continuous because both frames are continuous in $S$, times the constant change of the bases of $F/R(P)$. Lemma 6.5.3 (preprint 6.19) — exterior powers, duals, sums and tensor products of topological vector bundles — is applied here only to trivial bundles, and Proposition 6.5.4 (preprint 6.20) is proved with the explicit frames; the lemma in general is §VI.35 (gap G.59 closed); "in a natural way" is read as this relation between frames (Findings, Chapter 6, item 22) (preprint p. 216).

**Lemma 6.5.5 (preprint 6.21)** (V6.23). *For $Q \le P$, $\gamma^Q_{PS}$ maps the $P$-frame at $S$ to a continuous nowhere-zero multiple of the $Q$-frame, on the common ball of any two local determinant charts* ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.gammaProj_frame_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · lemma_6_5_5⟧. The text's sketch — extend the kernel sections of $PS$ to sections spanning $\ker(QS)$ — is the proof. For a basis $f_1, \dots$ of $R(P) \cap \ker Q$, $z_m(S) = (PS|_Y)^{-1}f_m$ is continuous and $PSz_m(S) = f_m$; the $k_i(S)$ and $z_m(S)$ span $\ker(QPS) = \ker(QS)$; and in the choice of (91) for $\mathbf E(PS, Q)$ these vectors go with the *constant* classes $[f_m]$. So $\gamma^Q_{PS}(\omega_P(S))$ is $(k(S) \wedge z(S)) \otimes (e \wedge [f])^*$, continuous in $S$, and its ratio to the $Q$-frame of the other chart is the determinant of a continuous change of basis. The lemma is stated for two charts with different centres and radii, the form Lemma 6.5.9 (preprint 6.25) uses (Findings, Chapter 6, item 23) (pp. 259–261 (preprint pp. 216–217)).

### VI.8 $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$: Definition 6.5.6 (preprint 6.22), Propositions 6.5.7 and 6.5.8 (preprint 6.23 and 6.24), Lemma 6.5.9 (preprint 6.25)

**The prebundle** (V6.24). The fibre over a Fredholm $S$ is $\det(S)$ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · DetFiber⟧. A local determinant chart gives the pretrivialization $(S, h) \mapsto (S, \omega(S)^*(\gamma^P_Sh))$ over its ball, with model fibre $\mathbb R$ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · LocalDetChart.pretriv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · LocalDetChart.coord⟧ — the text's $\gamma_{(T,P,\varepsilon)}$ read in the frame of Proposition 6.5.4 (preprint 6.20) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 24). Every Fredholm operator is the centre of one ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · exists_localDetChart⟧: $\Pi_T \ne \emptyset$ (§VI.4) and the finite-dimensional $\ker(PT)$ has a topological complement. The charts form a Mathlib vector prebundle ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · detPrebundle⟧, which needs exactly that the coordinate changes be continuous, Lemma 6.5.9 (preprint 6.25) below; its topology and bundle structure are those of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ (preprint p. 217).

**Lemma 6.5.9 (preprint 6.25)** (V6.28), proved first. *The transition between two charts is $(S, t) \mapsto (S, g(S)t)$ with $g$ continuous and nowhere zero on the common ball* ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · lemma_6_5_9_local⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · lemma_6_5_9⟧. The proof is the text's: a common lower bound $Q \le P, P'$ (Lemma 6.10 (preprint), §VI.4); Corollary 6.4.12 (preprint 6.13) to pass from $\gamma^P$ to $\gamma^{P'}$ through $Q$; and Lemma 6.5.5 (preprint 6.21) for each chart, which turns both frames into multiples of $Q$-frames (preprint p. 218).

**Definition 6.5.6 (preprint 6.22), Propositions 6.5.7 and 6.5.8 (preprint 6.23 and 6.24).** $\mathcal B$ is the collection of sets lying over the ball of some chart whose image in $\text{ball} \times \mathbb R$ is open (V6.25) ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · detBasis⟧. It is a basis of the topology of the prebundle (V6.26) ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · proposition_6_5_7⟧: its members are open, the charts being homeomorphisms onto $\text{ball} \times \mathbb R$, and every open set is the union of its intersections with chart domains, which are members; so the topology $\mathcal B$ generates is that one. $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is a topological vector bundle with model fibre $\mathbb R$, and every $\gamma_{(T,P,\varepsilon)}$, read in its frame, is a trivialization (V6.27) ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · proposition_6_5_8⟧ (preprint p. 218). The remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable, which does not hold as we read it for finite-dimensional $E$, $F$, and the classical case at the opening of §6.6 (preprint §6.5) are §VI.34 (gap G.60 closed; Findings, Chapter 6, items 26, 135).

### VI.9 Orientations of line bundles, Proposition 6.6.1 (preprint 6.26), Definition 6.6.2 (preprint 6.27)

**Orientations of line bundles** (V6.29). An orientation of a topological line bundle is a choice of rays of the fibres given near every point by a continuous nowhere-zero section ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · IsLineOrientation⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · LineOrientation⟧. Two orientations that agree on one fibre agree over a preconnected base ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · LineOrientation.eq_of_apply_eq⟧: the set where they agree is open and closed. The rays of the fibres form a two-sheeted covering ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · OrCover⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · isCoveringMap_orCover⟧, and an orientation is a continuous section of it; over a simply connected, locally path-connected base the lifting criterion extends every orientation of one fibre ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · exists_lineOrientation_apply_eq⟧, and over a nonempty such base there are exactly two orientations ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · exists_two_lineOrientation⟧. The text gives "since the base space is contractible" as the reason, without the theorem it needs (Findings, Chapter 6, item 25) (p. 263 (preprint p. 219)).

**Proposition 6.6.1 (preprint 6.26)** (V6.30). Over a nonempty convex set $C$ of Fredholm operators ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · fredholmIncl⟧, the restriction $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)|_C$ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · DetOn⟧ is a topological line bundle with exactly two orientations ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · proposition_6_6_1⟧: a nonempty convex set of a normed space is contractible, hence simply connected, and locally path-connected. The proposition is stated for every nonempty convex $C$; $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is one (§VI.1) (preprint p. 219).

**Definition 6.6.2 (preprint 6.27)** (V6.31). At a chart point the members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.isFredholm_of_mem_linSet⟧; $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ is the pull-back of $\mathrm{DET}(T_zO, K_z)$ to $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.detLin⟧, and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ is the set of its orientations ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.Or⟧, with exactly two elements ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.exists_two_or⟧. For each $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $o \mapsto o(L)$ is a bijection onto the two orientations of $\det(L)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.orEquivRay⟧: injective because an orientation is determined by one value over the connected base, onto because each ray extends. The category $\mathcal O_f$ is read through its objects, the two-element sets, with bijections as morphisms; between two two-element sets there are bijections ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · nonempty_equiv_of_two⟧, each determined by one value ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · equiv_eq_of_apply_eq_of_two⟧. No negation is set up on the tensor products, so $\{o_x, -o_x\}$ is stated as "exactly two elements" (Findings, Chapter 6, item 44) (preprint pp. 219–220). The comparison of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ in two charts is §VI.21.

### VI.10 Proposition 6.6.3 (preprint 6.28): the neighbourhoods of the propagation

The text: every smooth point $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ which (1) is sc-smoothly contractible, (2) has $\{y \in \mathrm{cl}(U) \mid f(y) = 0\}$ compact, (3) carries, for every sc-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to U$, an sc⁺-section $s : U \times [0, 1] \to Y$ with $s(\varphi(t), t) = f(\varphi(t))$, and (4) carries sc⁺-sections $q : U \times [0, 1] \to Y$ through every smooth point of every fibre over $U_\infty$, at every $t_0$. The proof takes local strong bundle coordinates, $P : K \to O$ with $x = 0$. This is the preprint's wording of (1). The 2021 text (p. 263) prints (1) with a second neighbourhood: $U' \subset U$ is sc-smoothly contractible in $U$ to the point $x$; that form is proved at the end of this section.

**The statement formalized** (V6.32) ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · proposition_6_6_3⟧. *With sc-smooth bump functions, every smooth $x$ has open $U \subseteq W$ in the domain of one chart of the atlas with* (1′) *any two sc-smooth paths in $U$ with the same end points are sc-smoothly homotopic in $W$ with the end points fixed* ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · IsScHomotopyRel⟧; (2) *$\{y \in \mathrm{cl}(U) \mid f(y) = 0\}$ is compact*; (3) *for every sc-smooth family $\Phi : \mathbb R^n \to X$ with $\Phi([0, 1]^n) \subseteq W$ there is an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R^n \times X$ with $(f + S)(q, \Phi(q)) = 0$ for $q$ near $[0, 1]^n$, depending on $q \in [0, 1]^n$ only through $\Phi(q)$*; (4) *$\pi^*P$ has sc⁺-sections through all smooth fibre points*. A path "in $U$" is one with $\gamma([0, 1]) \subseteq U$.

**The neighbourhoods.** Take a chart $c$ of the atlas at $x$, $u_0 = \varphi(x)$, the retraction $r$ on $U_c \subseteq C$ with $O = r(U_c)$. Choose $\delta$ with $B_\delta \cap C \subseteq U_c$ (the domain of the retraction is relatively open); $\delta_2$ with $r(B_{\delta_2} \cap U_c) \subseteq B_\delta$ (continuity of $r$ at $u_0$ on level $0$, $r(u_0) = u_0$); a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ whose closure meets the zeros of $f$ in a compact set ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_nhds_isCompact_zeros⟧ — at a zero by the local compactness of Theorem 5.2.3 (preprint 5.6) (§V.7), elsewhere because the zero set is closed and misses a neighbourhood of $x$; a closed neighbourhood $T \subseteq N$ of $x$ and $\delta_3$ with $\varphi^{-1}(B_{\delta_3} \cap O) \subseteq T$. With $\delta' = \min(\delta, \delta_2, \delta_3)$, $W = \varphi^{-1}(B(u_0, \delta) \cap O)$ and $U = \varphi^{-1}(B(u_0, \delta') \cap O)$.

**(1′).** Let $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$ be sc-smooth paths in $U$ with the same end points. Since paths are maps on $\mathbb R$ that lie in $U$ only for $t \in [0, 1]$, first take a $C^\infty$ map $\sigma : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ equal to the identity near $[0, 1]$ with values in the open set $\gamma_0^{-1}(U) \cap \gamma_1^{-1}(U)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_contDiff_eq_id_near_Icc_mapsTo⟧. Then $\Phi(\tau, t) = \varphi^{-1}\big(r\big((1 - \kappa(\tau))\,\varphi(\gamma_0(\sigma(t))) + \kappa(\tau)\,\varphi(\gamma_1(\sigma(t)))\big)\big)$. The convex combination lies in the convex set $B_{\delta'} \cap C$, hence in $U_c$; $r$ maps it into $B_\delta \cap O$, so $\Phi$ takes values in $W$; it is sc-smooth as a composite of sc-smooth maps in the chart; at $\tau = 0, 1$ it is $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$ on $[0, 1]$, because $\sigma$ is the identity there and $r$ fixes $O$; and the end points stay fixed, because $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ agree there. The text's contraction $\hat r(t, y) = r(ty)$ contracts $r(V)$ for a convex $V$; for $U = r(V')$ it needs $r(V') \subseteq V'$, which is not stated, and a convex domain of the retraction is not available in general. As we read it, the preprint's (1) is not established for $U$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 45); the 2021 wording of (1) is proved below. What Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35) uses is (1′).

**(2).** $\mathrm{cl}(U) \subseteq T \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(N)$, since $U \subseteq \varphi^{-1}(B_{\delta_3} \cap O) \subseteq T$ and $T$ is closed; so the zeros in $\mathrm{cl}(U)$ are a closed subset of a compact set.

**(3), sections along families** ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_family⟧. This is the text's $s(y) = R(y, f(x))$ made to depend on the parameter. An sc-smooth map on the finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^n$ takes values in the smooth points, and the principal part $q \mapsto \hat f(\Phi(q))$ lifts to a $C^\infty$ map into the level-$1$ fibre model. In the chart, the section over $(q, y)$ whose fibre coordinate is the projection onto $K_{\varphi(y)}$ of that lift of $-\hat f(\Phi(q))$ — after a reparametrization of the parameter, equal to the identity near $[0, 1]^n$, that keeps the family in the chart domain — is an sc⁺-section of the pull-back over the chart domain, and at $y = \Phi(q)$ it is $-f(\Phi(q))$. Cut off by an sc-smooth function on $X$ supported in the chart domain and equal to $1$ near a compact set containing $\Phi([0, 1]^n)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_isScSmoothMap_eq_one_nhdsSet⟧, it becomes a global sc⁺-section, with $f + S = 0$ at the points $(q, \Phi(q))$ where the cut-off is $1$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_mapsTo_of_bump⟧. For $q \in [0, 1]^n$ it is the projection of $-\hat f(\Phi(q))$, so it depends on $q$ only through $\Phi(q)$. The text's (3) is for paths; it is stated for families because the homotopies of Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35) need it (Findings, Chapter 6, item 46).

**(4)** ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · hasScPlusSectionsThrough_pullback_rn_of_bump⟧. Products of bump functions on $\mathbb R^n$ and on $X$ are bump functions on $\mathbb R^n \times X$, and they give the sections. $\mathbb R^n \times X$ ⟦Chapter2/FibredProduct · MPolyfold.paracompactSpace_prod⟧ and the total space of $\pi^*P$ ⟦Chapter2/StrongBundlePullback · paracompactSpace_pullbackSpace⟧ are paracompact, as the project's M-polyfolds and strong bundles must be. *Hidden hypotheses:* bump functions, for the global sections of (3) and (4), where the text assumes partitions of unity from §6.3 (preprint §6.2) on. The construction uses neither that $x$ is smooth nor that $X$ is tame (pp. 263–264 (preprint pp. 220–221)). (3) and (4) also hold as printed, with sections over the M-polyfolds $[0, 1] \times X$ and $[0, 1]^n \times X$ (§VI.37).

**(1), as printed in 2021** ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_Contractible · proposition_6_6_3_one⟧. *For every smooth $x$ and every open $U \ni x$ there are an open $U' \ni x$ in $U$ and an sc-smooth $H$ on the product M-polyfold $[0, 1] \times X$ with values in $U$ on $[0, 1] \times U'$, $H(0, \cdot) = x$, $H(1, \cdot) = \mathrm<built-in function id>$ on $U'$, and $H(t, x) = x$* ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_Contractible · IsScContraction⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_Contractible · exists_isScContraction⟧. In a chart $\varphi$ with retraction $r$ and $u_0 = \varphi(x)$, take $H(t, y) = \varphi^-1 r(u_0 + t(\varphi(y) - u_0))$ and $U' = \varphi^-1(B_\varepsilon(u_0))$, the ball chosen so that $B_\varepsilon \cap C$ lies in the domain of $r$ and $\varphi^-1 r(B_\varepsilon \cap C) \subseteq U$. The segment stays in the convex set $B_\varepsilon \cap C$; at $t = 1$ it is $\varphi(y)$, which $r$ fixes; at $t = 0$ it is $u_0$. The smoothness of $x$ is used: the constant $u_0$ must be a smooth point of $E$ for $H$ to be sc-smooth. The text's $\hat r(t, y) = r(ty)$ is this map for $x = 0$. The form with parameter $\mathbb R$ is ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_Contractible · exists_isScContractionRn⟧. `proposition_6_6_3_one` is the proposition with (1) in this form and with (1′), (2), (3), (4), for $U' \subseteq U \subseteq W$ in one chart (V6.32, restated; gap G.61, closed; Findings, Chapter 6, item 137).

**(1′) on $[0, 1]$** ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_IntervalHomotopy · exists_isScHomotopyI⟧. For paths on the M-polyfold $[0, 1]$ no reparametrization $\sigma$ is needed. For sc-smooth $\gamma_0, \gamma_1 : [0, 1] \to U$ with the same end points, the segment $H(\tau, t) = \varphi^-1 r(\varphi\gamma_0(t) + \tau(\varphi\gamma_1(t) - \varphi\gamma_0(t)))$ is sc-smooth on the M-polyfold $[0, 1]^2$: in the charts $t$ and $1 - t$ of $[0, 1]$ its representative is $(v, a, b) \mapsto r(a + s(v)(b - a))$ with $s(v) = v$ or $1 - v$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_IntervalHomotopy · chartSegment⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_IntervalHomotopy · isScSmoothOn_chartSegment⟧. The parameter has to stay in $[0, 1]$, since outside it the segment leaves the partial quadrant on which $r$ is defined. The edge conditions hold exactly, and they are the hypotheses of the invariance of the transport along $[0, 1]$-paths ⟦Chapter6/PathsInterval · orTransportI_eq_of_homotopy⟧ (§VI.37). Together, (1) with parameter $[0, 1]$, (1′) for $[0, 1]$-paths, (2) and (3), for one $U$: ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_IntervalHomotopy · proposition_6_6_3_interval⟧ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 138).

### VI.11 Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29): general position along a family

The text (preprint pp. 221–222): along a path $\varphi$ with a section $s(\cdot, t)$, the section $F(t, y, \lambda) = f(y) - s(y, t) + \sum\lambda_is_i(y, t)$ of the bundle over $[0, 1] \times \mathbb R^k \times X$; Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29) asserts that there are $s_1, \dots, s_k$ with property (P): for every $t$, the slice $F_t$ is in general position to the boundary of $X \times \mathbb R^k$ at $(\varphi(t), 0)$. The proof is the sentence "using the results from the transversality theory".

**The statement formalized** (V6.33) ⟦Chapter6/Lemma629 · lemma_6_6_4⟧. *Over a tame $X$ with bump functions, for $f$ with tame germ data, an sc-smooth $\Phi : \mathbb R^n \to X$ and an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P$ with $(f + S)(q, \Phi(q)) = 0$ near $[0, 1]^n$, there are finitely many sc⁺-sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ of $\pi^*P$ such that $F(\lambda, (q, y)) = f(y) + S(q, y) + \sum\lambda_is_i(q, y)$ is in general position at $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ for all $q$ near $[0, 1]^n$.*

**The proof** is that of Theorem 5.3.10 (preprint 5.18) (§V.20). The points $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ are zeros of $F$ ⟦Chapter6/Lemma629 · isZeroAt_paramSection_zero⟧, and for $q$ in a compact neighbourhood of $[0, 1]^n$ they form a compact set. At each of them finitely many sections make the parametrized section satisfy properties (i)–(ii) of §V.19; general position is open (§V.18); finitely many neighbourhoods cover the compact set, and the sections of all of them together do the job ⟦Chapter6/Lemma629 · exists_sections_isGeneralPositionGerm_of_isCompact⟧. *Hidden hypotheses:* $X$ tame, bump functions, tame germ data, the standing hypotheses of §6.6 (preprint §6.5) and of Theorem 5.3.10 (preprint 5.18). The conclusion is the general position of $F$ at the points $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, which the text derives from (P) and which Lemmas 6.6.5 and 6.6.6 (preprint 6.30 and 6.31) use. (P) itself, the general position of each slice $F_t$, follows from it by a chart computation — the tangent vectors of the family of zeros lie in $\ker F'$ and $\mathbb R^n$ has no boundary — and is §VI.36 (gap G.63 closed; Findings, Chapter 6, item 47).

### VI.12 Lemma 6.6.5 (preprint 6.30): kernels as continuous families of subspaces

The text (preprint p. 222): near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$ the solution set of $F$ is a manifold with boundary with corners, $\pi(t, y, \lambda) = t$ restricted to it is a submersion, and the kernels $L_t$ form a smooth vector bundle $L$ over $[0, 1]$. What the propagation needs is less: the kernels form a continuous family, so that an orientation of one of them can be continued to the others.

**The kernels** (V6.34). At a zero with surjective linearization and germ data of index $d$, $\dim\ker = d$ ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · StrongBundle.IsSurjLinOfIndex.finrank_linKer⟧. Near a zero in good position the kernel is the tangent space of the solution set (Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54), §III.45), the range of the derivative of an sc-retraction onto the solution set read in the chart. So along a continuous family $y_q$ of zeros in good position, read in one chart at continuously varying level-$1$ points $z_q$, near every $q_0$ the vectors $DS(z_q)b_i$, for a basis $b$ of the kernel at $q_0$ and that retraction $S$, are a continuous frame of the kernels ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · exists_local_frame_linKer⟧ — continuous because $(z, v) \mapsto DS(z)v$ is, independent near $q_0$ because independence is open, and spanning because the dimension is constant. The kernels form a continuous family of subspaces of the model space, of dimension the index ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · exists_subspaceFamily_linKer⟧. For an sc-smooth family of zeros $\mathbb R^n \to X$ read in a chart ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · hasFDerivAt_scDeriv_rn⟧, differentiating $\hat f(\Phi(q)) = 0$ shows that the derivative lies in the kernel of the linearization ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · fderiv_mem_linKer⟧. For the propagation the bundle $L$ is used as a continuous family of subspaces; the solution set as a manifold with boundary with corners near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, the submersion $\pi$ and the smooth structure of $L$ are §VI.36 (gap G.62 closed; Findings, Chapter 6, items 48, 126).

**Continuous families of subspaces** (V6.35). A family of $n$-dimensional subspaces $L_b$ of a normed space, spanned near every point by a continuous frame ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily⟧, has the line bundle $b \mapsto \lambda(L_b)$ ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.det⟧, with the wedges of the frames as trivializations ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.Frame.pretriv⟧; the coordinate change between two frames is the determinant of the matrix expressing one in the other, continuous because that matrix solves a linear system with continuous coefficients ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.Frame.coordChange_continuousOn⟧. Families and orientations restrict along continuous maps ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · LineOrientation.comp⟧. Over $[0, 1]$ an orientation of $\lambda(L_0)$ extends uniquely to an orientation of $\lambda(L)$ (§VI.9), and its value at $1$ is the continuation ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport_eq⟧, injective ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport_injective⟧ and compatible with restriction ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport_comp⟧; over a simply connected, locally path-connected base the continuation along a path depends only on its end points. This is the text's "an orientation of the lines … determines by continuation an orientation of all the other lines" (pp. 264–266 (preprint pp. 222–223)), and the bundles $\tilde L$ of pp. 266–273 (preprint pp. 224–227). "Vector bundle" is read as a family of subspaces of one model space with continuous local frames.

**Families of kernels and their images** (V6.36). The kernels of a norm-continuous family of surjective Fredholm operators over a connected base form a continuous family ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · exists_subspaceFamily_ker⟧: their dimension is the index, and near $q_0$ the kernel of $A_q$ is the graph over $\ker A_{q_0}$ given by Lemma 6.5.2 (preprint 6.18) with $P = 1$. The images of a continuous family under a jointly continuous family of linear maps injective on its members form one ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · SubspaceFamily.exists_map⟧, and continuous orientations are carried along ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · SubspaceFamily.isLineOrientation_map⟧. Cutting a continuous family by the kernel of a fixed $\ell$ that is onto on every member gives one ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · SubspaceFamily.exists_inf_ker⟧. "As $\tau$ varies, the bundle varies continuously" (pp. 265–272 (preprint pp. 223–226)) is read in the operator norm, and for maps into a model space as joint continuity.

### VI.13 The stabilized section in a product chart, and Lemma 6.6.6 (preprint 6.31)

The text (pp. 264–266 (preprint pp. 222–223)): with $T = (f - s(\cdot, t))'(\varphi(t))$, the kernel $L_t$ of $F_t'(\varphi(t), 0)$ fits into the sequence (96) $0 \to \ker T \to L_t \to \mathbb R^k \to \operatorname{coker}T \to 0$, and Lemma 6.6.6 (preprint 6.31) says that it is exact.

**The product chart** (V6.37). The parametrized section $F$ lives on $\mathbb R^k \times (\mathbb R^n \times X)$; it is read in the product chart $(\lambda \mapsto \lambda) \times ((q \mapsto q) \times \varphi)$ at $(0, (q, z))$, whose tangent space and fibre are products ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · PullbackChartData.ofProd_scDeriv_r_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · PullbackChartData.ofProd_mem_tangent_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · PullbackChartData.mem_K_ofProd_iff⟧. There the linearization of $F$ is $(\lambda, (\sigma, v)) \mapsto D(\hat g_q \circ r)(z)v + \sum\lambda_i\hat s_i(q, \cdot)(z) + D_q\sigma$, with $g_q = f + S(q, \cdot)$ and $D_q$ the derivative in the parameter ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundle.scDeriv_ofProd_slice_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundle.scDeriv_paramSection_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundleChart.paramDerivAt⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundle.scDeriv_paramSection_ofProd_ofProd⟧. With the projection to $\sigma$ and the inclusion of the slice $\sigma = 0$ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · sliceProj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · sliceIncl⟧, the kernel cut by $\sigma = 0$ is the image of $\ker(T \oplus \varphi)$ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · linKer_inf_ker_sliceProj_eq_map⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · exists_sliceOps⟧, where $T = g_q'(x)$ lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · mem_linSet_sectionAdd_pullbackSlice⟧ and $\varphi(\lambda) = \sum\lambda_is_i(q, x)$. *$T \oplus \varphi$ is onto when $F$ is in general position at $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$* ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · surjective_coprod_of_isLinSurjAt⟧: given $w$, the surjectivity of $F'$ gives $(\lambda, \sigma, v)$ with image $w$; the derivative of the curve of zeros, $(0, \sigma, D\Phi\,\sigma)$, lies in $\ker F'$ (§VI.12); subtracting it gives $(\lambda, 0, v - D\Phi\,\sigma)$ with the same image, a preimage under $T \oplus \varphi$. The kernel is then a closed subspace of the product with the right inclusion ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · exists_sliceKernel⟧. $\ker F_t'(\varphi(t), 0)$ is read as the kernel of the linearization of the whole $F$ cut by $\sigma = 0$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 49) (pp. 263–266 (preprint pp. 221–223)).

**Lemma 6.6.6 (preprint 6.31)** (V6.38) ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · lemma_6_6_6⟧. With these operators, (96) $0 \to \ker T \to \ker(T \oplus \varphi) \to \mathbb R^k \to K_z/R(T) \to 0$ is the stabilization sequence of $T$ and $\varphi$ (Lemma 6.4.14 (preprint 6.14), §VI.6), hence exact. The text has $c$ onto by (P); here it is onto by the general position of $F$ (§VI.11) and the derivative of the family of zeros, which absorbs the $\mathbb R^n$-directions (preprint p. 223).

### VI.14 Continuation, the sign, and the push-forward

The text (pp. 265–269 (preprint pp. 223–224)): $\Phi_{E_t}$ of (94) identifies $\det(T_t)$ with $\lambda(L_t)$; an orientation $o_0$ of $\det(T_0)$ gives one of $\lambda(L_0)$, continuation carries it to $\lambda(L_1)$, and $\Phi_{E_1}^{-1}$ carries it to $\det(T_1)$: this defines $o_1 = \varphi_*o_0$.

**Continuation** (V6.39). Over a simply connected, locally path-connected base the continuation of a ray of $\lambda(L_{q_0})$ to $\lambda(L_{q_1})$ is the value at $q_1$ of the unique orientation extending it ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_eq⟧. It is the identity from a point to itself ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_self⟧, composes ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_trans⟧, is a bijection of rays ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.contEquiv⟧, is compatible with pull-back ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_comp⟧, and along $[0, 1]$ it is the continuation of §VI.12 ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_eq_transport⟧. For a stabilization $T \oplus \varphi$ that is onto, $\det(T \oplus \varphi) \cong \lambda(\ker(T \oplus \varphi)) \otimes \lambda^*(\{0\}) \cong \lambda(\ker(T \oplus \varphi))$ ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · detEquivOfSurjective⟧, and through $\iota_\varphi$ (§VI.6) and an identification of the kernel with a member of $L$ the rays of $\det(T)$ and of $\lambda(L)$ correspond ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · stabRayEquiv⟧. The propagation is $\Phi_{E_0}$, then continuation, then $\Phi_{E_1}^{-1}$ on rays ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate⟧, with the identity on a constant family ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate_self⟧, composition ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate_trans⟧ and pull-back ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate_comp⟧. It is stated over any simply connected, locally path-connected base, so that one statement serves the paths and the squares; the fixed identification $\lambda^*(\mathbb R^k) \cong \lambda^*(\{0\})$ of (94) occurs at both ends.

**The sign** (V6.40). In a local determinant chart with projection $P$, the chart coordinate of $\iota_\psi(x) \in \det(S \oplus \psi)$ is $(-1)^{k\dim F/R(P) + \dim\operatorname{coker}S}\,D(S, \psi)$ times that of $x$ ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · coord_stabIota⟧, with $D$ ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · stabD⟧ continuous ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · continuousOn_stabD⟧ and nowhere zero ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · stabD_ne_zero⟧ near the centre. The first summand of the exponent is constant on a chart, the second is not. So where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ changes parity along a family, the rays carried by $\Phi_E$ jump. With $\alpha(T) = (-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}T}$ ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · stabSign⟧: *for a continuous orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}$, a norm-continuous family $T_q$ and a continuous stabilization $\varphi_q$ with $T_q \oplus \varphi_q$ onto, the rays $\alpha(T_q)\,\Phi(o(T_q))$ of $\lambda(\ker(T_q \oplus \varphi_q))$ form an orientation* ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · isLineOrientation_stabRay⟧. Without the sign they need not ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · not_isLineOrientation_stabRay_uncorrected⟧: $E = F = \mathbb R$, $k = 1$, $T_q = q/(1 + |q|)$ and $\varphi(r) = r_0$, where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T_q$ is $1$ at $q = 0$ and $0$ elsewhere. As we read it, the orientations carried by $\Phi_E$ of (94) along a continuous family are not continuous where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ changes parity, and Lemmas 6.6.8, 6.6.10 (preprint 6.33, 6.34) and the homotopy argument before Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35) use that they are. The propagation uses $\alpha(T)\Phi_E$, which on each operator carries the text's orientation or its opposite (Findings, Chapter 6, item 50) (p. 256 (preprint p. 212), as used on pp. 265–272 (preprint pp. 223–226)).

**The push-forward** (V6.41). At a chart point $p$ of a point $y$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · chartPt⟧, a section $S$ with $(f + S)(y) = 0$ and sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ give $T = (f + S)'(y) \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabT⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabT_mem_linSet⟧ and $\varphi(\lambda) = \sum\lambda_i\hat s_i(z)$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabPhi⟧, with appended sections giving the appended stabilization ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabPhi_finAppend⟧; $T \oplus \varphi$ is Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · isFredholm_stabCoprod⟧, and the sign is an involution ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · stabSign_inv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · toPerm_stabSign_symm⟧. A family of *stabilized kernels* ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels⟧ over a parameter space $Q$ consists of a global sc⁺-section $S$ of the pull-back with $f + S = 0$ at the points $(q, y(q))$, sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$, a continuous lift of $q \mapsto \varphi(y(q))$ to level $1$ of the chart, and a continuous family $\Lambda$ of subspaces of $E_0 \times \mathbb R^k$ such that at every chart point of $y(q)$ in the chart $T_q \oplus \varphi_q$ is onto and $\Lambda_q$ is the image of its kernel. It restricts along continuous maps ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.comp⟧. Its *push-forward* between two parameters $a, b$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push⟧: $o \in \mathrm{Or}^f_{y(a)}$ gives the ray $o(T_a)$, then $\alpha(T_a)\Phi_{E_a}(o(T_a))$, a ray of $\lambda(\Lambda_a)$; continuation carries it to $\lambda(\Lambda_b)$; $\alpha(T_b)\Phi_{E_b}^{-1}$ carries it to $\det(T_b)$; and $\mathrm{Or}^f_{y(b)} \cong \{\text{rays of }\det(T_b)\}$ (§VI.9) gives the image. It depends only on the data ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_congr⟧. With $\mathrm{orRay}_q(o)$, the ray of $\lambda(\Lambda_q)$ read from $o$ at $q$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.orRay⟧, $\varphi_* = \mathrm{orRay}_b^{-1} \circ \mathrm{cont}_{ab} \circ \mathrm{orRay}_a$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_eq_orRay⟧. *Along a path with continuously varying data and a fixed point, continuation carries the rays read at one parameter to those read at the next* ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.cont_orRay_path⟧: the operators $T_q$, $\varphi_q$ vary continuously; their kernels form a continuous family (§VI.12); the sign makes the rays $\alpha\Phi(o(T_q))$ an orientation; and the inclusion into $E_0 \times \mathbb R^k$ carries that orientation to $\lambda(\Lambda)$. The push-forward is compatible with pull-back ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_comp⟧ and with concatenation ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_trans⟧. For given end-point operators the result differs from the text's by $\alpha(T_a)\alpha(T_b)$; the sections enter pointwise, and the continuity in the parameter is that of $\Lambda$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 50) (preprint p. 224).

### VI.15 The stabilized kernels exist; push-forwards along paths

**Lemma 6.6.5 (preprint 6.30) for the push-forward** (V6.42) ⟦Chapter6/StabKernelsExist · exists_isStabKernels⟧. *For an sc-smooth $\Phi : \mathbb R^n \to X$ with $\Phi([0, 1]^n)$ in the domain of a chart, an sc⁺-section $S$ with $f + S = 0$ along $\Phi$ near $[0, 1]^n$, and sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ as in Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29), the stabilized kernels of the slices form a continuous family over $[0, 1]^n$.* The family $q \mapsto \varphi(\Phi(q))$ has a continuous lift to level $1$ ⟦Chapter6/StabKernelsExist · exists_continuousOn_lift_chart⟧, the values of an sc-smooth map on $\mathbb R^n$ being smooth points. The zeros $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ of $F$ are in general position, hence in good position; their kernels form a continuous family (§VI.12); cutting it by $\{d\sigma = 0\}$, a fixed functional onto on every member because the derivative of the family of zeros lies in the kernel, keeps it continuous (§VI.12); and §VI.13 identifies the cut with $\ker(T_q \oplus \varphi_q)$. The kernels also form a smooth vector bundle (§VI.36); the continuation uses only their continuity.

**Push-forwards along paths** (V6.43). The parameter points of $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PushData · pt1_mem_Icc⟧, level-$1$ lifts at smooth points ⟦Chapter6/PushData · exists_lift_of_smooth⟧ and the chart points they give ⟦Chapter6/PushData · chartPtOf⟧ are the bookkeeping. *$e : \mathrm{Or}^f_{\gamma(0)} \to \mathrm{Or}^f_{\gamma(1)}$ is a push-forward along an sc-smooth path $\gamma$ in a chart* ⟦Chapter6/PushData · IsPush⟧ if there are global sc⁺-sections $S, s_1, \dots, s_k$ of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R \times X$ with $(f + S)(t, \gamma(t)) = 0$ for $t$ near $[0, 1]$, and a family of stabilized kernels of their slices along $\gamma$ whose push-forward is $e$. Equal data give equal push-forwards ⟦Chapter6/PushData · IsStabKernels.push_eq_of_eq⟧. Pulled back along an affine reparametrization the sections still vanish along the reparametrized path ⟦Chapter6/PushData · isZeroAt_sectionAdd_reparamSection⟧ and give a push-forward along it ⟦Chapter6/PushData · isPush_reparam⟧; so a push-forward along $\gamma$ is the composite of push-forwards along its two halves, each reparametrized to $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PushData · IsPush.split⟧. *Along every sc-smooth path in a set with property (3) of Proposition 6.6.3 (preprint 6.28) there is a push-forward* ⟦Chapter6/PushData · exists_isPush⟧: (3) gives $S$, Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29) gives $s_1, \dots, s_k$, and the stabilized kernels exist. Global sections of the pull-back stand in place of the text's sections over $U \times [0, 1]$, and (P) is used only to construct a push-forward (preprint p. 224).

### VI.16 Lemma 6.6.8 (preprint 6.33) and sections over families
