### VI.28 Appendix §6.8.1 (preprint §6.7.1): the proof of Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5)

**The text's proof** (preprint pp. 234–235) has three steps: a change of the basis of the complement of $\alpha(A)$ multiplies both wedges of (91) by its determinant; a change of the bases of $A$ and $D$ multiplies the source by $\det(\tau)/\det(\varepsilon)$; and a change of complements adds to the basis of the complement of $\alpha(A)$ vectors of $\alpha(A)$, and to the $\gamma$-preimages vectors of $\beta(B)$, which leaves the wedges unchanged.

**The formalized proof** (V6.63) does the three steps at once. For two choices $\chi$, $\chi'$ there is a scalar $\mu$ with $\text{source}(\chi') = \mu\,\text{source}(\chi)$ and $\text{value}(\chi') = \mu\,\text{value}(\chi)$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice.exists_smul_source_value⟧. *Step 1.* Project the basis $b''$ of the new complement $Z'$ onto $Z$ along $\alpha(A)$; the projections form a basis of $Z$, related to $b'$ by some $\sigma$, and since $\beta \circ \alpha = 0$ they have the same $\beta$-images as $b''$. *Step 2.* In $B$, $\alpha(a') \wedge b'' = \alpha(a') \wedge p(b'')$, adding vectors of the span of the first block; with $a' = \tau a$ this is $\det\tau\,\det\sigma\;\alpha(a) \wedge b'$. *Step 3.* In $C$, the $\gamma$-preimages $c'$ of $d' = \varepsilon d$ in $V'$ differ from the $\gamma$-preimages in $V$ by vectors of $\ker\gamma = \beta(B)$, the span of the second block, so the wedge of the basis of $C$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice.wedgeC⟧ is $\det\varepsilon\,\det\sigma$ times that of $\chi$. *Step 4.* So the value scales by $\det\tau\,\det\sigma/(\det\varepsilon\,\det\sigma) = \det\tau/\det\varepsilon$, as the source does, and Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5) follows from the fixed choice that defines $\Phi_E$. The step "independent of the choices of the basis if and only if $\det(\tau) = \det(\varepsilon)$" is read as this homogeneity of (91) in the bases of $A$ and $D$, $\tau$ being the $\sigma$ just introduced; the corrections $p_i$ lie in $\beta(B)$, written $\beta(C)$, and are combinations of the $\beta$-images, whose names are exchanged with those of the $\gamma$-preimages in the last step (possible misprints; Findings, Chapter 6, item 1).

### VI.29 Appendix §6.8.2 (preprint §6.7.2): the proof of Proposition 6.4.11 (preprint 6.12)

(V6.64.) Let $P \le Q$ in $\Pi_T$. *Step 1, adapted bases.* Take a basis $a$ of $\ker T$ and classes $[d_i]$ forming a basis of $\operatorname{coker}T$ with $d_i \in \ker Q$, possible because $R(QT) = R(Q)$; complete $a$ by $b$ to a basis of $\ker(QT)$, and $(a, b)$ by $\tilde b$ to a basis of $\ker(PQT) = \ker(PT)$. *Step 2, the three values.* By (91) with these choices (Lemma 6.3.3 (preprint 6.5), §VI.3), $\gamma^Q_T(h_0) = (a \wedge b) \otimes ([d]_Q \wedge [Tb]_Q)^*$; $\gamma^P_{QT}\gamma^Q_T(h_0) = (a \wedge b \wedge \tilde b) \otimes ([d]_P \wedge [Tb]_P \wedge [QT\tilde b]_P)^*$, the classes $[d]_P$, $[Tb]_P$ being preimages of $[d]_Q$, $[Tb]_Q$ because $Pd_i = PQd_i = 0$ and $PTb \in R(P) \subseteq R(Q)$; and $\gamma^P_T(h_0) = (a \wedge b \wedge \tilde b) \otimes ([d]_P \wedge [Tb]_P \wedge [T\tilde b]_P)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj_wedge_tmul⟧. *Step 3, the spanning.* $[T\tilde b]_P - [QT\tilde b]_P = [(I - Q)T\tilde b]_P$, and $(I - Q)T\tilde b \in \ker Q$. If $Qg = 0$, then $g = \sum c_id_i + Tx$ with $x \in \ker(QT)$ — write $[g] = \sum c_i[d_i]$ in $\operatorname{coker}T$ and use $Qd_i = 0$ — so the classes of the $d_i$ and of the $Tb_j$ span what the text calls $\ker\tilde Q$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · mem_span_append_of_ker⟧. *Step 4.* The last block of the third value differs from that of the second by vectors of the span of the first two blocks, which does not change the wedge (§VI.2), and with the identification of $\det(P(QT))$ with $\det(PT)$ the two values agree ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · comp_comp_eq_of_projLE⟧. The spanning is proved directly in $F$; the name $\alpha_q$ in the last part is read as $\alpha^P$ (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, items 6, 7) (pp. 280–286 (preprint pp. 235–237)).

### VI.30 What is not formalized

Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43), the admissible sections, the orientation of the solution set and of $\hat f$, Lemma 6.5.3 (preprint 6.19), Lemmas 6.6.4 and 6.6.5 (preprint 6.29 and 6.30) as statements about manifolds, the remarks of §§6.3–6.6 and after Theorem 6.6.17, and the facts on paths are now formalized, and so is Proposition 6.6.3 (1) in its 2021 wording (gaps G.54–G.64, G.66–G.69, G.81, G.90, G.91 closed). What remains:

- **Proposition 6.6.3 (1) in the preprint's wording** (gap G.61 is closed): "$U$ is sc-smoothly contractible". As we read it, the proof does not establish it for its $U$: it needs $r(V') \subseteq V'$, which is not stated. No counterexample is known to us. The 2021 wording, a smaller $U'$ contractible in $U$, is proved, and the proofs use (1′) (§§VI.10, VI.18, VI.19, VI.23).
- **Paths and families on $[0, 1]$** (gap G.65, in part): most statements hold on $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n \times X$ as printed (§§VI.36, VI.37), and so does Proposition 6.6.3 (1′) for paths on $[0, 1]$ (§VI.10). For $n = 1$ the bundle $L$ of Lemma 6.6.5 is a smooth vector bundle over the manifold with boundary $[0, 1]$ itself, the pull-back along the inclusion ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_SmoothLInterval · lemma_6_6_5_smoothBundle_interval⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_SmoothLInterval · SmoothSubspaceFamily.comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP3_K4_SmoothLInterval · contMDiff_unitIntervalToOpens⟧. Still read on $\mathbb R$ (decision D2): $L$ over a neighbourhood of $[0, 1]^n$ for $n \ge 2$ (V6.34; Mathlib has no manifold structure on the cube, estimated at 300–600 lines), the stabilized kernels and their continuation for families with sections over $[0, 1]^n \times X$ (V6.42, 400–700 lines), and Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42) over $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ (V6.62, 1,500–2,500 lines), with the cobordisms of Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43).
- **The narrower rows.** V6.48, Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35): the section $f$, which the statement does not introduce, is supplied (presumably an omission), and the neighbourhood is not shown contractible in itself (the preprint's (1)). V6.80, the remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable: it does not hold as we read it for finite-dimensional $E$, $F$ (`exists_two_lineOrientation_det_of_finiteDimensional`), and it is proved only for spaces isomorphic to an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space or to $H \times H$ with $H \cong \mathbb R \times H$, and under complex structures with an odd-dimensional kernel; infinite-dimensional Banach spaces without such structures are not covered (§VI.34). V6.81, the classical case: $C^1$ in place of smooth, and the smoothness of the line bundle is not formalized (§VI.34). V6.32, Proposition 6.6.3, is restated since 2026-11-13.
- **The chart-free objects** $T_xX$, $Y_x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ (gaps G.6, G.7, G.13 of Chapter 2): they are made in chart points and identified between charts (§VI.21).

### VI.31 What the formalization taught us

**The sign of (94).** The main change of substance is a sign. The coordinate of $\Phi_E$ in a local determinant chart carries the factor $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}S}$, which jumps where the parity of the cokernel dimension changes; the orientations it carries along a continuous family are then not continuous, as we read it, and an example on $\mathbb R$ shows it (§VI.14). The continuity statements of pp. 265–272 (preprint pp. 223–226) are not written in coordinates in the text, and it is in coordinates that the sign appears. The normalized $\alpha(T)\Phi_E$ at both ends of every propagation changes nothing on surjective operators — the tangent orientations of Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41) are the text's — and the same sign is used in Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42) (§VI.26).

**Lemma 6.10 (preprint) and the 2017 remark.** The common lower bound of two good left-projections exists, but not with the range $R(P) \cap R(P')$: a projection onto a smaller, finite-codimensional piece of it, along a complement containing both kernels, is below both (§VI.4). This keeps the preprint's construction of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ — one lower bound, Corollary 6.4.12 (preprint 6.13), Lemma 6.5.5 (preprint 6.21) — intact.

**Contractibility was never needed.** Proposition 6.6.3 (1) (preprint 6.28) in the preprint's wording is not established for the neighbourhood its proof builds, as we read it; the 2021 wording, with a smaller $U'$, holds (§VI.10). Every later use of contractibility is a use of (1′): two paths in $U$ with the same end points are homotopic in a larger region where sections along families exist. Orientable neighbourhoods become pairs $V \subseteq U$, and property (∗) of Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37) holds on every set with the local propagation property (§§VI.10, VI.19, VI.23).

**Paths on $\mathbb R$ cost reparametrizations.** With paths and homotopies on $\mathbb R$ whose conditions hold on $[0, 1]$ (decision D2), the homotopy of (1′) has the right edges only on $[0, 1]$ while push-forward data need zeros near $[0, 1]$; transitivity of homotopy, associativity of concatenation and Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.35) all pass through the smooth transition function $\kappa$ (§§VI.18, VI.20).

**Charts must be compared.** The text's chart-free $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ becomes a set read in a chosen chart, and the invariance of the local propagation under a change of chart — the naturality of the stabilization isomorphism, of the sign and of continuation — is a file of its own (§VI.21).

**"By a covering argument" and "one verifies".** The covering argument of Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37) is a dyadic transport with a square lemma, proved for any family of types (§VI.22); the "simple computation" of Lemma 6.6.8 (preprint 6.33) is an exact identity of stabilization isomorphisms, with no sign, once the appended sections come last (§VI.16); and the equivalence of Definitions 6.6.14 and 6.6.15 (preprint 6.38 and 6.39), stated without proof, needs the transport computed on dyadic pieces inside orientable neighbourhoods (§VI.24).

**Theorem 6.7.1 is proved as the text proves it, with two changes of route.** The invariant is defined from one admissible perturbation, made a map on cohomology by Stokes' theorem, and compared along a cobordism, as in the text. The decomposition $\partial S_F = S_0 \cup S_1 \cup \tilde S$ is replaced by a cut-off in time: $\int d(gA) = 0$ for a closed form $A$ with vanishing face restriction, while $d(g_iA)$ lives on the product ends, where Fubini gives the integrals over $S_0$ and $S_1$. This avoids face integrals over $\tilde S \subseteq \partial X \times (0, 1)$ and the signs of the pieces of $\partial S_F$. And the relative form is built on inner ends, because gluing $p_1^*\gamma_i$ to an extension needs room in time inside the product end (§VI.27).

**The extension $\bar\omega$ has one degree too many, as we read it.** The proof extends $\omega$ to $X \times [0, 1]$ by $p_1^*\omega \wedge p_2^*dt$, a form of degree $k + 1$ on the $(k + 1)$-dimensional $S_F$, whose integrals over the $k$-dimensional pieces of $\partial S_F$ vanish. The comparison goes through with $p_1^*\omega$ and $p_1^*\tau$ (§VI.27, reading R-e).

**The orientation of the cobordism is a computation, and has no sign.** "Taking the orientations into account" is: the linearization of $F$ on an end is that of a $t$-constant lift, its kernel is $\mathbb R \times \ker$, the 2021 map puts $e$ in front of the kernel orientation, and the tangent map of the end is $(s, w) \mapsto (s, T\iota(w))$; with the time vector first on both sides, $e \wedge o$ is the product orientation $e \wedge o_{S_i}$ (§VI.27). The 2021 convention $\tilde h = e \wedge h$ also removes the sign that the preprint's $h \mapsto \tilde h$ needed: it differs from the continuous map by $(-1)^{\mathrm{ind}L}$, which is locally constant (§VI.26).

**Hidden data of the theorem.** The neighbourhood $U$ needs a margin, $\mathrm{cl}\{N(f) \le 2\}$ compact, for the cobordism between two admissible sections; Theorem 5.3.10 (preprint 5.18) is needed relative to a compact part of a zero set that need not be compact; the degree of a form is paired with the part of $S_{f+s}$ of that index, since the index need not be constant; the proper oriented homotopy, which the text does not define, is read through Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42); and $p_1$ maps the faces of $S_F$ to faces of $X$ because the degeneracy index of $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ is that of $X$ (§VI.27).

**$\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ and dimension.** The remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable does not hold as we read it for finite-dimensional $E$, $F$: there $L(E, F)$ is convex and Proposition 6.6.1 (preprint 6.26) gives two orientations (`exists_two_lineOrientation_det_of_finiteDimensional`). It holds for infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, through a loop of surjective operators whose kernels form a Möbius band; in finite dimension the cokernels form a second Möbius band and the two cancel in $\det$ (§VI.34).

**Orientations of manifolds with corners.** Mathlib has none. An oriented atlas, the usual definition, does not fit the quadrant model: $[0, 1]$ has no atlas of quadrant charts with positive changes, and in dimension $0$ every atlas is oriented. A continuous tangent orientation does, and it is the form in which Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41), Stokes' theorem and the cobordism argument use orientations (§§VI.25, VI.27).

**(P) follows from the general position of $F$.** The text derives the general position of $F$ along the family from property (P) of the slices. The formalization goes the other way: general position of $F$ is proved by the method of Theorem 5.3.10 (preprint 5.18), and (P) follows from it by a chart computation, since the tangent vectors of the family of zeros lie in $\ker F'$ and have reduced $X$-components; on the cube $[0, 1]^n$ the two are equivalent (§VI.36).

### VI.32 The Springer 2021 edition: Lemma 6.4.4, Proposition 6.4.13, Lemmas 6.6.8 and 6.6.9

The 2021 edition adds index equalities to Lemma 6.4.4 (2017: 6.3), makes the hypothesis of Proposition 6.4.13 (2017: 6.6) explicit, and splits preprint Lemma 6.33 (2017: 6.15) into Lemmas 6.6.8 and 6.6.9. Neither Lemma 6.4.4 nor Proposition 6.4.13 has a preprint counterpart. The file is `Chapter6/Book2021.lean` (Findings, Chapter 6, items 110–115).

**Lemma 6.4.4 (2017: 6.3)** ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · lemma_6_4_4⟧. *Statement.* Let $E$, $F$ be Banach spaces, $T_0 : E \to F$ Fredholm and $P_0 \in \Pi_{T_0}$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj⟧. There is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $T$ and every projection $P$ with $\|T - T_0\| < \varepsilon$, $\|P - P_0\| < \varepsilon$: $T$ is Fredholm, $P \in \Pi_T$, and $\mathrm{ind}(P \circ T) = \mathrm{ind}(T) = \mathrm{ind}(T_0) = \mathrm{ind}(P_0 \circ T_0)$, all indices of maps $E \to F$ ⟦Chapter1/FredholmIndex · fredholmIndex⟧. *Proof.* (a) With a quasi-inverse $v$ of $T_0$, every $T$ with $\|T - T_0\| < 1/(\|v\| + 1)$ is Fredholm of the index of $T_0$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · isFredholm_add_of_norm_lt⟧ ⟦Chapter1/FredholmIndex · fredholmIndex_add_of_norm_lt⟧. (b) Instead of the text's map $\Phi_{(P,T)}(x, h) = PTx + (I - P)h$, take the intertwiner $J(P) = PP_0 + (1 - P)(1 - P_0)$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · projIntertwiner⟧. It is continuous in $P$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · continuous_projIntertwiner⟧, $J(P_0) = 1$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · projIntertwiner_self⟧, so $J(P)$ is a unit for $P$ near $P_0$; and $J(P)P_0 = PJ(P)$ for every projection $P$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · projIntertwiner_mul⟧, so $P = JP_0J^{-1}$. (c) $J^{-1}T$ is near $T_0$, so by Lemma 6.5.1 (preprint 6.17) $P_0 \in \Pi_{J^{-1}T}$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · lemma_6_5_1⟧. Then $R(P) = JR(P_0)$ has finite codimension, $(1 - P)F$ complements it, and $R(PT) = JR(P_0J^{-1}T) = JR(P_0) = R(P)$: $P \in \Pi_T$. (d) The indices of $P \circ T$ and $P_0 \circ T_0$ are those of $T$ and $T_0$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.fredholmIndex_comp⟧. $\square$ As a map onto $R(P)$ the operator $P \circ T$ would have index $\dim\ker(PT)$; the text's equalities hold for the map $E \to F$. $E$ and $F$ are taken in the universe `Type`, that of (a).

**A common complement** ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · exists_isCompl_isCompl_of_finrank_eq⟧. *Statement.* Two finite-dimensional subspaces $K_1$, $K_2$ of the same dimension of a real vector space have a common algebraic complement. *Proof.* Induction on $n = \dim(K_1 + K_2) - \dim K_1$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · exists_isCompl_isCompl_of_finrank_eq_aux⟧. For $n = 0$, $K_1 = K_2$. Otherwise neither contains the other; take $a \in K_2 \setminus K_1$, $b \in K_1 \setminus K_2$. Then $a + b$ lies in neither, $K_i + \mathbb R(a + b)$ has dimension $\dim K_i + 1$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · finrank_sup_span_singleton_of_notMem⟧ and their sum is still $K_1 + K_2$, so the induction gives a common complement $X'$ of $K_1 + \mathbb R(a + b)$ and $K_2 + \mathbb R(a + b)$, and $X' + \mathbb R(a + b)$ complements $K_1$ and $K_2$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · isCompl_sup_span_singleton⟧. $\square$ The text takes $X$ closed; that is not needed for the algebraic part below, and a closed one is §VI.33.

**Proposition 6.4.13 (2017: 6.6), the algebraic part** ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · proposition_6_4_13⟧. *Statement.* Let $T$ be Fredholm and $P, Q \in \Pi_T$ with $R(P) = R(Q) = H$ (the 2021 hypothesis $\Pi_T \cap \mathcal P_H \ne \emptyset$ is the existence of such projections). There are linear isomorphisms $A_T : \ker(PT) \to \ker(QT)$, $B_T : F/R(P) \to F/R(Q)$ with $A_T \circ j_P = j_Q$, $\Phi_Q \circ A_T = B_T \circ \Phi_P$ and $\pi_Q \circ B_T = \pi_P$, for the maps of $E(T, P)$, $E(T, Q)$ (§VI.5) ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqJ⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqPhi⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqPi⟧. *Proof (the text's).* $PT$ and $QT$ are Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.isFredholm_comp⟧ of index $\mathrm{ind}(T)$, and $F/R(P) = F/R(Q)$, so $\dim\ker(PT) = \dim\ker(QT)$; let $X$ be a common complement. $QT$ maps $X$ isomorphically onto $R(Q)$; for $e \in \ker(PT)$ let $x(e) \in X$ solve $QTx = QTe$ and put $A_T(e) = e - x(e) \in \ker(QT)$. It is injective ($A_T(e) = 0$ puts $e$ in $X \cap \ker(PT) = 0$), the identity on $\ker T$, and onto by the dimensions. For $f \in F$ write $(1 - P)f = Tx + \tilde f$ with $x \in X$, $\tilde f \in (1 - Q)F$ (solve $QTx = Q(1 - P)f$), and put $B_T(f + H) = \tilde f + H$. The three identities are direct computations; $B_T$ is injective by a direct computation, hence an isomorphism, the two quotients having the same finite dimension (the text uses the five lemma). $\square$ The last sentence, that $A_T$ and $B_T$ depend continuously on $T$, is §VI.33, with a closed $X$ (gap G.81, closed).

**Lemmas 6.6.8 and 6.6.9** ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · lemma_6_6_8⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · lemma_6_6_9⟧. *Statement.* For stabilized kernels of the data $(f, s_1, \dots, s_k)$ along a family ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels⟧ and of the data with $d$ sections appended, the push-forwards of orientations agree: for zero sections (Lemma 6.6.8, the parameters $\mu$ as dummy variables) and for arbitrary sections $\bar s_1, \dots, \bar s_d$ (Lemma 6.6.9). *Proof.* Both are §VI.16 ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_append⟧, Lemma 6.6.8 with $\bar s_j = 0$. $\square$ The statement of preprint Lemma 6.33 (2017: 6.15) is Lemma 6.6.9, and the first step of its proof is Lemma 6.6.8; the formalization of §VI.16 never needed that step.

**Already covered.** The other 2021 changes of the chapter concern statements verified before: Proposition 6.4.15 with its hypotheses made explicit (§VI.6) ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · proposition_6_4_15⟧, Proposition 6.6.3 for a tame $X$ and sections valued in $Y \times [0, 1]$ (§VI.10, without tameness) ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · proposition_6_6_3⟧, and Lemma 6.6.5 with the solution set near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$ in the points $(t, y, \lambda)$, whose kernel family (§VI.12) is unaffected ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · exists_subspaceFamily_linKer⟧.

### VI.33 The Springer 2021 edition, continued: Proposition 6.4.13 (last sentence) and Theorem 6.6.17

The last sentence of Proposition 6.4.13 (2017: 6.6), the continuity of $A_T$ and $B_T$ in $T$, is proved with a closed common complement. Theorem 6.6.17 is new in the 2021 edition: a topology on the orientation space $O_f$ of pp. 274–275, whose proof the text leaves to the reader. It is proved with properties (1)–(3); property (2) uses a hypothesis on $X$, connected smooth neighbourhoods, which every M-polyfold satisfies (gap G.90, closed). The files are `Chapter6/Book2021Continuity.lean` and `Chapter6/OrientationSpace.lean` (Findings, Chapter 6, items 116–121).

**A common closed complement** ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · exists_isClosed_isTopCompl_isTopCompl_of_finrank_eq⟧. *Statement.* Two finite-dimensional subspaces $K_1$, $K_2$ of the same dimension of a real normed space $E$ have a common closed complement $X$: $E = K_1 \oplus X = K_2 \oplus X$ topologically. *Proof.* Let $X_0$ be a common algebraic complement (§VI.32) ⟦Chapter6/Book2021 · exists_isCompl_isCompl_of_finrank_eq⟧ and $Z$ a closed complement of the finite-dimensional $K_1 + K_2$. Then $X = Z + X_0 \cap (K_1 + K_2)$ complements $K_i$: inside $K_1 + K_2$, $X_0 \cap (K_1 + K_2)$ complements $K_i$, and $Z$ complements $K_1 + K_2$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · isCompl_sup_inf_of_isCompl⟧. $X$ is closed, a closed subspace plus a finite-dimensional one, and an algebraic complement of a finite-dimensional subspace that is closed is a topological one. $\square$

**Proposition 6.4.13 (2017: 6.6), the last sentence** ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · proposition_6_4_13_continuity⟧. *Statement.* Let $T$ be Fredholm and $P, Q \in \Pi_T$ with $R(P) = R(Q) = H$. There are a closed $X \subseteq E$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that on $\|S - T\| < \varepsilon$ the maps $S \mapsto A_S = 1 - \xi_S \circ S$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · kerTransition⟧ and $S \mapsto B_S = (1 - P) - S \xi_S (1 - P)$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · cokerTransition⟧, where $\xi_S = (QS|_X)^{-1} \circ Q$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · solveOp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · projCod⟧, are continuous into $L(E)$, $L(F)$ in the operator norm, and jointly with the vector; and for every such $S$: $P, Q \in \Pi_S$, $E = \ker(PS) \oplus X = \ker(QS) \oplus X$ topologically, $e - A_S e \in X$ and $QSA_S e = 0$ (6.15)–(6.16) ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · kerTransition_apply⟧, $QB_S f = 0$ and $Sx + B_S f = (1 - P)f$ for some $x \in X$ (6.18)–(6.19) ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · cokerTransition_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · solveOp_mem⟧, and $A_S$, $B_S$ induce isomorphisms $\ker(PS) \to \ker(QS)$, $F/R(P) \to F/R(Q)$ filling the diagram of $E(S, P)$, $E(S, Q)$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · diagram_of_solveOp⟧. *Proof.* Take $X$ from the previous statement for $\ker(PT)$, $\ker(QT)$, which have the same dimension (§VI.32). (a) By Lemma 6.5.1 (preprint 6.17) ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · lemma_6_5_1⟧ there is $\varepsilon$ with $P, Q \in \Pi_S$ and $QS|_X : X \to R(Q)$ an isomorphism for $\|S - T\| < \varepsilon$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · projRestrict⟧. (b) $S \mapsto QS|_X$ is continuous ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · continuous_projRestrict⟧ and inversion is continuous at isomorphisms, $X$ being complete; so $\xi_S$ is continuous in $S$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · continuousAt_solveOp⟧, and so are $A_S$, $B_S$, which are built from $\xi_S$, $S$ and $P$ by composition. (c) $QS\xi_S = Q$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · apply_solveOp_of_projRestrict_eq⟧ gives (6.15)–(6.19). (d) $\ker(QS) \cap X = 0$ because $QS|_X$ is injective, and $\ker(QS) + X = E$ because $e - \xi_S Se \in \ker(QS)$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · disjoint_ker_comp_of_projRestrict_eq⟧; the projection $1 - \xi_S S$ onto $\ker(QS)$ along $X$ is continuous ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · isTopCompl_ker_comp_of_projRestrict_eq⟧; the same for $P$, $R(P) = R(Q)$. (e) The diagram is §VI.32 for $S$ with this $X$. $\square$ *Satisfiable:* $T = 1$ on $\mathbb R$ and $P = Q$ any element of $\Pi_T$ ⟦Chapter6/Book2021Continuity · proposition_6_4_13_continuity_hyps⟧. "Depend continuously" is read as the continuity of $A_S$ on $E$ and $B_S$ on $F$; these determine the maps between the varying kernels $\ker(PS)$, $\ker(QS)$ and on $F/H$, and the joint continuity is continuity on the kernel bundle $\bigcup_S \{S\} \times \ker(PS)$ of Remark 6.4.5 (gap G.81, closed).

**The orientation space** ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · OrSpace⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · orProj⟧. *Definition.* $O_f$ is the set of pairs $(x, o)$ with $x \in X_\infty$ and $o \in \mathrm{Or}^f_x$, read in the chosen chart (§VI.21) ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · Orx⟧, and $\pi_f(x, o) = x$; $X_\infty$ carries the topology of Theorem 2.3.10 (§II.7) ⟦Chapter2/Metrizable · MPolyfold.SmoothLevel⟧. For an sc-smooth path $\varphi$ (a map $\mathbb R \to X$, decision D2) the pull-back $\varphi^* O_f$ is the subspace of $[0, 1] \times O_f$ of the $(t, p)$ with $\varphi(t) = \pi_f(p)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · OrPullback⟧, and a continuous section over an open $U$ is a continuous $\sigma : U_\infty \to O_f$ with $\pi_f \circ \sigma = \mathrm{id}$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · IsContSectionOver⟧. The three properties of the theorem: (1) $\pi_f$ is a local homeomorphism; (2) every $x \in X_\infty$ has an open $U$ in $X$ over whose smooth part there are exactly two continuous sections ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · HasTwoContSections⟧; (3) for every sc-smooth path $\varphi$ and continuous section $t \mapsto (\varphi(t), o_t)$ of $\varphi^* O_f$, for every $t_0$ and $t$ near $t_0$, $o_t$ is the push-forward of $o_{t_0}$ along the segment $\varphi|[t_0, t]$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · segPath⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · isScSmoothMap_segPath⟧ in a set with the local propagation property ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsPropagationNbhd⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orPush⟧, which does not depend on the set ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orPush_compat⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · IsPropagationContinuous⟧. An *orientation topology* is a Hausdorff topology with (1)–(3) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · IsOrientationTopology⟧. This is our reading of the text's "local propagation of $o_{t_0}$".

**Sc-smooth paths in $X_\infty$** ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · continuous_smoothMk_comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eventually_exists_scPath_smoothLevel⟧. *Statement.* (a) An sc-smooth $\Gamma : \mathbb R^n \to X$ is continuous into $X_\infty$. (b) If $N$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X_\infty$, every $y \in X_\infty$ near $x$ is joined to $x$ by an sc-smooth path with all its points in $N$. *Proof.* (a) Its values are smooth points ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · mem_smoothSet_of_isScSmoothMap⟧; in a chart, $\Gamma$ is continuous into every level $m$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · continuousOn_levelLift_comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · rnChart_toBase⟧, which is continuity into $X_\infty$. (b) In a chart at $x$, take the retracted segment $t \mapsto r((1 - t)u_0 + tu_1)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · chartSegPath⟧, sc-smooth ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · isScSmoothMap_chartSegPath⟧; for $y$ near $x$ in $X_\infty$ its points are near $x$ in every level, hence in $N$. $\square$ The neighbourhood version for open sets of $X$ is ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · exists_nhds_scPath_of_isOpen⟧, from §VI.18 ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · exists_nhds_scPath⟧.

**The topology** ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · orTopology⟧. *Definition.* Fix local transport data $L$ (§VI.22) ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport⟧. A *continuous orientation* over an open $U$ is a family $y \mapsto o_y$ on $U_\infty$ carried along by the transport of $L$ along every sc-smooth path in $U$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · IsContOrOn⟧; its sheet is $\{(y, o_y) : y \in U_\infty\}$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · orSec⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · orBasic⟧. A set $W \subseteq O_f$ is open if $\{y \in U_\infty : (y, o_y) \in W\}$ is open in $X_\infty$ for every continuous orientation $o$ over an open $U$. *Properties, for every $L$.* (a) Two continuous orientations that agree at a point agree near it ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · IsContOrOn.eventually_iff⟧; so the sheets are open ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · isOpen_orBasic⟧ and $\pi_f$ is continuous ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · continuous_orProj⟧. (b) Every point of $O_f$ lies on a sheet ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · exists_isContOrOn⟧: push the orientation from $x$ along the paths of §VI.18 in a good set of $L$. (c) On a sheet $\pi_f$ is a homeomorphism onto $U_\infty$, with inverse $y \mapsto (y, o_y)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · continuousOn_orSec⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eq_orSec_of_mem_orBasic⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · orSec_mem_orBasic⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · orChartHomeo⟧; with (b), property (1) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · isLocalHomeomorph_orProj⟧. (d) Hausdorff ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · t2Space_orTopology⟧: points over different $x$ are separated by $\pi_f$, $X_\infty$ being metrizable ⟦Chapter2/Metrizable · MPolyfold.metrizableSpace_smoothLevel⟧; the two points over one $x$ lie on two sheets which, by (a), are disjoint over a neighbourhood of $x$. $\square$ The text gives no construction ("in view of Proposition 6.6.3 and Theorem 6.6.11").

**Property (2), under connected smooth neighbourhoods** ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · hasTwoContSections_orTopology⟧. *Statement.* Suppose every smooth point has, inside every open $W \ni x$, an open $U \ni x$ with $U_\infty$ preconnected in $X_\infty$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · MPolyfold.HasConnectedSmoothNbhds⟧, and every $\mathrm{Or}^f_y$ has two elements. Then the topology has property (2) for every $L$, the two sections being $y \mapsto (y, \pm o_y)$. *Proof.* Take a sheet of $o$ over $V \ni x$ (property (b)) and such a $U \subseteq V$. Every point over $y$ is $(y, o_y)$ or $(y, -o_y)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eq_orSec_or_eq_orSec⟧, and both sheets are open; so for a continuous section the sets where it equals $(y, o_y)$ and where it equals $(y, -o_y)$ are open and complementary in $U_\infty$, which is preconnected. $\square$ The hypothesis holds for $\mathbb R^n$ (convex balls) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · rnPolyfold_hasConnectedSmoothNbhds⟧ and for every M-polyfold on a subsingleton ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · MPolyfold.hasConnectedSmoothNbhds_of_subsingleton⟧. It holds on every M-polyfold (below; gap G.90 closed).

**Theorem 6.6.17** ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · theorem_6_6_17_hyp⟧. *Statement.* Let $X$ be tame with bump functions and $f$ an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data and sc⁺-sections through the smooth fibre points, the hypotheses under which $\Gamma_f$ is built (§VI.23) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · theorem_6_6_13_hyp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orLocalTransport⟧. If $X$ has connected smooth neighbourhoods, $O_f$ carries exactly one Hausdorff topology with (1), (2), (3). Without that hypothesis, $O_f$ carries exactly one Hausdorff topology with (1) and (3) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · existsUnique_orientationTopology⟧. *Proof.* Existence: the topology for the transport data of $\Gamma_f$. It has (1) and is Hausdorff (above), has (2) by the previous statement, every $\mathrm{Or}^f_y$ having two elements ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · exists_two_orx⟧, and has (3) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · isPropagationContinuous_orTopology⟧: near $t_0$ a continuous section of $\varphi^* O_f$ stays in one sheet ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eq_orSec_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eventually_segPath_mem⟧, and a sheet is carried along the segments of $\varphi$ by the transport. Uniqueness: let $t$ be any topology with (1) and (3) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eq_orTopology_of⟧. (i) A $t$-continuous local section $s$ over an open $N \subseteq X_\infty$ that agrees with a continuous orientation $o$ at $y_0$ agrees with it near $y_0$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationSpace · eventually_eq_orSec_of_continuousOn⟧: join $y$ near $y_0$ to $y_0$ by a path in $N$ (statement (b) above), which is continuous into $X_\infty$ (statement (a)); then $s$ along the path is a continuous section of the pull-back, and by (3) the set of parameters where it equals $o$ is open and closed in $[0, 1]$. (ii) Through every point a local inverse of $\pi_f$ for $t$ is such a section. By (i) the $t$-open sets and the open sets of the topology coincide. $\square$ Neither Hausdorffness nor (2) is used in the uniqueness. The text's "uniquely defined" is read as "exactly one".

**Property (2) without the hypothesis** (V6.74). *Every M-polyfold has connected smooth neighbourhoods* ⟦Chapter6/OrientationMainClean · MPolyfold.hasConnectedSmoothNbhds⟧: inside an open $W \ni x$, the connected component $U$ of $x$ in $W$ is open, M-polyfolds being locally connected (Proposition 2.3.7), and $U \cap X_\infty$ is path connected in $X_\infty$ ⟦Chapter2/SmoothPaths · MPolyfold.isPathConnected_smoothVal_preimage⟧, since nearby smooth points are joined by paths in $X_\infty$ ⟦Chapter2/SmoothPaths · MPolyfold.exists_nhds_joinedIn_smooth⟧ and $U$ is connected. So property (2) holds without the hypothesis, and *Theorem 6.6.17 holds with (1), (2), (3) under the text's hypotheses* — $X$ tame with bump functions, $f$ with tame germ data ⟦Chapter6/OrientationMainClean · theorem_6_6_17⟧ (gap G.90 closed; Findings, Chapter 6, items 120, 122). The remarks after the theorem — the orientation bundle, orientability as a global continuous section, the $\mathbb Z_2$-action and $\det_f$ — are §VI.38 (gap G.91 closed).

### VI.34 §§6.4–6.6 (preprint §§6.3–6.5), remarks: the alternative determinant, the identification (6.25) (preprint (95)), the remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable, and the classical case

Four remarks of the text, without proofs, are formalized here; the chapter's statements do not use them (Findings, Chapter 6, items 10, 26, 135). The files are `Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions.lean`, `Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable.lean`, `…Ell2.lean`, `…Transport.lean` and `Chapter6/GapP1_ClassicalDetBundle.lean`.

**The alternative determinant** (V6.78; after Definition 6.4.1 (preprint 6.7), p. 246 (preprint p. 208)). *Some authors use $\lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$; it is naturally isomorphic to $\det(T)$.* The map $\iota : \lambda(A^*) \to \lambda^*(A)$ of Definition 6.3.1 (preprint 6.3) is a nonzero map of lines (§VI.2), hence an isomorphism ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · iotaDualEquiv⟧, natural by Proposition 6.3.2 (preprint 6.4). With $A = \operatorname{coker}T$, $\mathrm{id} \otimes \iota$ is the isomorphism ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · altLinDetEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · altFredholmDetEquiv⟧, and on a cokernel basis $d$ with its dual basis it is $(a_1 \wedge \dots) \otimes (d_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge d_m^*) \mapsto (a_1 \wedge \dots) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_m)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · altLinDetEquiv_tmul_dualBasis⟧, since the matrix of the pairing is the identity. (Gap G.57 closed.)

**The identification (6.25) (preprint (95)) and the maps after Proposition 6.4.15 (preprint 6.15)** (V6.79). $\mathbb R \cong \lambda(\mathbb R^n)$, $1 \mapsto e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n$, has inverse $c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n \mapsto \det[c_1, \dots, c_n]$, the matrix with columns $c_j$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · stdLine⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · stdLine_symm_wedge⟧, by the change-of-basis rule of §VI.2; its transpose $\lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \cong \mathbb R^*$ maps $(e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n)^*$ to $1^*$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · stdLineDual_dualVec⟧, the isomorphism (94) of Proposition 6.4.15 (preprint 6.15). The maps $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ and $V \otimes \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to V$, $v \otimes (e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n) \mapsto v$ and $v \otimes (e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n)^* \mapsto v$, are isomorphisms ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · tensorStdLine_tmul_stdWedge⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetConventions · tensorStdLineDual_tmul_dualVec⟧ for every vector space $V$; the text asks $V$ finite-dimensional, which is not needed (stronger). (Gap G.58 closed.)

**The remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable** (V6.80; end of §6.5, p. 262 (preprint p. 218)). The text: $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is known to be non-orientable, but orientable over certain subsets (Proposition 6.6.1 (preprint 6.26)); no hypothesis on $E$, $F$, and no proof or reference. "Not orientable" is read as: no orientation in the sense of §VI.9. *For finite-dimensional $E$, $F$ the remark does not hold as we read it*: every operator is Fredholm, the base $L(E, F)$ is convex, and $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ has exactly two orientations by Proposition 6.6.1 (preprint 6.26) ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable · exists_two_lineOrientation_det_of_finiteDimensional⟧ — the Lean counterexample. *It holds under hypotheses.* (a) *A loop criterion*: a line bundle with a continuous nowhere-zero section along a map from a preconnected space that takes the values $v$ and $-v$ in one fibre has no orientation ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable · isEmpty_lineOrientation_of_loop⟧ — an orientation would have to agree with the section everywhere or nowhere. (b) *A section of $\mathrm{DET}$ from kernel bases*: for surjective Fredholm $A_x$, norm-continuous in $x$, and continuous bases $v_x$ of the kernels, $(v_{x,1} \wedge \dots \wedge v_{x,n}) \otimes 1^*$ is a continuous section of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ along $x \mapsto A_x$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable · continuous_kerDetMk⟧: in a local determinant chart with $P = 1$ its coordinate is the determinant of the projections of the $v_{x,i}$ to the kernel at the centre. (c) Hence, *if such a family has $A_{x_1} = A_{x_0}$, $v_{x_1} = -v_{x_0}$ and odd $n$, $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ has no orientation* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_of_kernel_loop⟧, since $(-v_1) \wedge \dots \wedge (-v_n) = -(v_1 \wedge \dots \wedge v_n)$. (d) *If $E$ and $F$ carry bounded $J$, $J'$ with $J^2 = -1$, $J'^2 = -1$ and there is a surjective $T : E \to F$ with kernel of odd finite dimension, $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ has no orientation* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_of_complexStructure⟧: with $R_\theta = \cos\theta + \sin\theta\,J$ and $R'_\theta$ likewise, the loop $A_\theta = R'_\theta TR_{-\theta}$, $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, consists of surjective operators with kernels $R_\theta(\ker T)$ and bases $R_\theta v$; at $\theta = \pi$, $R_\pi = -1$, so $A_\pi = T$ and $R_\pi v = -v$, and (c) applies. The kernels form a Möbius band. (e) *Consequences*: $\mathrm{DET}(H \times H, H \times H)$ has no orientation when $H$ has a surjective operator with kernel of odd finite dimension ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientable · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_prod⟧, for instance $H = \ell^2$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientableEll2 · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_ellTwo⟧; orientability depends only on the isomorphism classes of $E$ and $F$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientableTransport · nonempty_lineOrientation_det_iff_of_equiv⟧; so $\mathrm{DET}(H, H)$ has no orientation for every infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space $H$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientableTransport · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_hilbert⟧, nor $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ for $E$, $F$ isomorphic to such an $H$ or to $H \times H$ with $H \cong \mathbb R \times H$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientableTransport · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_of_equiv_hilbert⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_DetNonOrientableTransport · isEmpty_lineOrientation_det_of_equiv_prod⟧. Infinite dimension enters through the surjective operator with a kernel; on a finite-dimensional space the same loop also has a Möbius band of cokernels, and the two cancel in $\det$. *Not claimed*: infinite-dimensional Banach spaces without such structures. The remark presumably intends infinite-dimensional $E$, $F$ of the kind met in the applications (Findings, Chapter 6, item 135). (Gap G.60 closed, with this corrected form; row V6.80 narrower.)

**The classical case** (V6.81; opening of §6.6, p. 262). The text: for a smooth $f : U \to F$ on an open $U \subseteq E$ with Fredholm derivatives, the determinant lines of the $Df(x)$ form a continuous, even smooth, line bundle, with two orientations when $U$ is contractible. For $f$ of class $C^1$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is a continuous map into the Fredholm operators ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_ClassicalDetBundle · derivFredholm⟧, the pull-back of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ along it is a topological line bundle over $U$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_ClassicalDetBundle · ClassicalDet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_ClassicalDetBundle · classicalDet_vectorBundle⟧, and for contractible $U$ it has exactly two orientations, every orientation of one line extending to exactly one of the bundle ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_ClassicalDetBundle · classicalDet_two_orientations⟧: $U$ is then simply connected, and locally path connected as an open subset of a Banach space (§VI.9). *Narrower* (V6.81): $C^1$ in place of smooth, which is weaker, and the bundle is topological; its smoothness, which would need smooth frames of the local determinant charts, is not formalized.

### VI.35 Lemma 6.5.3 (preprint 6.19): determinant bundles of vector bundles

The text (p. 260 (preprint p. 216)): *for finite-dimensional topological vector bundles $E$, $F$ over $X$, the bundles $\lambda(E)$, $\lambda^*(F)$, $E \oplus F$ and $E \otimes F$ have in a natural way the structure of topological vector bundles*, a standard lemma whose proof is left to the reader. §VI.7 applied it only to trivial bundles (V6.22). The file is `Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021.lean` (Findings, Chapter 6, item 125).

**The statement formalized** (V6.22) ⟦Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021 · DetBundle.lemma_6_5_3⟧. *For Mathlib topological vector bundles $E$, $F$ with finite-dimensional normed model fibres over a topological space, the fibrewise $\lambda(E_b)$, $\lambda^*(E_b)$, $E_b \times F_b$ and $E_b \otimes F_b$ are Mathlib topological vector bundles, with trivializations induced by those of $E$ and $F$.* *Proof, $\lambda(E)$.* A trivialization $e$ of $E$ and a basis $f_1, \dots, f_n$ of the model fibre give the frame $b \mapsto e^{-1}(b)f_1, \dots, e^{-1}(b)f_n$ over the base set of $e$, whose wedge $w_e(b)$ is a continuous nowhere-zero section of $\lambda(E)$; the trivialization is $x \mapsto w_e(b)^*(x)$ ⟦Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021 · DetBundle.lamPrebundle⟧. By the change-of-basis rule of §VI.2 the coordinate changes are the determinants of those of $E$ ⟦Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021 · DetBundle.coord_wedgeAt_eq_det⟧, continuous because the coordinate changes of $E$ are; this is what a Mathlib vector prebundle asks, and it gives the topology and the bundle structure. *$\lambda^*(E)$*: $\xi \mapsto \xi(w_e(b))$, with the inverse determinants ⟦Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021 · DetBundle.lamDualPrebundle⟧. *$E \oplus F$* is Mathlib's fibrewise product with its vector bundle structure. *$E \otimes F$*: a pair of trivializations gives $u \otimes w \mapsto (i \mapsto (eu)_i\,e_1w)$ into $F_1^n$, $n = \dim F_0$ ⟦Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021 · DetBundle.tenPrebundle⟧, with the matrices of $A \otimes C$ as coordinate changes for those $A$, $C$ of $E$, $F$ ⟦Chapter6/DetVectorBundles2021 · DetBundle.tenMap_tenInv_eq⟧. $\square$ *Readings.* "In a natural way" is read as: the trivializations of the new bundles are induced by those of $E$ and $F$, so that local frames give local frames. The model fibre of $E \otimes F$ is $F_1^n$, since Mathlib puts no norm on $F_0 \otimes F_1$; this does not change the bundle. Proposition 6.5.4 (preprint 6.20) is still proved with the explicit frames of §VI.7. (Gap G.59 closed; row V6.22 restated.)

### VI.36 Lemmas 6.6.4 and 6.6.5 (preprint 6.29 and 6.30) as statements about manifolds: property (P), the solution set near the family, $\pi$ a submersion, $L$ a smooth bundle

§§VI.11–VI.12 proved what the propagation uses: the general position of $F$ along the family, and the kernels as a continuous family of subspaces. The text says more: property (P) for every slice $F_t$; the solution set of $F$ near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$ is a manifold with boundary with corners on which $\pi(t, y, \lambda) = t$ is a submersion; its fibres $S_t$ are manifolds with tangent spaces $L_t$; and $L$ is a smooth vector bundle (pp. 264–265 (preprint p. 222)). All of it is now formalized, on $\mathbb R^n$ (decision D2) and on the cube $[0, 1]^n$ itself. The setting is that of §VI.11: $G = \tilde f + S$ with $G(q, \Phi(q)) = 0$ near $[0, 1]^n$, and $F(\lambda, (q, y)) = G(q, y) + \sum\lambda_is_i(q, y)$ (Findings, Chapter 6, items 47, 48, 126).

**Property (P) for the slices** (V6.33) ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SlicePropertyP · lemma_6_6_4_propertyP⟧. *Under the hypotheses of Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29) there are finitely many sc⁺-sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ such that for every $q$ near $[0, 1]^n$ the slice $F_q(\lambda, y) = G(q, y) + \sum\lambda_is_i(q, y)$ is in general position at $(0, \Phi(q))$ — property (P) — and $F$ is in general position at $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$.* The second clause is §VI.11. The first is derived from it, the reverse of the text's order ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SlicePropertyP · isGeneralPositionGerm_slice⟧. *The chart computation* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SlicePropertyP · isParamGP_slice_of_isParamGP⟧: in a tame chart centred at $\Phi(q)$ and the product chart $(r \mapsto r - q) \times c$, properties (i)–(ii) of §V.19 for $G$ and the $s_i$ at $(q, \Phi(q))$ give (i)–(ii) for the slice at $\Phi(q)$. The $\mathbb R^n$-directions are absorbed by the derivative of the curve of zeros $q' \mapsto (q', \Phi(q'))$, which lies in $\ker G'$ (§VI.12); and its $X$-component lies in the reduced tangent space, because every corner coordinate of $\varphi \circ \Phi$ is $\ge 0$ near $q$ and vanishes at $q$, so its derivative vanishes ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SlicePropertyP · fderiv_mem_minimalSubspaceWith_of_centre⟧ — $\mathbb R^n$ has no boundary. *The fibres*: the zeros of $F_q$ are the fibre $S_q$ of the solution set of $F$ over $q$; the slice is tame sc-Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SlicePropertyP · isScFredholmSectionTame_slice⟧, and given (P), $S_q$ is near $(0, \Phi(q))$ a Mathlib manifold with boundary and corners ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SlicePropertyP · lemma_6_6_5_fibre_isManifold⟧, by Theorem 3.1.26 (Part III) for $F_q$. (Gap G.63 closed; row V6.33 restated.)

**The solution set near the family, and $\pi$** (V6.34, V6.42). *For $q$ near $[0, 1]^n$, $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ has an open neighbourhood in which the solution set of $F$ is a Mathlib manifold with boundary and corners* ⟦Chapter6/SolutionManifoldFamily2021 · lemma_6_6_5_isManifold⟧, *a smooth submanifold of dimension the index* ⟦Chapter6/SolutionManifoldFamily2021 · lemma_6_6_5_isSubmanifoldOfDim⟧ (Theorems 3.1.26 and 3.6.8 applied to $F$). *At the points of the family $d\pi$ maps the tangent space onto $\mathbb R^n$* ⟦Chapter6/SolutionManifoldFamily2021 · lemma_6_6_5_submersion⟧: in the product chart the tangent space is $\ker F'$, $d\pi$ is the projection to the parameter, and the derivative of the curve of zeros lies in $\ker F'$ with parameter component the identity. *Off the family* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SubmersionNearFamily · lemma_6_6_5_submersion_nhds⟧: surjectivity of $d\pi$ on the kernels is open along the zeros ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SubmersionNearFamily · exists_nhds_surjective_linKer⟧, because the zeros near a point in good position are the image of an sc⁺-retraction, so the level-$1$ chart points vary continuously along them, the kernels have a continuous frame (§VI.12), and a determinant that is $1$ at one point is nonzero nearby. So $\pi$ is a submersion on a neighbourhood of every point of the family. (Gap G.62 closed; rows V6.34, V6.42 restated.)

**$L$ is a smooth vector bundle** (V6.34) ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SmoothL3 · lemma_6_6_5_smoothBundle⟧. *In the setting of §VI.15 (with (P)), there are an open connected $V \supseteq [0, 1]^n$ and a smooth family of subspaces over the manifold $V$ whose fibre at $q$ is $L_q = \ker F'(0, (q, z_q)) \cap \{dq = 0\}$, a Mathlib $C^\infty$ vector bundle.* *Step 1.* An sc-smooth map on $\mathbb R^n$ read in a chart is $C^\infty$ into every level on the open sets it maps into the chart ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SmoothL1 · IsScSmooth.contDiffOn_levelMap_const⟧. *Step 2.* The kernel vectors of an sc-Fredholm linearization are smooth points ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SmoothL1 · IsSc1With.apply_mem_smooth_of_finiteDimensional⟧. *Step 3, a smooth frame* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SmoothL3 · exists_local_smooth_frame_linKer⟧: with an sc-retraction $S$ onto the solution set (Theorem 3.6.8) and a basis $b$ of one kernel, $e_i(q) = DS(z_q)b_i$ is $C^\infty$ into every level, since $q \mapsto (z_q, b_i)$ is sc-smooth into the tangent bundle and the tangent map of $S$ is sc-smooth; it is a frame near the base point, as in §VI.12. *Step 4.* A family of subspaces of a normed space with smooth local frames is a smooth vector bundle ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SmoothL2 · SmoothSubspaceFamily.contMDiffVectorBundle⟧, and cutting it by $\{dq = 0\}$, onto which the projection is surjective, keeps it smooth ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_SmoothL2 · SmoothSubspaceFamily.infKer⟧. The continuation of orientations still uses only continuity. (Rows V6.34, V6.42 restated.)

**On the cube itself** (V6.33, V6.34). The same statements hold for families on $[0, 1]^n$, boundary and corners included, with sections over the M-polyfold with corners $[0, 1]^n \times X$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeSections · cubePolyfold⟧, whose degeneracy index counts the coordinates in $\{0, 1\}$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeSections · cubePolyfold_degIndex⟧. The pull-back of a tame sc-Fredholm section to $[0, 1]^n \times X$ is tame sc-Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeFredholm · StrongBundle.IsScFredholmSectionTame.paramCube⟧, with charts of $[0, 1]^n$ centred at every point ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeCharts · UnitCube.cChart⟧ and basic germs extended by the mixed quadrants ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeGerms · IsConjugateToBasicGerm.quadExtend⟧. Lemma 6.6.4 (preprint 6.29) holds there ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeLemmas · lemma_6_6_4_cube⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeLemmas · lemma_6_6_4_cube_family⟧, and near the family the solution set is a manifold with boundary and corners and a submanifold of dimension the index ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeLemmas · lemma_6_6_5_isManifold_cube⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeLemmas · lemma_6_6_5_isSubmanifoldOfDim_cube⟧. On the cube, *(P) at $q$ is equivalent to the general position of $F$ at $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$*, boundary and corners included ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeBoundaryP · isGeneralPositionGerm_cubeSlice_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeBoundaryP · lemma_6_6_4_propertyP_cube⟧: the tangent vectors of the family of zeros in reduced directions of $[0, 1]^n$ have reduced $X$-components, by a one-sided minimum argument ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeBoundarySlice · mem_minimalSubspaceWith_of_hasFDerivWithinAt⟧. At these points $\pi$ is a submersion in the corner sense: $d\pi$ maps $\ker F'$ onto $\mathbb R^n$ and its reduced part onto the reduced tangent space of $[0, 1]^n$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeBoundarySubmersion · lemma_6_6_5_submersion_cube⟧.

### VI.37 Paths and families on $[0, 1]$; the facts on paths before Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2)

Decision D2 reads the paths, homotopies and families of the chapter on $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^n$. Most statements now also hold as printed, for maps on the M-polyfolds $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$ (gap G.65, in part; Findings, Chapter 6, items 102, 122, 124).

**$[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$ and $X \times [0, 1]$.** $[0, 1]$ is a tame M-polyfold with boundary ⟦Chapter3/UnitIntervalPolyfold · unitIntervalPolyfold⟧, and every sc-smooth path on it is the reparametrization by $\sin^2(\pi r/2)$ of an sc-smooth path on $\mathbb R$ ⟦Chapter3/UnitIntervalPolyfold · MPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap.exists_rn_reparam⟧; this transfers the statements on $\mathbb R$. $X \times [0, 1]$ is tame for tame $X$, with $d(x, t) = d_X(x) + d_{[0,1]}(t)$ ⟦Chapter6/PathsInterval · isTame_prod_unitInterval⟧, and $[0, 1]^2$ is an M-polyfold with corners ⟦Chapter6/PathsInterval · unitSquarePolyfold⟧.

**Theorems 6.6.11, 6.6.13 and 6.6.17 for paths on $[0, 1]$** (V6.48, V6.57, V6.71). The push-forward along $\varphi : [0, 1] \to U$ is read along the path $\varphi \circ \sin^2(\pi r/2)$ on $\mathbb R$, independently of the reparametrization ⟦Chapter6/PathsInterval · theorem_6_6_11_interval⟧; the transport of Theorem 6.6.13 (preprint 6.37) is invariant under sc-smooth homotopies $[0, 1]^2 \to X$ with fixed end points ⟦Chapter6/PathsInterval · orTransportI_eq_of_homotopy⟧, and Theorem 6.6.17 holds with property (3) for paths on $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PathsInterval · theorem_6_6_17_interval⟧.

**The path category on $[0, 1]$** (V6.52). Sc-smooth homotopies $[0, 1]^2 \to X$ with fixed end points ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · ScHomotopicI⟧ are an equivalence relation, and two paths on $[0, 1]$ are homotopic in this sense iff their reparametrized paths on $\mathbb R$ are homotopic in the sense of §VI.20 ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · scHomotopicI_iff⟧. The composition is the text's $\gamma(s) = \varphi(\beta(s))$ on $[0, 1/2]$ and $\psi(\beta(s) - 1)$ on $[1/2, 1]$, with $\beta(s) = \kappa(3s) + \kappa(3s - 2)$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · betaConcat⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · ScPathI.concat⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · ScPathI.concat_toFun_of_le⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · ScPathI.concat_toFun_of_ge⟧. The classes form a category ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · PathCatI⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · PathCatI.category⟧, a groupoid ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · PathCatI.groupoid⟧, and $[\varphi] \mapsto [\varphi \circ \sin^2(\pi r/2)]$ is a full and faithful functor to the category of §VI.20, bijective on objects ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_PathCategoryInterval · PathCatI.toPathCat_isEquivalence⟧, so the two readings give isomorphic categories.

**Proposition 6.6.3 (3) and (4) on $[0, 1] \times X$ and $[0, 1]^n \times X$** (V6.32). *With bump functions, for an sc-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to X$ in the domain of a strong bundle chart there is an sc⁺-section $S$ of the pull-back of $P$ to the M-polyfold $[0, 1] \times X$ whose fibre part is the text's $-\beta(y)R(y, f(\varphi(t)))$, $\beta$ an sc-smooth cut-off equal to $1$ near $\varphi([0, 1])$, with $(f + S)(t, \varphi(t)) = 0$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_UnitIntervalSections · proposition_6_6_3_three_interval⟧. The construction works in any product chart $\chi \times \varphi_c$ of $Q \times X$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_UnitIntervalSections · PullbackChartData.ofProdChart⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_UnitIntervalSections · exists_isScPlusSection_prodChart⟧; on $[0, 1]$ the principal part lifts to level $1$, the parameter space being finite-dimensional, and the two charts $t$, $1 - t$ of $[0, 1]$ are glued with a partition of unity in $t$. $[0, 1] \times X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions when $X$ does, which gives (4) ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_UnitIntervalSections · proposition_6_6_3_four_interval⟧. The same holds for families on $[0, 1]^n$, with sections over $[0, 1]^n \times X$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeSections · proposition_6_6_3_three_cube⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeSections · proposition_6_6_3_four_cube⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_CubeSections · admitsBumpFunctions_prod_cube⟧. The sign is that of $f + s$ (structural choice (1)).

**The facts on paths before Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2)** (V6.49) ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · MPolyfold.paths_before_proposition_6_2_2⟧. The text recalls (p. 240 (preprint p. 201)): *an M-polyfold is locally path connected, and two smooth points in one connected component (preprint: path component) are joined by an sc⁺-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to X$.* *Step 1, the local step* ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · MPolyfold.exists_nhds_scJoinedIn⟧: every $u$ in an open $U$ has an open $N \ni u$ in $U$ whose smooth points are pairwise joined by sc-smooth paths in $U$ — the retracted segment of a chart of $X$, without a strong bundle chart. Local path connectedness is proved from the charts, which are retracts of open sets of partial quadrants ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.locallyPathConnectedSpace⟧. *Step 2, the global step* ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · MPolyfold.scJoinedIn_of_isConnected⟧: in a connected open $U$ any two smooth points are joined by an sc-smooth path in $U$, by a chain argument over the neighbourhoods of Step 1, with the concatenation of paths (§VI.18), using that $U$ is connected. *Step 3, sc⁺* ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · MPolyfold.IsScSmoothMap.exists_scPlus_lift⟧: $[0, 1]$ is modelled on sc⁺-retracts, so the inclusion $[0, 1] \to [0, 1]^1$ is sc-smooth, and an sc-smooth path on $[0, 1]$ lifts to an sc-smooth path into $X^1$. For smooth points, being in one connected component, in one path component and being joined by an sc-smooth path on $[0, 1]$ are equivalent ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · mem_connectedComponent_iff_exists_scPath⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · MPolyfold.mem_pathComponent_iff_exists_scPath⟧, which justifies reading "in the same path component" in Definitions 6.6.2 and 6.6.14 (preprint 6.27 and 6.38) as "joined by an sc-smooth path" (§VI.24); and two smooth points of one connected component have the same index ⟦Chapter6/SmoothPathComponents2021 · proposition_6_2_2_connectedComponent_2021def⟧. "Sc⁺-smooth path" is read as an sc-smooth path that lifts to $X^1$; every sc-smooth path on $[0, 1]$ does. (Gap G.56 closed.)

**What is still read on $\mathbb R$** (gap G.65, in part; Proposition 6.6.3 (1′) holds on $[0, 1]$ since 2026-11-13, §VI.10): the smooth bundle $L$ of Lemma 6.6.5 (preprint 6.30) over a neighbourhood of $[0, 1]^n$ in $\mathbb R^n$ (V6.34), the stabilized kernels and their continuation (V6.42), and Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42) over $\mathbb R^1 \times X$ (V6.62), with the cobordisms of Theorem 6.7.1 (preprint 6.43) (§VI.27).

### VI.38 The remarks after Theorem 6.6.17: the orientation bundle, orientability, $\mathbb Z_2$ and $\det_f$

The text (p. 275, new in the 2021 edition): with the topology of Theorem 6.6.17, $\pi_f : O_f \to X_\infty$ is the orientation bundle of $f$; $f$ is orientable iff $\pi_f$ has a global continuous section; $\mathbb Z_2$ acts continuously on $O_f$ by $(x, o_x) \mapsto (x, -o_x)$; and $\det_f = \mathbb R \otimes_{\mathbb Z_2} O_f \to X_\infty$ is the determinant bundle of $f$. The file is `Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle.lean` (V6.82; Findings, Chapter 6, item 121).

**Sections** (V6.82). For local transport data whose fibres have two elements, with the topology of §VI.33: *$y \mapsto (y, o_y)$ is continuous iff the transport along every sc-smooth path carries $o$ along* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · continuous_orSec_iff⟧ — near each point a continuous section stays in one sheet, and a sheet is carried along by the transport (§VI.33) — and every section of $\pi_f$ has this form ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · exists_eq_orSec⟧. For the transport of $\Gamma_f$: *$y \mapsto o_y$ is an orientation of $f$ (Definition 6.6.16 (preprint 6.40)) iff $y \mapsto (y, o_y)$ is continuous* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · isSectionOrientation_iff_continuous⟧, by §VI.24, and so *$f$ is orientable iff $\pi_f$ has a global continuous section* ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · isOrientableSection_iff_exists_continuous_section⟧.

**The $\mathbb Z_2$-action.** $(x, o) \mapsto (x, -o)$, $-o$ the other element of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$, maps each sheet onto the sheet of the opposite continuous orientation, so it is a homeomorphism ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · orNegHomeomorph⟧, an involution without fixed points over $\pi_f$; it is the action of $\mathbb Z^\times \cong \mathbb Z_2$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · orMulAction⟧, continuous ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · continuous_orUnitsAct⟧.

**$\det_f$.** A Mathlib vector bundle core with fibre $\mathbb R$ over $X_\infty$, with a trivialization for every continuous orientation $(U, o)$ and coordinate changes $\pm 1$ according as two continuous orientations agree — locally constant by §VI.33 (a) ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · detCore⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · detBundleCore⟧. Its fibre over $x$ is $\mathbb R \otimes_{\mathbb Z_2} \mathrm{Or}^f_x$: $r \otimes a$ and $r' \otimes a'$ have the same class iff $(r', a') = (r, a)$ or $(-r, -a)$ ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · detMk_eq_iff⟧, and $r \otimes a$ has coordinate $r$ in the trivialization of $(U, o)$ if $a = o_x$, and $-r$ if not ⟦Chapter6/GapP1_OrientationBundle · localTriv_detMk⟧. (Gap G.91 closed; row V6.82 restated.)

## Part VII. Ep-groupoids (HWZ Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.3, 7.5, 7.6 (2017 §§7.1–7.5))

Chapter 7 opens Part II of the book. Part II has no 2014 preprint, so its numbers and pages are those of the book (Springer 2021, pp. 287–356), with the 2017 text's in parentheses (2017 pp. 225–256; see `BookConcordance.md`). The chapter introduces ep-groupoids, the sc-smooth version of étale proper Lie groupoids. §7.1 defines groupoids, isotropy groups and ep-groupoids (Definitions 7.1.1–7.1.3 (2017: 7.1–7.3)), the local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ of a morphism and its tangent (Definition 7.1.4 (2017: 7.4)), the levels and the degeneracy index of the orbit space (Definition 7.1.5 (2017: 7.5)), tame ep-groupoids and the category $\mathcal{EP}$ (Definitions 7.1.6, 7.1.7 (2017: 7.6, 7.7)). It proves that $\pi$ is open, that $|X|$ has countable bases of neighbourhoods, the local closure relation and the finiteness of the isotropy groups (Propositions 7.1.8–7.1.12 (2017: 7.1–7.4), Lemma 7.1.11 (2017: 7.1)). It states the natural representation of $G_x$ (Theorem 7.1.13 (2017: 7.1)), discusses the translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ and the action $\hat\Phi$ (pp. 293–297 (2017 pp. 231–233)), extends the natural representation to finite sets of isomorphic objects (Proposition 7.1.15 (2017: 7.5), Definition 7.1.18 (2017: 7.8)), identifies $|U(x)|$ with $G_x\backslash U(x)$ (Proposition 7.1.19 (2017: 7.6)) and defines local uniformizers and ep-subgroupoids (Definitions 7.1.20, 7.1.21 (2017: 7.9, 7.10), Proposition 7.1.22 (2017: 7.7)). §7.2 treats effective ep-groupoids, the subgroups $T_x$, the reduced morphism space $\mathbf X^R$ and the reduced ep-groupoid $X_R$ (Definitions 7.2.1–7.2.15 (2017: 7.11–7.13), Lemmas 7.2.2, 7.2.3 (2017: 7.2, 7.3), Propositions 7.2.4, 7.2.10 (2017: 7.8, 7.9) and Proposition 7.10 (2017; rewritten in 2021 as Theorem 7.2.14)). §7.3 proves that $|X|$ is locally metrizable, regular and Hausdorff (Theorem 7.3.1 (2017: 7.2), Lemmas 7.3.2–7.3.5 (2017: 7.4–7.7), Corollaries 7.3.6, 7.3.8 (2017: 7.1, 7.2), Definition 7.3.7 (2017: 7.14)) and lifts ep-groupoids to level $1$ (Proposition 7.3.9 (2017: 7.11)). §7.5 (2017 §7.4) defines paracompact orbit spaces and sc-smooth partitions of unity (Definitions 7.5.1, 7.5.5 (2017: 7.15, 7.16), Remarks 7.5.2, 7.5.6 (2017: 7.1, 7.2)), proves Proposition 7.5.3 (2017: 7.12) and Theorems 7.5.4, 7.5.7 (2017: 7.3, 7.4), and characterizes the closed subsets of $|X|$ (Definition 7.5.8 (2017: 7.17), Propositions 7.5.9, 7.5.10 (2017: 7.13, 7.14)). The appendix §7.6 (2017 §7.5) proves Theorem 7.1.13 (2017: 7.1) as Theorem 7.6.1 (2017: 7.5) (Lemmas 7.6.2, 7.6.3 (2017: 7.8, 7.9)) and Theorem 7.5.7 (2017: 7.4) as Theorem 7.6.4 (2017: 7.6) (Lemma 7.6.5 (2017: 7.10)), and ends with Corollary 7.6.6 (2017: 7.3). This Part retells §7.1 in §§VII.1–VII.12 — Definitions 7.1.1, 7.1.2 (2017: 7.1, 7.2) (§VII.1), Definition 7.1.3 (2017: 7.3) and properness (§VII.2), Definitions 7.1.4–7.1.6 (2017: 7.4–7.6) (§VII.3), Definition 7.1.7 (2017: 7.7) and the remark after it (§VII.4), Propositions 7.1.8–7.1.10 (2017: 7.1–7.3) (§VII.5), Lemma 7.1.11 (2017: 7.1) and Proposition 7.1.12 (2017: 7.4) (§VII.6), Theorem 7.1.13 (2017: 7.1) (§VII.7), pp. 293–297 (2017 pp. 231–233) (§VII.8), the uniqueness of natural representations (§VII.9), Proposition 7.1.15 (2017: 7.5) and Definition 7.1.18 (2017: 7.8) (§VII.10), Proposition 7.1.19 (2017: 7.6) and Definition 7.1.20 (2017: 7.9) (§VII.11), Definition 7.1.21 (2017: 7.10) and Proposition 7.1.22 (2017: 7.7) (§VII.12); §7.2 in §§VII.13–VII.17 — Definition 7.2.1 (2017: 7.11) and Lemmas 7.2.2, 7.2.3 (2017: 7.2, 7.3) (§VII.13), Proposition 7.2.4 (2017: 7.8) (§VII.14), $T_x$ and Definition 7.2.7 (2017: 7.12) (§VII.15), Proposition 7.2.10 (2017: 7.9) (§VII.16), $X_R$, Proposition 7.10 (2017; Each item carries the number of its comparison item (V7.1–V7.68) in `Exposition/verification/ch07.md`. The additions of the 2021 edition (V7.69–V7.104) are retold in §§VII.33–VII.43: §7.1 (§VII.33), §7.2 (§§VII.34–VII.35), Appendices 7.6.3 and 7.6.4 (§VII.36), §7.4, new in the 2021 edition (§§VII.37–VII.39), Appendix 7.6.5 (§VII.40), what is not formalized and what they taught us (§VII.41), Theorem 7.6.9 in full, the boundary ep-groupoid (§VII.42), and §7.4 on every lift $X^i$ (§VII.43). The work that closed the remaining gaps is retold in §§VII.44–VII.50: $T\varphi$ as an sc-isomorphism, the facts (3), (4), $|X_\infty|$ and the density of $X_\infty$ (§VII.44), the Part I facts of §7.4 as theorems (§VII.45), Theorem 7.6.7 and Corollary 7.6.8 for every $i$ (§VII.46), Zhou's retract of Appendix 7.6.3 (§VII.47), the 2021 forms of Propositions 7.2.10, 7.2.16, Theorem 7.2.14 and Corollary 7.6.6 as printed (§VII.48), an ep-groupoid whose orbit space is not paracompact (§VII.49), and Theorem 7.6.9 for every representative and in the book's form (§VII.50).

**What is proved, and what is not.** Every statement of the chapter is formalized, and every gap of the chapter is closed: G.70 ($T\varphi$, §VII.44), G.71 (the M-polyfold $\mathbf X^R$, §§VII.34, VII.48), G.72 ($|X_\infty|$, §VII.44), G.73 (the density of $X_\infty$, §VII.44), G.82 (Theorem 7.6.7 for every $i$, §VII.46), G.83 (Zhou's retract, §VII.47), G.84 (§7.4 on every lift, §VII.43) and G.85 (the Part I facts of §7.4, §VII.45). Theorems 7.1.13–7.6.4 (2017: 7.1–7.6) are proved, and so are Propositions 7.1.8–7.2.4 and 7.3.9–7.5.10 (2017: 7.1–7.8 and 7.11–7.14), Lemmas 7.1.11–7.6.5 (2017: 7.1–7.10) and Corollaries 7.3.6–7.6.6 (2017: 7.1–7.3); Corollary 7.6.6 (2017: 7.3) as printed, Part I's Theorem 5.5.16 (2017: 5.14) of Godefroy–Troyanski–Whitfield–Zizler being now a theorem (§§VII.29, VII.48). Proposition 7.2.10 (2017: 7.9) and Proposition 7.10 (2017) are proved in their 2021 form: the natural charts of $\mathbf X^R$ with no hypothesis (Proposition 7.2.10), paracompactness for every ep-groupoid (Proposition 7.2.12), and the reduced ep-groupoid under the 2021 text's hypothesis that $T_R$ is Hausdorff (Theorem 7.2.14, Proposition 7.2.16) (§§VII.34, VII.48); for every ep-groupoid, as the 2017 text states them, they do not hold as we read it, and $\mathbb Z/2$ acting on a dimension-jumping retract is the counterexample ⟦Chapter7/ReducedNotHausdorff · EpGroupoid.Examples.exists_not_t2Space_reducedMor⟧ (§VII.16). The 2021 additions to §§7.1, 7.2, the new §7.4 and Appendices 7.6.3–7.6.5 are proved (§§VII.33–VII.50). Remark 7.5.6 (2017: 7.2) is an assessment, with nothing to formalize (row V7.57). One statement is formalized in a narrower form: in Theorem 7.6.9 (row V7.98), "$\Phi$ is a homeomorphism onto $\theta$" holds as we read it only for $V$ centred at $x$; for the other representatives $\Phi$ is an sc-diffeomorphism onto the open set $\theta \cap V^x$, and both are proved (§§VII.40, VII.50). The open question of p. 340 (2017 p. 249), whether property (5) follows from (1)–(4), is settled negatively: the Čech groupoid of a Prüfer-type surface is an ep-groupoid whose orbit space is not paracompact ⟦Chapter7/PropertyFiveResearch · EpGroupoid.Examples.Pruefer.exists_epGroupoid_not_hasParacompactOrbitSpace⟧ (§VII.49). Five places of the 2017 text needed more than a reading. The remark after Definition 7.1.7 (2017: 7.7), that a functor sc-smooth on objects is sc-smooth on morphisms, does not hold as we read it, and a counterexample on the trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action on $\mathbb R$ shows it; it holds for functors continuous on morphisms, which is what its argument uses and what the 2021 text asks (§§VII.4, VII.33). The proof of Proposition 7.2.10 (2017: 7.9) gives the charts of $\mathbf X^R$ and their sc-smooth transitions but, as we read it, neither Hausdorffness nor paracompactness; Hausdorffness is the hypothesis of the 2021 Theorem 7.2.14, and paracompactness is proved (§§VII.16, VII.34). The natural representation of Theorem 7.1.13 (2017: 7.1) is taken on a connected neighbourhood, which the text chooses on 2017 p. 231 but does not put in the statement; connectedness makes $\Phi$ a homomorphism and $\Gamma$ a functor, and the local path connectedness of M-polyfolds that supplies it is proved (§VII.7). The tameness of $X^1$ in Proposition 7.3.9 (2017: 7.11) needs that the index lift of a tame retraction is tame, which Part I left open; it is proved (§VII.22). And several omitted steps are supplied: the uniqueness of natural representations behind "adapting restrictions" (§VII.9), the conjugation $\varphi T_x\varphi^{-1} = T_y$ that the composition of $X_R$ needs (§VII.15), the passage from compact to component compact sets in Corollary 7.3.8 (2017: 7.2) (§VII.21), the support bound that makes the sum in the proof of Theorem 7.5.7 (2017: 7.4) locally finite (§§VII.27–VII.28) and Michael's theorem on unions of closed paracompact sets (§VII.20). Proposition 7.1.15 (2017: 7.5) is proved by a construction without induction (§VII.10), Proposition 7.5.3 (2017: 7.12) by Smirnov's theorem pulled back to $|X^1|$ (§VII.23), Proposition 7.5.10 (2) (2017: 7.14) without Lemma 2.7.3 (2017: 2.7) (§VII.25), Lemma 7.3.4 (2017: 7.6) from the closedness of points and regularity (§VII.19), and the normalization of Theorem 7.5.7 (2017: 7.4) by bump coverings (§VII.28). Nothing of the chapter is left unformalized (§VII.31).

**Seven structural choices.** (1) *A groupoid is a structure of maps.* Objects and morphisms are types; $s, t, u, \iota$ are maps and the composition $m$ is a total map whose value on a non-composable pair is a junk value never used; the groupoid laws are required on composable pairs. A bridge to Mathlib's groupoids makes "full" and "faithful" Mathlib's. (2) *Properness is Mathlib's.* Definition 7.1.3 (3) (2017: 7.3) is the properness, in Mathlib's sense, of $t$ restricted to $s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X V)$, for some open $V \ni x$, per point; on metrizable spaces it is equivalent to the sequential form the text uses (§VII.2). (3) *Condition (4) in two forms.* It is stated literally, on the fibred product of Part I's Proposition 2.5.20 (2017: 2.15; preprint 2.46, §II.17), and used in the equivalent *sheet form*: for every local inverse $\sigma$ of $s$, the map $\psi \mapsto m(\sigma(t\psi), \psi)$ is sc-smooth. (4) *Natural representations are data.* "An open neighbourhood $U(x)$ equipped with the natural $G_x$-action" is always a datum $(U, \Phi, \Gamma)$ with $U$ open, connected and containing $x$, never a hypothesis "for every such $U(x)$". (5) *$G \times U$ is a product with a discrete M-polyfold*, the finite disjoint union of copies of $U$, on which sc-smoothness is sc-smoothness on each slice (§VII.8). (6) *The reduced morphisms* $\mathbf X^R$ are a quotient whose M-polyfold structure is built under the hypothesis that it is Hausdorff, the 2021 text's hypothesis on $T_R$; its paracompactness is proved, for every ep-groupoid (§§VII.16, VII.34). (7) *Michael's theorem without Hausdorff.* Part I's Lemma 2.7.3 (2017: 2.7) and Proposition 2.7.4 (2017: 2.17) (gap G.15 there) are proved for regular spaces, and Mathlib's paracompactness, like Definition 7.5.1 (2017: 7.15), does not include Hausdorff (§VII.20).

Throughout, $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ is an ep-groupoid: $X$ is the object M-polyfold and $\mathbf X$ the morphism M-polyfold, both Hausdorff and paracompact, as every M-polyfold of the project (Definition 2.3.4 (2017: 2.8), §II.5); $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are source and target, $m(\varphi, \psi) = \varphi \circ \psi$ the composition, $u(x) = 1_x$ the unit and $\iota(\varphi) = \varphi^{-1}$ the inverse. $|X|$ is the orbit space with the quotient topology and $\pi : X \to |X|$ the projection; $G_x$ is the isotropy group of $x$, $\mathrm{cl}_X$ the closure in $X$, and $\mathbf U(x)$ the set of morphisms with source and target in $U(x)$. For a natural representation $(U, \Phi, \Gamma)$ at $x$, $g \ast y = \Phi(g)(y)$. A *sheet* is an open set $\mathbf W \subseteq \mathbf X$ on which $s$ is an sc-diffeomorphism onto an open set, its inverse a *local inverse* of $s$. Part I results are cited in the same way, by their 2021 numbers with the 2017 numbers in parentheses; the Lean names carry the 2021 numbers (Lemma 2.7.3 and Proposition 2.7.4, 2017 Lemma 2.7 and Proposition 2.17, are `lemma_2_7_3` and `proposition_2_7_4`; Theorem 5.5.10, 2017 Theorem 5.12, is `theorem_5_5_10`), and the Lean names of Chapter 7 carry the 2021 numbers too, with `_2017` for the statements that exist only in 2017. Findings are those of `Exposition/Findings.md`, "Chapter 7".

### VII.1 Definitions 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 (2017: 7.1 and 7.2): groupoids, the orbit space, isotropy

**Definition 7.1.1 (2017: 7.1)** (V7.1). A groupoid is a structure of maps $s, t, m, u, \iota$ on a type of objects and a type of morphisms ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr⟧, with associativity, units and inverses required on composable pairs; the morphisms $x \to y$ are a set ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.mor⟧, and so are the morphisms between points of a set $A$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.morOn⟧. The composition of a non-composable pair is a junk value; no statement uses it. The text's list of consequences — $(\varphi^{-1})^{-1} = \varphi$, $1_x^{-1} = 1_x$, $(\varphi \circ \psi)^{-1} = \psi^{-1} \circ \varphi^{-1}$, uniqueness of inverses — is derived from the laws ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.inv_inv⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.inv_unit⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.inv_comp_rev⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.eq_inv_of_comp_eq_unit⟧. Objects are isomorphic if there is a morphism between them ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isomorphic⟧, an equivalence relation ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.orbitSetoid⟧ whose quotient is $|X|$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.OrbitSpace⟧ with projection $\pi$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.π⟧; $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ iff $x \cong y$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.π_eq_π_iff⟧, $\pi(s\varphi) = \pi(t\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.π_src_eq_π_tgt⟧ and $\pi$ is onto ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.surjective_π⟧. The saturation $\pi^{-1}(\pi(A))$, used from Definition 7.1.21 (2017: 7.10) on, is defined here ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.saturation⟧, with saturated sets ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.IsSaturated⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isSaturated_iff⟧. The bridge to Mathlib's groupoids is a type synonym of the objects ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Ob⟧ with the groupoid instance ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.instGroupoid⟧, whose isomorphism classes are those of the orbit relation ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.orbitSetoid_eq⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 1) (pp. 287–288 (2017 pp. 225–226)).

**Definition 7.1.2 (2017: 7.2)** (V7.2). $G_x$, the morphisms $x \to x$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy⟧, is a group under composition with $gh = g \circ h$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy.val_mul⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy.val_one⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy.val_inv⟧, the text's order. Mathlib's vertex group multiplies in the other order; it is identified with the opposite group ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isotropyEquivVertexGroup⟧, and $G_x$ with the automorphisms of $x$ in the bridge ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isotropyEquivAut⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 2) (p. 288 (2017 p. 226)).

### VII.2 Definition 7.1.3 (2017: 7.3), and properness

**Definition 7.1.3 (2017: 7.3)** (V7.3) ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid⟧. An ep-groupoid is a groupoid with M-polyfold structures on the objects and on the morphisms such that (1) $s$ and $t$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, (2) $u$ and $\iota$ are sc-smooth, (3) every $x$ has an open neighbourhood $V(x)$ with $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X V(x)) \to X$ proper, and (4) $m$ is sc-smooth on $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$. "In particular all structure maps are sc-smooth": $s$ and $t$ are ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothMap_src⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothMap_tgt⟧, and continuous ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_src⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_tgt⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_unit⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_inv⟧ (pp. 288–290 (2017 pp. 226–227)).

*Condition (3).* It is existential, one open $V(x)$ per point, as the text writes it. The universal reading, "for every open $V \ni x$", fails: in the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$ (objects $\mathbb Z$, one morphism between any two objects) $t$ is proper over $s^{-1}(\{x\})$ but not over $s^{-1}(\mathbb Z)$ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.pair_isProperMap⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.pair_not_isProperMap_univ⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.pair_not_forall_isProperMap⟧; every smaller open neighbourhood of $x$ works as soon as one does (§VII.25) (Findings, Chapter 7, items 3, 103).

*Condition (4).* The text cites "Lemma 2.8 in [38]" for the M-polyfold structure of the fibred product; this is an external reference, and the statement used is Part I's Proposition 2.5.20 (2017: 2.15) (§II.17): since $s$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X \times \mathbf X$ ⟦Chapter2/FibredProduct · MPolyfold.isSubMPolyfold_fibredProduct⟧, and (4) is stated on it ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · IsScSmoothComp⟧. The proofs use an equivalent *sheet form* ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · IsScSmoothCompSheet⟧: for every sc-diffeomorphism $s : \mathbf W \to V$ with inverse $\sigma$, the map $\psi \mapsto m(\sigma(t\psi), \psi)$ is sc-smooth on $t^{-1}(V)$. *Step 1.* The graph of $\sigma \circ t$ over $t^{-1}(V)$ is an open piece of the fibred product, and the second projection is an sc-diffeomorphism from it onto $t^{-1}(V)$, with inverse $\psi \mapsto (\sigma(t\psi), \psi)$. *Step 2.* So the literal (4) gives the sheet form by composition, and conversely the fibred product is covered by such graphs ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · isScSmoothComp_iff_sheet⟧. Every ep-groupoid satisfies the sheet form ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothCompSheet⟧. The "for every $\sigma$" of the sheet form carries no vacuity risk, being equivalent to the literal condition (Findings, Chapter 7, item 4).

**Properness in sequential form** (V7.4). The text uses properness through sequences: in Proposition 7.1.10 (2017: 7.3), Lemma 7.1.11 (2017: 7.1), Proposition 7.1.22 (2017: 7.7), Proposition 7.3.9 (2017: 7.11), Proposition 7.5.9 (2017: 7.13) and Lemma 7.6.2 (2017: 7.8). For a continuous map between metrizable spaces, properness is equivalent to: every sequence whose images converge has a convergent subsequence ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_iff_exists_tendsto_subseq⟧. *Step 1, from properness.* The images and their limit form a compact set, whose preimage is compact, hence sequentially compact ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · exists_tendsto_subseq_of_isProperMap⟧. *Step 2, to properness.* Preimages of compact sets are sequentially compact, hence compact in a metrizable space, and a continuous map with compact fibres of compacta into a compactly generated space is proper (Mathlib's characterization) ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_of_exists_tendsto_subseq⟧.
